A DEAR little thing—A diamond. A LOVELY parcel—A beautiful young lady rapt In herself. A WELL-DRESSED man is a neat one, but a glutton- ous man is an eater. WHAT is the prime object of soldiers' drill ?—To snake holes in the enemy. WHO is supposed to be about the sharpest old lady known ?—The mother of vinegar. "You see,' said a school-boy, "I like gain' to school well enough; it is the stayin' there that I WHEN people establigh a partnership, they are said to lay a firm found“._on—that is, they found a firm. THERE is one thief/ which the poorest man can always borrow plenty of on his own personal security, said that is trouble. "I'LL b blovved if Igo out 1" said a candle on the mantel-piece. "And I'll go out if I'm not blowed 1" said the fire on the hearth. A REPORTER, who had escaped from a fighting crowd, said "there was too much missile-laneous matter in the affair to suit him." •
AN Ohio paper says that the tramp law in that State is working well. If it is, then it beats the tramp, for he doesn't work worth a cent.
- - "IN these wintry days," says a kind-hearted old scientist, "it is to be hoped that the poor little chick, before it is hatched, wears an ova- coat." . .

"NEIGHBOUR Jones, you occupy a position of very great trust in this community ?" "Yes, neigh- bour Smith, I find that I have to trust almost every- body." THE boy asked: "Why do you blow down the muzzle of your gun ?" And the man replied: "To see if—" and just then he discovered that it was. The boy attended his funeral. "'lima works wonders," said a young man of 27, • when he returned home and found his elder sister only 18. "EXCUSE mo, madam, but I should like to ask why you look at me so savagely ?" "Oh, I beg pardon, sir; I took you for my husband." " AN impecunious fop said that his straitened circumstances were owing to his failure in the "yarn business ; " that is, nobo'dfwritild his stories. FATHER,'with much solemnitY'=" Whatever you do, my boy, beOn at the bottom and work up." Son, deferentially—" But, father, suppose I was going to dig a well ?" "A Bias is known by the company he keeps," said a musician to his dissipated son. "And a . musician is known by the accompaniment hekeeps," retorted the unfilial young man.
AN English chiropodilt, who had determined to settle in Cornwall, being asked his reason therefor,, said he "thought the best place for a corn doctor would be among the Cornishmen."

"My boy," said a pompous old gentleman, "don't be too prolix. You'll always find truth in a nutshell." "I don't know about that," responded the boy; "I most always find a worm in 'em." "WHEN you have leisure," said a caller to the' Snake Editor, "I would like to speak to you."l " Leisure !" replied the Snake Editor, "what is that ?"—Pittsburgh Chronicle Telegraph. AN Irishman who was reprieved the night before his execution, and who wiebed to, get rid of his wife, wrote to her as follows ;--" I was yesterday , hanged, and (lied like a hero; do as I did, and bear t like a man."

FATHER, to fast son—" My father never gave lila money to spend for race horses, opera tickets, late dinners, and the like." Fast 8011—" Oh, yes; but you forget that I come of a more aristocratic family than you did." TALK to woman about religion, she 'sighs ; talk to her of love, she simpers ; talk to her.of art, she yawns; talk to her of science, she goei to sleep; but talk to her of dress, and she will open her .eyes and give you the entire attention of her ears. SWEET Gira..—" And so you have been on the plains for ten years ?" Ilandbome Cowboy—" Yea; this is the first time I've been ba4 into real civiliyation." "Now please tell me, in that lonely life so far removed from the rtfining ences you know, what did you miss most ?" " Oysters."—Omahrt Woild. . "Loox here, waiter," said a man in a city restaurant the other day, "is there any difference In your roast lamb and roast mutton ? I don't detect any." "Oh, yes," said the waiter ; " you would notice that yesterday, when you had roast lamb, I.gave you a is. 6d. check. To-day, when you had roast ;nutton, I gave you Is. cheek. _Chore's the difference."

SOME young fellows of various nationalities had been toasting the particular heaut.es of their sweet- hearts till it came to the turn of a young Scotsman, whose loved one was more distinguished for the absence than the possession of good looks. "Wed, lads," he exclaimed, looking round at his smiling companions, "at least ye'll allow she's got a bony dimple in her elbow 1" EMPEROR WILLIAM, of Germany, recently made a joke, for the first time in his life. On the eightieth anniversary of his entry into the army, one of the doctors tried to prevent him from going to the open window to return the salutations of the assemblage outside. His Majesty replied—" I must go. It is noon, and Baedeker's guide says that I am always visible at the window at this hour." "SEE here," said a fault-finding husband, "we must have things arranged in this house so that we shall know just where everything is kept." " With all my heart," sweetly answered his wife, "and let us begin with your late hours, my love. I should dearly love to know where they are kept." He let things run on as usual. " ANOTEIEK statesman gone !" .exclaimed a wag, In Washington, as he stood on the sidewalk of Pennsylvania Avenue. "Indeed !" said a by- stander. "How sad ! Thus our great men, one after another—" "Don't take it too hard," interrupted the wag. "He'll soon be back. He's only gone around the corner to get a glass of water with something in it just to kill the animal- cules."
POOR J3CT UONEST. —Two Englishmen, one of

whom is k own to love his money, were at dinner in a Paris restaurant. "Let's have a bottle of Corton," said Reckless, who is very poor. "Well, Corton is deuced dear," said Dives ; " let's have some ordinary Bordeaux." So they did , and when it came, Dives tasted it, and said : "Now, that's what I call an honest wine." " Yes," replied his friend, "poor, but honest." "Do you consider that the poetic instinct is fostered by allowing the hair to grow long?" asked a young lady of her poetical admirer. "I really couldn't say, was the reply. "I think it must be just a habit, for I don't know why Ido it." "I know," interrupted the enfant terrible. " Well, tell us, then," said the poet, patting the youngster on the head. "It's because you haven't the money to get it cut,' proudly roared the little man. "Do you know that I am going to whip you ?" said a teacher to one of his small pupils. "I sup- pose you will now,, replied the boy, with a gleam in his eye, "as you are so much bigger than I am. But remember that I have a future before me." "You see," said a dissipated old bachelor, on being advised to get married—‘, you see, I can't do it, because I could not marry a woman that I didn't respect, and it would be impossible for me to respect a woman that would consent to marry me." -Ix advertisement appeared in a paper recently which read:—" Wanted, a young man, to be partly out of doors and partly behind the counter." It appeared a trifle too late, however, for the Siamese twins are defunct; but if a female would fill the bill, the advertiser might hire the double-headed nightingale. A FRIEND said to a grocer who had retired from business, Why, my dear fellow, you are looking thin ! Idleness does not agree with you." " Well, no," responded the grocer, "I don't weigh as mudh as did. '

--- The return of Mr. S. Whitbread for Bedford on the sth inst., was rendered more than usually in- teresting from the fact that it was within two days of the anniversary of his first return forty years ago, he 'having sat continuously for the borough since 1852, a record second only to that of Mr. C. P. Villiers, the member for Wolverhampton.

The members of the Governmeni :have, by the way, suffered very severely. Two are among the slain—Mr. Ritchie and Mr. Walter Long, so that the Local Government department is deprived of its heads. The following have been condemned by the country by having their majorities, as compared with'the results in 1885 and 1886, reduced :—Mr. Balfour, leader of the House, Mr. Chaplin, Mr. Stan- hope, and Sir J. Pergusson.

. It is satisfactory to learn that the loss from the lamentable fire at St. Jan's, Newfoundland, is less than the original estimate. The damage is now put at 4,500,000 sterling, a terrible loss for a town like St. John's to have to bear, but a good deal less than it was siad to be on the morrow of the.disaster. It is pleasant to note that the neighbouring colony of Nova Scotia has promptly sent a supply of provis- ions for the use of the homeless poor; and we do not doubt that Lord Knutsford's appeal, through the Lord Mayor, for English help will meet with hearty response.

Liberals, while busy with the present election, should not forget to prepare for the next, which, like that of 1886, may coin d like a thief in the night. They must remember that, this is the registration season. The. oversners are notoriously., neglectful uf their duty, and voters who are qualified must not omit to apply before, the 20th ,of this month. Lodg,u.s must prepare to send in their claims dur- ing the first two weeks of August. It would be well if Liberal organisations whic4 are now in working order were kept in full operation until the registration teasonis over.,

"Terence" writes: "I have failed to discover, as a consequence of the growing majority of the " Separatists," the advocates of the disruption of the Empire," in union with traitors, murderers, and the like, any depreciation in the prices of the British Funds. On the contrary, I hoive remarked that whereat before the dissolution Consols were quoted 961, they are to-day even better, (961). 1 have always understood that the Stock Excbange is peculiarly sensitive to the prospects of revolu- tion and civil war. Perhaps our expert Chancellor of the Exchequer can explain."'

London has been so long accustomed to identify- ing the Rev. Newman Hall with the handsome gothic church which has been reared during his thirty-eight years,' Ministry in ,South LOgon that it will find it diffiehlt to realise that theltwo are no longer inseparable. Nevertheless, it is a fact that Dr. Rail- has ceased to be a pastor of Christ Church. The powerful preacher, who not many years ago was at the very zenith of his popularity, was on Tuesday night the central figure of one of those gatherings which for Nontonformists especi- ally are singularly pathetic.

Captain Penton,' Of Pentonville, takes this beat- ing by Lard Salisbury's " black man very He has had the votes counted several times, and is not yet satisfied. He wants o scrutiny. It is true that Mr. Naoroji's majority is only three; but in 1886 Captain Penton's majority was only five; and he did not then rake such a tremendous fuis to find if the odd few were absolutely justified. If the ballot papers had been placed under the micro- scope then as they are now, it is very 4oubtful whether Captain Penton's five would have stood the test to which Mr. Naoroji's three are being sub- jected.

Mr. B. B. Finley, as welt Lis Mr. Gainsford Bruce, is mentioned in connection with the vacant judg- ship. Most probably, however, Mr. Finlay,although he has lost his seat, would not care to take an ordinary judgeship. Moreover a seat is wanted for Mr. Ritchie, and perhaps he would have a Walk over in Holborn, Mr. Gainsforci Bruce may, therefore, he regarded as likely to be the new judge. He is not a brilliant politician, but he has the reputation of being a sound lawyer. In personal appearance Mr. Gainsford Wine is tall, strongly built, and grey- haired. Ile ought to look well enough in the robes of a judge,

Strangely in contrast to the present disturbed state of his Pittsburg ironworks is the unmixed quietude which Mr. Andrew Carnegie enjoys at Co- worth Park. For the moment the ironmaster is in the Highlands. So Coworth Park is quieter than ever. Mr. Carnegie has rented Coworth Park,which is near Sunningdale Station,and not far from Ascot, from Sir William Farmer. The house makes little pretension to outside show, but if externally it is plain, internally it is commodious and cosily com- fortable. There is a beautiful greenhouse, and the gardens are full of freshness, colour, and perfume. Woods and spreading fields surround the house,and the chimneys of three or four other country houses rise in the distance.

Dr. Hall was bidding farewell to his pastoral haunts in the Westminster-bridge-road, end the great congregation which gathered to afford him a final impression of their lasting esteem was sur- charged with that emotion which denotes more impressively than anything else the magnetic forcs of one man's individuality. Although Dr. Hall is now seventy-six years of age, his personality amongst his own people is apparently as attractive as ever, and it was evidently only by severe ordeal that the ties of long years were at last sundered. Tributes of admiration came from all quarters and from all sorts and conditions of men, and a service of silver plate, supplemented by a cheque for £2OO, was the hist gift of the people to their pastor.

Said:the " Spectator ' ~a 6aturday :—The most 6ignal victory obtained by any personal influence as yet is the victory of hr. Chamberlain in the Iklidlands, where he has not only carried all his candidates by vastly increased majorities, but has won for us Walsall, Wednesbury, and West Wolver- hampton. It is clear, we think, that while Mr. Chamberlain's influence is yearly waxing," &c. No, Mr. Chamberlain's personal influence is not " wax- ing.' It ia greasing. The Government virtually granted him, as readers of "The star" know, an imperial subsidy of £350,000 with which to grease the palms of the thousands interested in the Bir- mingham gun trade. If Liberal Unionism cannot flourish under such conditions, well—what do you think?

Dr. Daniel Murphy; the Archbishop of Tasmania, who is now the guest of Archbishop Croke, is an even grander old man than Mr. Gladstone himself. The incoming Prime Minister would probably not dream of circumnavigating the globe even if relieved from the cares of politics, but that is what Archbishop Murphy, who is two years Mr. Glad- stone's senior, is engaged in doing. Ile has travelled from the Antipodes via the Suez Canal to pay his respects to the Pope, who has received him very graciously in special audience, and he is going to return to his diocese "down under "by way of America. He was consecrated bishop as far back as 1846, and was for years in charge of a diocese in sultry India before he was promoted to mild and temperate Tasmania. His Indian experiences, cov- ering the whole of the Mutiny period, would make a thrilling volume,

According to private news received in Berlin the Emperor's cruise has this year had a very beneficial effect upon his health. He never left the decks of the Kaiseradler, except when business took him into his cabin, lie has not only improved in appearance, but is in the best of spirits, Although some days the weather was unfavourable and the sea rough the Emperor did not suffet. The Imperial party have been spending their time on board in the same way as on previous trips: at eight or half-past there is breakfast, which his Majesty takes with his suite —this is always served in the English style; at one o'clock ha has a solid lunch, and at seven or eight dinner. The suite and the commander of the ship are always present at meals, and of the other six officers—including the doctor—always two in tarns. The Emperor hears reports generally between break- fast and lunch. In the afternoon he writes letters and reads diplomatic reports. In the evening his Majesty generally promenades on deck for some time with one or the other of his suite. He then goes down to tea in the saloon, and spends an hour or so in conversation or in listening to music.

THE CURSE OF Tn CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN. Author of" Some Fisher Folic," "Judith," " Where the North Wind Blows," ctec., Jae.
CHAPTER LV. CHANGING pLAcas.

As Cuddy WiddringtOn retreated from this scone of his triumph—or of his defeat, whichever it might be—his pace gradually slackened, and his steps grew more and more slow and hesi- tating. The blood that, under the influence of his un- ehristianlike passion, had boiled and surged with- in his veins, gradually cooled, and as it did so the tempest within subsided also. He began to feel a little conscience stricken; although his brain worked so slowly that only by degrees did the full enormity of the thing he had clone dawn upon him.

"Judge not, that ye be not judged." This text Of Scripture came across his mind Very appositely. The high position he had taken up and arro- gated to himself—was he fitted for it by nature and discipline? Had he sufficient control of his own temper for example, to weigh calmly the rights and wrongs of the case upon which he pronouAced judgment ? Was there not an unjudicial bias within him against the condemned? Without doubt Justice ought to be entirely unbiassed and unprejudiced. Could he honestly declare this to be the case with him?
NI) He had allowed envy, hatred, and malice to enter into his heart under the guise of zeal, and of enthusiasm for the Lords work, and therefore was he not fitted for the position of accuser. _ _
Besides, it was not the business of any mere mortal to accuse his fellow.

God alone could judge the heart. Had not even the sinner in question appealed to that higher tribunal? The mercy of God was more to be trusted than the humanity of man. Rather would the old man Carr place himself in the hands of his Maker, than would lie appeal to his enemy for help and succour, in this his sore need. "If Thou, Lord, wilt he extreme to mark what is done amiss ; 0, Lord, who may abide it ? For there is mercy with Thee ; therefore shalt Thou be feared." The Psalmist knew more about judgment when he made use of these words, so full of deep and profound thought, and deep and profound know- edge of both the human and the Divine nature also. Suppose the positions to be changed; and he, Cuddy Widdrington, were to be put in the place of the judged instead of old Carr? Why, the crime of which he would stand ac- cused would then be identically the same. Strange that he should not have recognised this sooner. He had left an ofd man to die a horrible death when rescue would have been quite easy. There- fore the guilt of the murder of the old man would certainly rest upon his soul. Good God? What a dastardly act it was that he had done, now that he saw. it aright, the lurid light of passion having ettied out; to leave a man, a grey-haired man; old enough to be his father, to such a fate; simply because the said old man would not acknow- ledge his, Cuddy Wicldrington's, judgment to be infallible. Was it too late for rescue? Surely not. In frantic haste Cuddy now tore back to the cliff, eager to save his adversary; and to save himself at the same time from the committal and the unbearable weight of a hideous crime. His brain was slow, but when once he had arrived at a determination he could act quickly enough. "Hallo, Cuddy man! where are ye gannin' at such a pace ?" cried a voice, as the young fisher- man ran past a figure seated on one of the upturned boats, upon the headland which formed one of the horns of Frenchman's Bay. Cuddy looked round without pausing, and saw that the voice proceeded from one of his com- rades, a stalwart, bearded man, Jack Lisle by name, who had apparently just sauntered up to look after his boat.

"Come on, Jack, aw'll maybe want yer help," Widdrington shouted back, breathlessly. "And Carr's below us yonder there's been a land- slip !" Jack Lisle rose and followed Cuddy, wonder- ingly; but without wasting further words. The former young man's heart stood still for fear as he neared the fatal spot, and could dis- tinguish no sound, save the lapping of the sea against the stones, far below. The piteous cries for help had ceased, and a terrible silence reigned instead. Too late ! Was he too late to save tat grey head from being dashed to pieces upon_ tilt jagged rocks?

He threw himself down, and crawled cautiously to the edge. No ! Thank Heaven! The ledge ,of rock was still there ; and a dark mass huddled together, showed that the old man retained Isis place npon it, although he had most probably fainted. Quick as lightning, Cuddy slipped the noose in the rope round his own shoulders, and with Jack Lisle's assistance, lowered himself down to the perilous ledge. Although tall, he was a spare, muscular man, and this was in his favour, since it was impossible for the rock, in its shaky position, to bear a much greater weight than that already upon it. He felt it quiver, and vibrate dangerously under his feet, gently as •he descended upon it. There was no tins t to he lost.

When down, he found that it was as he had con- jectured. The old man, between despair and dis- comfort, had lost consciousness, and now lay huddled together, waiting for the end, an inert mass, with not the slightest power to help him- self. Cuddy raised him, and managed to place the rope round his body; then giving the signal to his assistant above, and himself carefully lifting the dead weight as far as he could reach, the young , fisherman was relieved to see the helpless burden hauled at last out of danger. Not a moment too soon, for the double weight had proved too much for the shaky ledge, and it gave way under Cuddy's feet, overturning and falling sideways with a tremendous crash. Making a desperate effort for life, Cuddy leaped the other wax, landing with his toes upon a slight projection in the face of the cliff; a pro- jection which he had noticed previously, and clinging with his hands to another a little way above it. It was a frightful situation—the yawn- ing gulf beneath, the perpendicular cliff above. The support to which he clung was too slight to sustain him for long, and it required all his mus- cular strength to support the terrible strain caused by the weight of his CAV/1 body. After a moment indeed it became keen agony. His fingers, grasp- ing with the tenacity of desperation the pointed rock, became each a separate point of fiery agony ; and kis body seemed weighted with lead, so heavy did it appear. No breath had he left to call for more haste on Jack's part : Ms breath came in gasps ; and the beating of his heart was as one great pulsation, penetrating and moving his whole frame. But Jack Lisle recognised the perilous nature of his friend's situation at once by the noise of the falling stone, and leaving the insensible body of old Carr upon the ground, rushed back to the edge of the precipice, without even taking time to recover his breath after the tremendous exer- tion he had just made. It was some moments before he discovered Caddy, clinging like a limpet to the face of the rock ; and then the rope he threw with no weight to keep it steady, swung too far out. There was fortunately no wind to complicate matters.
He drew it up, and fastening a block of wood to the end, lowered it gradually and with great steadiness.
This contrivance answered the purpose admir- ably. It brought the rope within Cuddy's reach. But bow was he to relax his bola sufficiently in order to fasten it around him?

If he let go the point of stone above, he must inevitably fall! And yet he could not hold 011 longer, another minute would be too much to endure in his present position. He managed to seize the rope with his teeth, and then gm,lually sliding his hand along, event- ually to grasp it. There was no ehance of fasten- ing it 'properly ; but he somehow got one arm through the noose, and clung on to the rope with the other.

It was nothing but the strength of despair which enabled him to do this; and had he not been both a fisherman and an athlete, he must certainly have perished in the attempt. However, the feat, impossible as it appeared, was accomplished at last, and Cuddy was lauded in safety upon the top of the cliff. That night, when old Carr was sitting by biz own firosideo smoking quietly, as though nothing extraordinary had taken place during the day, the door opened suddenly, And Cuddy Widdrianzton came in.

Ailsie; who know-nothing aS yet of the danger in which her father had been placed, and who certainly would never hear it from his lips, was surprised to see Cuddy go up to the old fisherman and hold out his hand.

" AW was a daft, self-righteous fyule," he said, in a low hesitating voice, very unlike to the strident tones in which he was wont to lay down the law, "an' the Lord's, gien me a sharp lesson ? If ye wad gie Inc a shake o' the fist' just to show there's no ill feclin', aw wad sleep better for it the fleet ?"

"What ? Wad ye shake lw-nds with such a deep dyed sinner ?" asked the old fisherman, with a queer twinkle in his light coloured eyes. "Are ye sartin sure ye'll get to heaven, efter such a home down as that ?"
Cuddy coloured, and shifted uneasily from one foot to the other. _ _ _

"Aw knaw it's a deal to ax, efter aw behaved like a cowardly brute," he went on with curious humility; "but ye niver were one to bear malice." "Aw left that for saints like thou !" was the stinging reply. " Wey, wey, let bygones be by- gones, an' dinna bother thy head about other folks so much. Let every tub stand on its own bottom, say aw. There's ma' hand, wiv all ma heart ;" and the old man shook the other's muscular fist heartily. "An' look here, Cuddy ma man, aw canna explain matters to thee, 'cause there's no sense 'i rakin' up the past; but aw'm none so much to blame as thou's thinkin' for !" Cuddy certainly slept better that night, for his own confession of wrongdoing, and for leaving judgment and vengeance to a Higher Power.
CHAPTER LVI. THE SIBYL.

One grey day in November, Lady Callerley, who had been riding out with her husband, called at the Widdringtons' cottage, and dismounting, announced that she had come to have a chat with Bell, while Sir Lancelot went on to Breamish ; where he was to meet his steward about some business connected with hisTroperty there. Silvia had seen very little of Bell lately, and reproached herself that her own great pre- occupation and happiness had apparently caused her to slight that of her humble friend, whom she heard was on the eve of matrimony. Not expecting to make a long visit, Lady Callerley led Britomart up to the door, and fastened the reins there to a crook in the wall.

Then she stood for a moment listening to the rushing sound made by Yarrop water, which was greatly swollen by the long continuance of rain amongst the hills. "What a noise it makes, Bell," she said, rather awed by the thunderous roar. " Did you ever hear it rush so strongly before l" Bell, who had come out to greet Lady Callerley with smiles and delight, nodded in assent. "Once. When aw was a bit lass, it corned down i' the like fashion, when it swept away Farmer Todd's hay ricks fro' Heathery Rigg, an' landed them right ower on yonder bank. Aw mind Bill an' me climbed o' the top o' the byre te be able to see a long way, an' te count the things that came doon wi' the stream. An' granny thowt we'd tumbled in an' been drooned, an' wes that mad ' with us that she gave us both a good licking, only the worst was for me, cause aw said aw'd led him into the scrape. That wes afore the bridge wes built. AW often think it'll not stand a spate, an' this'll surely try it !" Lady Callerley walked to the top of the bank, a short distance from the house, and looked down into the current.

It was indeed a scene of wild turmoil, a restless, excited, whirling mass of water, a mass such as only those who have seen a spate in a mountain stream can realise. Sometimes it would appear to quiet down and subside a little, and at such times the dark, swift- running stream eddied round the banks in a com- paratively gentle fashion; then suddenly a great solid ponderous wall of water Would come thunder- ing and pounding down, carrying everything before it, tearing at the banks, and roaring, like a hungry monster eager for prey. As Silvia gazed at it Bell noticed that her face grew very pale, and that she shuddered slightly. " Are ye feared?" asked the fisher girl, who could not understand such emotion being excited by the spectacle in one whom she knew to have faced a much worse scene without quailing. Lady Callerley passed her hand over her eyes and looked bewildered.

"I do not know. Yes, lam rather afraid, 1 think, because—because it seems as though I had seen it all somewhere before—l know not where— in a dream perhaps? Strange dreams have come to me of late. I have been so happy in my waking hours, oh, so happy, Bell ! Is it not wonderful, therefore, that I should dream of horrors? "Did you ever feel as though you had seen a place before in some previous state of existence—as though each word and action was but the shadow of another which had preceded it ?" Bell stared at the speaker with surprise. Such mental phenomena was utterly unknown to her healthy organisation. "When I first came to Seaton Callerley I had the same impression, followed by a feeling of in- tense loneliness and misery. What does it mean, Bell? Is it a presentiment of evil, I wonder ?" The fisher girl smiled incredulously. " Hoots ! Diana fash yer canny heid wi' them sort o' notions, ma leddy !" she said, with fine scorn, "if aw wes to take heed to all granny's warnings aw wad never go nowhere nor do owt at all. She's gettin' worse than ever, poor, daft, fanciful and body ! But then she's sore failed o' late, an' the deith o' wor Bill's been a sad blow for. bye !" she ended, with pity. Come thee ways in an' rest a bit afore Sir Lancelot returns," she said coaxingly, "it's not well for anybody to look over long at Yarrop burn. An' granny'll be wonderiu' who aw'm talkin' to, and gettin' sore put oot at ma absence !"

Sure enough, when they entered, tho old woman was querulous and ill-tempered ; imagining herself neglected and slighted, wishing she were out of the world, since all the folks who had ever cared for her had gone before ; lamenting Bill's untimely demise and Cuddy's religious proclivities alternately, and wondering how long it would be before Bell took a man and left her to fend for herself.

"Come, come, Nanny, you must not welcome me in such a fashion as this, there's a good soul ! See, I have not forgotten you! I've brought you a basket with all sorts of good things that Mrs. Moot has packed at my request. You must try and be sweet with Bell too, because she is the very best girl in the country, and because there is not the slightest fear of her leaving you." " Darrsay I._ Young folks are all selfish, an' Bell's clean daft about her man, forbye ! If he axed her te chop me up into little bits, she'd do it without thinkin' twice."

Bell laughed. "She canna help being aggravatin', poor aad body," she said, with good-natured tolerance, " aw never Mind her, cause she means nowt bad, an' she's had a peck o' troubles." "It's easy to be sweet-tempered when one is happy," remarked Silvia, her eyes shining with the consciousness of her own supreme contentment, "Oh, Bell, I do hope you may be as perfectly con- tented as lam when you are married! It some- times makes me afraid though It is too great, too satisfying a bliss to last." " Nonsense ! We dinna serve God better for bein' miserable, as some folks would have us believe. Whatfor shouldna' ye be the happiest leddy i' the land? Sir Lancelot's a fine man an' a bonny, noo that he's getten a brighter look on his handsome fyece, an' he worships the very ground ye tread on, a body can see that wi' half an eye." "And what of your own sweetheart, Bell? I'll warrant he is not far behind mine in devotion?"
Bell's face lighted up in a moment, but she was shy of expressing her feelings, even to Lady Caller- ley. So she turned away and began vigorously polishing one of the brass candlesticks on the table.
"Eh weigh, he's well enough, is Dick! We hey both wor tempers, but we understand one another, an' that's the main thing !" Silvia laughed gaily, and patted the fisher girl's rich cheek. _

"Oh Bell, you are just as fond of him as ever you can be, only you are too proud to own .it. Silly c4ild ! When you come to be an old married woman like me, you'll have got over all that sort of thing." Now it was Bell's turn to laugh. And Lady Callerley asked her very sharply why she did so? "Aw dinna ken ! Ye look such a bairn to be talkin' to an' lecturin' me !" "Oh, but indeed I am old—old in experience, if not in years," replied Lady Callerley with eager- ness, "Indeed I do not want to keep too young, because I must be Lancelot's companion and friend as well as his wife. That is where women make the mistake, I think," went on the sage matron in a solemn voice, "they are not content to study their husband's requirements, and expect him to play the lover alwity§, _What lit gat matter 3.v.ith

-- Those who care to open their eye e may See the signs of what is coiling. What is England's commercial standingo-day ? Is it not true that her seasons of prosperity are getting few, and far between ? Urban;growing at the expense of suburban, Mighty cities, and no outl ? It is mere foolishness to talk of emigration. The trade Unionist insists upon eight hours, 'and a Labour Departmeut in the Cabinet. He will and ought to have,these, but be will handicap himself into ruin, it is said. Not much: he has all to gain, and without a doubt, he will have

div.head: SOLVED THE LAND QUESTION,
div.p: SOLVED THE LAND QUESTION,

and then Mr. Chamberlain's apt quotStion about those who neither toil, nor yet spin, will have a little show. I see much capital is tried to be made out of some of the paltry measures passed by the present Government. Most of them can only be likened to tinkling cymbals, noisy and hollow. What benefit is it to the farm labourer to tell him that he can rent small lots, of land, when such rent is four, and five times the amount per acre more than the farmees over the hedge? This is noeX4g- aeration. See evidence given before Committee of the House of Commons. I am pleased to see that at last the real terror connected with Holum Rule is being trotted out. Well, an airing wilt do it good. It is the, sectarian .bogey.' No one can tell. the Nopeonformista of England's country sides about the abounding charity of the cultured gentle- men who are known as Protestants and Tories. Why, the love these gentlemen have been showing, even in recent years, towards - their dissenting brethren has become proverbial.

I CAN FANCY THE WARRINGTON ORANGEMEN meeting some of the Cairo-st. Unitarians and giving the kiss of love and peace. See how generously the Protestants of Ireland treat their Catholic brethren! No Catholic, whatever his qualifications, can have any hope of election to the Town Council of Belfast. From the Town Clerk to the humblest scavenger, every official and workman employed by the Town Council is a Protestant. The bitterness of sectarian zeal not only fills all official channels, but over- flows and permeates society. To show ally sym- pathy for oppressed or outraged Catholics has always brought upon the more liberal Protestants a social boycott, before ever that convenient word , was invented. The sincere, devout, and honest 1 Wesleyan who represents an almost exclusively ' Catholic constituency in Clare, is jealously excom- municated from co-operation in the public religious movements of his Protestant brethren. Mr. Jere- miah Jordan, to whom I refer, had been expected to take part in a certain religious Conference in Belfast. But, to the shame of Protestantism be it spoken, he received a letter informing him that his appearance on the platform would be unwelcome, and might even cause disorderly scenes.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre I (Chairman) presided, and there were also present thA Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Knowles, Speak- man, Taylor, Aaron, Stokes, J. Parr, Brandreth, W. Whitlow, P. Hall, Baxter, J. G. Heywood, T. Lewis, Norman, T. Lee, Williams, J. Baguley, J. W. Bagu- ley, Pickering, Bretherton, Jones, Wilkinson, T. J. Weir, Joseph Hall, Smith, Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).
THE ELECTION OF GUARDIANS.

A letter was read from. the Local Government Board with reference to the request of the Guardians that their period of service be altered from one year to three years, and stating that they would issue the necessary order for a poll of the ratepayers to be taken on the subject. They also inquired if it was intended that all the guar- dians sheuld retire at the end of three years. The Clerk said he had replied in the affirmative to this last inquiry.

div.head: _PROPOSED NEW VAGRANT WARDS.
div.p: _PROPOSED NEW VAGRANT WARDS.
The Local Government Board wrote laaking some ob- jections to the plans of proposed new vagrant wards which had been submitted to them. It was agreed to refer the plans back to the Committee.
-APPOINTMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICER.

The next business before the meeting was that of the appointment of a relieving officer for Runcorn to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. G. Ward, of Run- corn. The salary was fixed at £lOO a year.—Mr. Speak- man moved that the appointment be made in Committee, and that the reporters should retire from the room. This proposal on being put to the meeting was, however, negatived.—Mr. Heywood, Chairman of the Committee of Selection, said there had been 17 applications for the post, and through these the Committee had gone very carefully. Five of the applicants, as the most suitable, had been selected to appear before the Board that day before the final appointment was made. The Committee were strongly of opinion that the voting should be done by ballot. (Hear, hear.)—The applications and testi- monials of the five selected candidates were then read. The candidates were Messrs. Thomas Kirkham, G. T. Wainwright, A. S. Rigby, Thomas Cook, Thomas John- son, all of whom belonged to Runcorn. The candidates were afterwards separately called into the room and questioned by the members of the Board.—ln the end, Mr. Thomas Cook received the appointment.

div.head: DESERT ISLAND.
div.p: THE DESERT ISLAND.
FROM " THE TALMUD."

A very wealthy man, who was of a kind, benevo- lent disposition, desired to make his slave happy. lie gave him, therefore, his freedom, and presented him with a shipload of merchandise. " Go, " said he," sail to different countries, dis- pose of these goods, and that which thou mayest receive for them shall he thy The slave sailed away upon the broad ocean, but before he had been long upon his voyage a storm overtook him ; his ship was driven on a rock and went to pieces ; all on board were lost, all save this slave, who swam to an island shore near by. Sad, despondent, with naught in the world, he traversed this island, until he approached a large and beauti- ful city ; and many people approached him joyously shouting, " Welcome ! welcome ! Long live the king !" They brought a rich carriage, and placing him therein, escorted him to a magnificent palace, where many seivants gathered about him, clothing him in royal garments, addressing him as their sovereign, and expressing their obedience to his will. _ _ _
• The slave was amazed and dazzled, believing that be was dreaming, and all that he saw, heard, and

experienced was mere passing fantasy. Becoming convinced of the reality of his condition, he said to some men about him for whom he experienced a friendly feeling: "how is this? I cannot understand it. That you should elevate and honour a man whom you know not, a poor naked. wanderer, whom you have never seen before, making him your ruler, causes me mole wonder than I can readily express." " Sire," they replied, " this island is inhabited by spirits. Long since they prayed to God to send them yearly a son of man to reign over them, and he answered their prayers. Yearly he sends them a son of man, whom they receive with honour and elevate to the throne ; but his dignity and power ends with the year. With its close his royal gar- ments are taken from him, he is placed on board a ship and carried to a vast and desolate island, where, unless he has previously been wise and pre- pared for this day, he will find neither friend nor subject, and be obliged to pass a weary, lonely, miserable life. Then a new king is selected here, and so year follows year. The kings who preceded thee were careless and indifferent, enjoying their power to the full,and thinking not of the day when it snould end. Be wiser thou ; let our words find rest within thy heart." The newly-made king listened attentively to all this, and felt grieved that he should have lost even the time he had already missed for making prepar- ations, for his loss of power. He addressed the wise man who had spoken, saying, "Advise me, oh, spirit of wisdom, how I may prepare for the days which will come upon me in the future." " INaked thou camsst to us and naked thou will be sent to the desolate island of which I have told thee," replied the other. "At present thou art Icing, and may do as pleaseth thee ; therefore send workmen to this island ; let them build houses, till the ground, and beautify the surroundings. The barren soil will be changed into fruitful fields, people will journey there to live, and thou wilt have established a new kingdom for thyself, with subjects to welcome thee in gladness when thou shalt have lost thy power here. The year is short, the work is long; therefore be earnest and energe- tic."

The king followed this advice. Ile sent workmen and materials to the desolate island, and before the close of his temporary power it bad become a blooming, pleasant, and attractive spot. The rulers who had preceded him had anticipated the day of their power's close with dread, or smothered all thought of it in revelry ; but he looked forward to it as a day of joy, when he should enter upon a career of permanent peace and happiness. The day came ; the freed slave, who had been made king, was deprived of his authority ; with his power he lost his royal garments ; naked he was placed upon a ship, and its sails set for the desolate isle. When he approached its shores, however, the people whom he had sent there came to meet him with music, song, and great joy. They made him a prince aniowthem, and he lived with them ever after in pleasantness and peace. The wealthy man of kindly disposition is God, and the slave to whom He gave freedom is the soul which lie gives to man. The island at which the slave arrives is the world ; naked and weeping he appears to his parents, who are the inhabitants that greet him warmly and make him their king. The friends who tell him of the ways of the country are his " good inclinations." The year of his reign is his span of life, and the desolate island is the future world, which he must beautify by good deeds, "the workmen and material," or else live lonely and desolate for ever.

LATEST WINNERS OF THE VICTORIA CROSS, -It was announced in Tuesday night's " Gazette ', that the Queen has signified her intention of con- ferring the decoration of Victoria Cross upon three officers of her Majesty's Army, whose claims have been submitted for her Majesty's approval, for the conspicuous bravery displayed by them during the recent operations in the Hunza and Nagar Country on the Gilgit frontier in December, 1891. The officers are Captain Fenton John Aylmer, of the Royal Engineers, and Lieutenants G. H. Boisragon and John Manners Smith of the Indian Staff Corps. _ .

Captain Aylmer receives his cross for his con- spicuous bravery in the assault and capture of the Nilt Fort, on 2nd December, 1891. According to the official record, this officer accompanied the storming party, burst open the inner gate with gun-cotton. which he placed and ignited, and though severely wounded, once in the leg and twice in the right hand, fired nineteen shots with his revolver, killing several of the enemy, and remained fighting, until, fainting from loss of blood, he was carried out of action. •

Lieutenant Guy Hudleston Boisragon also earns the Victoria Cross for his conspicuous bravery in the assault and capture of the Nilt Fort. He is de- scribed as having led the assault with dash and de- termination, and forced his way through difficult obstacles to the inner gate, when he returned for reinforcements, moving intrepidly to and fro under a heavy cross-fire until he had collected sufficient men to relieve the hardly pressed storming party and drive the enemy from the fort. The Victoria Cross to be given to Lieutenant John Manners Smith, is awarded for his conspicuous bravery when leading the storming party at the attack and capture of the strong position occupied •by the enemy near Nilt, in the Hunza-Nagar Country, on the 20th December last. The official record says the position was, owing to the nature of the country, an extremely strong one, and had barred the advance of a force for seventeen days. It was eventually forced by a small party of 50 rifles, with another of equal strength in support. The first of these parties was under the command of Lieutenant Smith, and it was entirely owing to his splendid leading, and the coolness, combined with dash, he displayed while doing so, that a suc- cess was obtained. For nearly four hours, on the face of a cliff which was almost precipitous, he steadily moved his handful of men from point to point, asthe difficulties of the ground and showers of stones from above gave him an opportunity, and during the whole of this time he was in such a position as to be unable to defend himself from any attack the enemy might choose to make. He was the first man to reach the summit, within a few yards of one of the enemy's sungars, which Was immediately rushed, Lieutenant Smith pistolling the first man.

your grandmother ? - See how strangely she is look- ing at me." The old woman was indeed looking strangely in Lady Callerley's direction. The girls did not imagine that she was paying ally attention to their conversation, because she had kept on muttering all the while about her grievances and about the days of her youth in a muffled voice, and they fancied her quite absorbed in her own meditations. • But quite suddenly her mood seemed to change, and she ceased her garrulous chattering about the times of her youth. Once more her eyes shone with gloomy prophetic fire, and she rose to the dignity of a sibyL "Aw can hear it comin' from afar, the evil that. follows the Callerleys fra' generation to generation! Aw can hear it i' the wind, i' the sound o' the sea, i' the runnin' water o' Breamish, as it flows ower; the shiftin' sands below us. There's no way 0, escapin' fra' the curse, for any male descendant o that cruel man who killed his foster-mother, lang syne. Ye are happy noo, say ye, Leddy Callerley? Make the most ont then, for it'll be short lived, ma little beauty. Eh, weary on us! Whatten sense is there in lettin' an aad wife outlive strong, fine, brave, handsome men? An' him the last o' them. noo, the varry last o' the prood race." "Oh, stop her, Bell ; do stop her, for Heaven's sake !" exclaimed Lady Callerley, trembling in every limb; "I dare not listen while she seems to. fortell evil to my husband !" "She is queer just noo, Leddy Callerley._ manna mind her, or think twice of her daft sayin • Mebbe she's gannin' back on some of her sad stories o' things that happened lang syne. She wanders on about folks she met an' lived wi', an' lads that made love to her when she was a young lass, till aw'm fair sick o' hearin' her sometimes." Bell was doing her best to reassure Silvia, but the latter could not help fancying that the girl her- self was anything but easy in her mind. "Yes, yes, I have heard her talk like that," replied Silvia, hastily, "but this is a different' matter. Has she been long in this strange state of mind ?" The fisher girl nodded : " For the last few days she's been neither to hold nor to bind, as the sayin' goes! Aw Ilawna seen her so queer for years. It's the noise o' the water affects her mind a bit, aw believe !" " Eigh weigh, aw'll not be long after ye, Ina canny master, ina canny little Lancelot ;ma Laney, that aw held i' my arms when ye were a bit bairn an' took into ma bed to sleep by ma side when Yer, mother weaned ye. We'll all gan tegither, that'll not be so bad. If only them 'at went fort wad wait of us 'at comes after. There wes rna, Willie, ma first sweetheart, wi' the bonny curls an the glint in eyes; an wor Bill, that died the other day, an' had a look of him. ANY moist broke Ina heart when young Willie went ;but mebbe aw hare no tears left, for aw've been dry eyed ever since. It's a pity, though, for aw wad wish te do the right thing an' weep like the rest; when the held o' the family, an' the last on them, gans !" Lady Callerley kept her eyes fixed on the speaker. Every word seemed to piece her heart, for WO there not within her own .inner consciousness an. echo to it ? "Bt ye're not alone i' yer sorrow, Ina little leddy, an' ye bein' young an' innocent of anY offence, will mebbe be better able to bide it, than she who has guilt upon her soul? Hark ye! Here comes the other! Neither Lady Callerley nor Bell heard any foot- bonny steps, but the old woman's senses must have became preternaturally sharpened : for no sooner were the words out of her mouth than a tap came • to the door, the latch was lifted, and Dorothy Breannah entered.

div.head: OTHER POLLING DISTRICTS.
div.p: OTHER POLLING DISTRICTS.

At llaydock, the miners, however, voted largely for the Liberal candidate. There was, it was understood, an absence of anything approaching enthusiasm. Shortly after noon a little life was infused into the pro- ceedings by the appearance of Mr. S. Woods, M.P., a representative miners' man. On his departure, however, ! the interest flagged, and when thelbooth was closed at eight o'clock the miners viewed it with indifference. At Burtonwood the polling was very slow all day. The district was formerly purely an agricultural one, but on the establishment of the collieries the electorate became a mixed one. There was no display of feeling of any character.
At Newton the polling was very tedious. DECLARATION OF THE POLL. AN EXCITING SCENE...

At the conclusion of the polling the ballot boxes were despatched as quickly as possible in cabs to the Town Hall at Newton-le-Willows, where the counting took place. Owing to the great distance of one or two of the polling places from Newton, the last of the ballot boxes was not received until half-past nine. Both candidates and their agents were present,Mr. C. Appleton,of Wigan, acting as ldeputy returning officer. Shortly after eight o'clock elebtors from all parts of the division commenced to assemble in the street in front of the Town Hall to wait the declaration of the poll, and they conducted themselves in a very creditable manner, cheer after cheer being given for Mr. Legh by his supporters, and cheer after cheer for his opponent by the Liberals. A large number of policemen were in attendance, but they had comparatively little to do, owing to the good temper displayed by the crowd. The result of the poll was formally declared, although it is doubtful whether a single voter could hear what was said, shortly before eleven o'clock. The wildest excitement prevailed. Mr. Leah was warmly cheered and congratulated upon the result, and the Liberals, nothing daunted, also accorded a hearty reception to their defeated candidate. The result was a surprise, even to Mr. Leg,h's supporters. It was, of course, a greater surprise to the Liberals, who had been cheered during the day by the rumour that the colliers intended to vote in a body for Mr. Neill. As soon as it was understood that Mr. Legh had been returned, rockets and cannon were fired,and the result of 'the poll was soon telegraphed all over the country. The 'figures were as follows : Mr. Legh (C) Mr. Neill (L)

Majority 894 Mr. Legh, M P., endeavoured to speak to his suppor- ters from one of the windows of the Town Hall, but wing to the incessant cheers not a word he said could I.be heard by them. Recognizing this fact Mr. Legh spoke 1 directly to the reporters as follows :—Gentlemen,— : For the third time the Newton constituency has asserted its devotion to the Conservative and Unionist cause. We have achieved a remarkable triumph, and I have no , hesitation in saying that if other issues had not inter- vened we should have obtained even a larger majority 1 than that which has been gained to-night. It must be obvious to everyone of you that other questions, besides that of Home Rule, have entered into the decision of this contest. I will not enter into those questions now, but I should like to say on behalf of my opponent, Mr. Neill, and his supporters, that the election has been conducted in a manly and in a straightforward manner. This is not a personal triumph, it is a triumph of principle. Gentlemen, we have once more vindicated the Conser- vative cause and the cause of the Union. We have done what we could to maintain the unity and dignity of this empire, and from the 'bottom of my heart I desire to thank you all for the assistance that you have given to me during this election. Believe me, gentlemen, thit as long as I live I shall always remember with the utmost gratitude the devotion and the assistance which I have received from the members of the Conservative and Unionist party. ,Once more I have to thank you for your efforts on behalf of the Conservative and Unionist oause. Mr. Neill, who was ,received with loud cheers, said : Gentlemen,—l cannot say that lam not disappointed with the result of tbecontest to-day, but I will say that I am more disappointed for the sake of those earnest Liberals than lam for my own sake. I desire to express my appreciation of the great courtesy I have received from Mr. Legh, and the manly and straightforward manner in which bedgas conducted this fight. I ask you not to be disheartened, brit to have hope for the future, when we may be able to secure a Liberal victory in this division. (Cheers.) 1• thank all those who have so heartily supported me in this struggle. (Cheers.) The large crowd shortly afterwards dispersed. We understand that there were 51 spoiled votes.

„ Mr. Legh afterwards drove to the Gentlemen's Club, Newton, where he received numerous congratulations, and Mr. Neill, after calling at the residence of his agent, drove on to Eccleet.m. On Tuesday night the Tories again showed their en- thusiasm by alarming the neighbourhood with the ascent of several rockets, which on each occasion ex- ploded with a loud report. MR. R. PIERMINT, M.P., ON THE NEWTON 'ELECTION. The news of Mr. Legh's return was received at the Conservative Club at Warrington, shortly befora mid- night, and there was a good deal of jubilation in con- sequence. Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M.P., who arrived shortly after the treeipt of the news, was loudly cheered and asked to make a speech. In a brief address he expressed the delight it, had afforded him to hear of Mr. ' Legh's return, because he had had the pleasure of working for him. There was a feeling at one time in the division that perhaps the ;little side issue of the eight hours question would go against the Conservatives, but he was delighted to see that notwithstanding that feel- ing that the election had been fought on the one great question before them. When they remembered the molerate majorities by which their friend Lord Cross used to be returned for the \Newton Division, the larae majority by whichldr.,Legh was returned in 1886, and the magnificent majority by which he had been returned ' that night, they cold not but congratulate themselves ! exceedingly. (Cheers.) He felt certain that in the Newton Division there had been hundreds of men who had been willing to work heart and soul to secure Mr. Legh's return, and there were men in Warrington who had worked equally hard for the Conservative cause,and for him as their representative. Whatever the less edu- cated county constituencies might do, men such as they were, and who knew something of the world, were standing true to the Ccnstitution, to the Church,. and to the State. (Cheers.) They did not intend to hai,e the :Union of the United Kingdom disturbed. Perhaps, in times gone by, when he was their chairman, now and then he had to scold them a little, but after what had recently taken place in Warrington, and after the result of the poll att Newton, lie could only speak of them in terms of the highest praise. (Applause.)
! ALLEGED OUTIMGE AT THE NEWTON ELECTION.

A report has gone the round of the press of an attempt to shoot a returning officer. The report says-:-.--" The acting returning officer at the Newton election was Mr. Charles Appleton, solicitor, Wigan, and shortly after the declaration of the poll Mr. Appleton, accompanied by one of his clerks and several gentlemen, commenced the journey to Wigan in an open landau, drawn by a pair of horses. When a,short distance from Newton a one was thrown at the carriage from behind a hedge, the missile carrying away the,clerk's hat. This was immediately followed by a revolver shot, the bullet striking the pipe which Mr. Appleton had in his mouth. The pipe was smashed, though, fortunately, no other damage was done." From ioquiries made by our representative we learn that the above report, must be received with a certain amount of reservation. The affair was reported to the Newton police. who pursued inquiries into the matter, and found that as Mr. Appleton was driving past the Oak Tree Inn, at the end of Crow-lane. about half-past eleven, on'Monday night, a .number of mea made a rush at the carriage, and shouted something about Whigs and Tories at the occupants. Mr. Appleton's clerk's hat was knocked off, and whether by a stone ar not, is a doubtful point, and after the passage of the carriage, the men indulged in game of football with the bat. The question as to whether a revolver was fired or not, is open to doubt. The police incline to the belief that the excitement consequent on the victory has led Mr. Appleton 'astray ; and, as at the moment of his passing the" Oak tree,' a rocket was fired from Mr. Pardey's garden close by, the flash and report have caused him to think that he was fired at. The pipe may have been dislodged from his mouth by a stone. Further investigations are being made.

THE GEOGRAPHICAL ARGUMENT against Home Rule was concerned, it was said that because nature had thrown Ireland and England so closely together therefore they must be under one Government and one Parliament. What a remarkable intermingling of geography and politics ! Canada and the United States had been thrown together by nature therefore they must be under on 3 Government. France and England had been thrown together by nature, and therefore they must also be under one government. Germany and France for similar reasons must be under one government. Really the•geographical argument did not carry much weight.

THE DIRTY ROTTEN TOWEL OF COERCION. It was further argued that because for 700 years Ireland had been under the control of England therefore she must continue to be so for another 700 years. This was very like the argument they often heard of " It did for our fathers and grand- fathers, it did for our great grandfathers, it will do for us." To compare great things with small, it reminded him of what a certain steward on board ship was re- ported to have said to some one who complained that the towel was not as clean as it ought to be, " I don't know what you expect," exclaimed the steward, " do you know that 44 people have wiped themselves on that towel? I should think it would do for you." People had 13,-en wiped by that towel of coercion long enough. It was a rotten dirty rag, and would have to be thrown away, and cleanly linen would have to be substituted for it. Mr. Watson's spaech evoked repeated and loud cheering.

div.head: MR. BRUNNER AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MR. BRUNNER AND THE SHIP CANAL.

Speaking to a large meeting of working-men, at Wes- ton, Mr. Brunner said he had done something for the Ship Canal. In 1887 he remembered Lord R. Grosvenor saying that he wished the Ship Canal to be made. He (Mr. Brunner) not only wished it to be made, but he pot his hands in his pockets, and .pulled out money to help the undertaking. In 1888, when they were considering the Local Government Bill, he ventured to suggest that it would be a very good thing if the County Council should have what was now called a Joint Committee for the prevention of the pollution of rivers. In times gone by the rivers of England were a source of food and plea- sure to the people living or. their banks. In many parts of thecountry the rivers were befouled and a danger to the people living near them, in consequence of the sewage from the towns and the refuse from factories beim, deposited in them. The Irwell at Manchester was as braok as ink, and emitted in summer time an ex- tremely disagreeable odour. 'The waters of the Irwell were to be the feeder at the ship Canal. If the people of Runcorn had the foul waters et the Irwell placed in front of the town, there was not a shadow of a doubt that the water, being stagnant, would seriously affect the people living in close proximity. As a result of the amendment being introduced into the bill, a Joint Committee was formed of the County Councils of Lan- cashire and Cheshire to prevent the waters of the Mersey and Irwell and their tributaries being fouled. The au- thorities had been notified to keep the sewage out of the waters unless it had been filtered first, and a notice had been sent to manufacturers that they were not to allow any disagreeable or noxious fluid to flow into the rivers. The notices would be enforced, and the water in the Ship Canal would be clear, and they would have hun- dreds and hundreds of lives saved in Cheshire through his work in the House of Commons. (Applause.) EXPOSURE OF UNIONIST FALLACIES BY A WES- LEYAN MINSTER. The Rev. A. P. Watson,of Preston,who up till recently was stationed for several years in the Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit, has been taking an active pazt in the election at Preston. In a speech reported in the "Lancashire Evening Post," he sairt he had no hope whatever of obtaining any redress of his political grievances from the Tory party nor with regard to any other grievance which as a Nonconformist he might labour undiir did he hope to obtain any redress from the Tory party, unless circumstances should so come about, as they had occasionally come about in the past—whereby they were forced, as it had been cleverly said "to steal the clothes of the Whigs while they were bathing." It would be a monstrous misrepresentation of Methodism if it were to be supposed that English Methodists at this election were going to vote against Home Rule. Perhaps it would be known to many that there were 35 Methodist candidates in the field and not one of them was an anti-Hume

div.head: MR.. BRUNNER REPLIES TO HIS TRADUCERS.
div.p: MR.. BRUNNER REPLIES TO HIS TRADUCERS.

Speaking at an open air meeting at -NVinnington on Saturda7 Mr. Brunner, who was enthusiastically cheered, said their opponents in the division were getting un- commonly hard up for argument. They were giving up trying to argue and getting to abuse, and that was al- ways a sign of weakness. Mr. Ward had said that no man at Winnington dare declare himself to be a Tory— that if a man did not promise straight out t* vote for Mr. Brunner the foreman put a black mark against his name. (Cries of "It's a lie.") lie wanted them to defend their own character. (Loud cheers.) He was ready to declare before any set of people in this world that they were men and not cowards—(cheers)—that they were prepared to assert their opinions against any amount of screw, and that they hated it as much as he did. (Cheers.) Everybody in Winning,ton, at any rate, knew that every man in the service of Brunner Mond, and Co. was as free as he was. (Cheers.) When they heard the Tories repeating this statement, he hoped they would not hesitate to express their opinion of it. His word for it would be a very short one. (Laughter.) Mr. Whiteley had said that he (Mr. Brunner) denounced Blackburn men as scoundrt Is. He never said that Back. burn men were scoundrels, nor by implication, or in any other way that Mr. Whiteley was a scoundrel. He had never uttered that ugly epithet, and there was no neces- sity to accuse hi:n of it. Mr. Whiteley asked, " Had Mr. Brunner at his request last week a deputation of deputation of delegates of the licensed victuallers at his house at Winnington, and was he going to receive a similar deputation next week ?" He had very clear answers to both those questions. Mr. Whiteley had read his (Mr. Brunner's) address, and he noted with great care how he had voted on the questions of temperance reform, and then he finished hi remarks by saying that he was acting in a double-faced manner upon that point. No, he did not receive a deputation of licensed victuallers last week ; he was not asked to, and none came. He was not going to receive a similar deputation next week, as far as he knew. Mr. Whiteley seemed to be going to the moon for his infor- mation. "He (Mr. Whiteley) was not talking off the book; but he simply wanted to gain facts, in order to clear the matter. But Mr. Bruntser told various mem- bers of the deputation that he was not in favour of Sunday closing, and that he was not in favour of depriving the workingman of his beer on a Sunday." He certainly did not tell them anything of the sort, because he never saw them. He believed this to be a garbled account of an interview he had with a deputation of licensed victuallers in 1887. (Laughter.) He then did declare against Sunday closing, and he did say that lie did not want to deprive the workingman of his beer on the Sunday. He did not mean to deprive the working- man of his beer on Sunday ndiv, and he had only been persuaded to vote for Sunday closing because he had been convinced since 1887 that the vast majority of the men of this country wanted Sunday closing, and he felt bound as their representative in Parliament to accede to their wishes. (Cheers.)

with interest and compound interest from the time that he raised the rent ; and a Bill making a landlord pay for all buildings put up by the tenants ?" That ques- tion seemed like a Chinese puzzle. There was a law which compelled landlords to pay a tenant when he left for all improvements he had made. Third, "Will you bring in a Bill making it a penal offence for a landlord Ito compel his tenants to keep dogs and each tenant to give the landlord a cheese ?" (Laughter.) He did not think they required a Bill for that. 4. " Will you bring in a Bill making all game the property of the tenants ?" No. He thought game should belong to those who paid for it. 5. •• Will you make a landlord pay for all dam- age done by keeping an artificial lake ?" He thought if a landlord caused a tenant any loss he sh)uld pay for it. (Applause.) 6. " Will you bring in a Land Bill for England of the same nature of the Irish Land Bill ?" He considered that was for a Goverment to do, not an individual member of Parliament. 7. " Will you vote for the law of distress to be abolished, and allow a tenant to sell all produce on his farm when he leaves ?" What belonged to the tenant he ought to sell. 8. "Will you bring in a Bill allowing people to pasture cattle on -road sides when there is someone in charge, and one abolishing the law by which a magistrate can fine a person when his cattle accidentally stray on the highway ?" He was not aware that this was an offenco. 9. "Will you vote against judges' expenses being paid when on circuit ?" He certainly believed the judges' expenses should be paid. (A Voice: "Then why are not the expenses of men sitting on juries paid ?") Because they did not go on circuit. (Laughter.) 10. " Will you vote against al pensions ?" No. There were members of Mr. Gladstone's late Government receiving pensions at the present time. 11. " Will you give County Councils full control of the police ?" No. He thought the present arrangement worked very well. 12. "Will you bring in a bill allowing a person appealing against income tax to be represented by a solicitor, and one making it a penal offence for income tax commissioners to assess a person for more than his income, and for the income tax to be abolished on foreign securities ?" He would not bring in a Bill, but he should support it. 13. " Will you votel for all magistrates to be appointed by the County Council." He thought the present arrangement worked satisfactorily.
MR. DEACON'-§-CANDIDATU RE. UPROAR AT HALEWOOD.

-- -- A Liberal meeting was held on Saturday evening in the National Schools,lialewood,in support of the candidature of Mr. Henry Wade Deacon. The majority of those present were Tories. Although the candidate himself was quietly listened to while delivering a short address, the speakers who followed were constantly interrupted. Mr. Gladstone's name was on each occasion it was mentioned received with groans and general uproar, which completely drowned the applause. Cheers were given for the Tory leaders and the Tory candidate for the division. The speakers could not obtain a hearing, and an elector present rose to pro- pose, as an amendment, a v.te of confidence in Mr. Gilliat, the Tory candidate, but the chairman would not put it to the meeting, as there had been no proposition. Subsequently, it was attempted to put a motion to the meeting in favour of Mr. Gilliat, but the Liberal can- didate left the platform, and the meeting broke up in confusion.

H selected his text from Philippians i. 27, and gave as the literal translation "as citizens act worthily of the Gospel of Christ." As citizens, he said, they ought to take a pride in ail their nation's doings, and feel an intense desire for its welfare. A man who was incapable of that was incapable of all noble affections. They who refused to take an interest in the affairs of their country were cowards and traitors. For what did it mean when christians abstained from voting, and left the Government in the hands of un-christian citizens ? It meant that vital questions were not settled by the stunt of Christ, but by the spirit of individual interest. The nation was marching, on towards some higher social reconstruction, and if men could not get the socialism of Jesus Christ, they must get the socialism of the Devil. They must, as citizens, act worthily of the Gospel of Christ. It was their solemn duty to God and to their fellow-men to vote on the side of truth and equity. It was as much a religious duty as attending divine service ; aye, even as saying their own prayers. They should act, as citizens, worthily, of the Gospel of Christ, and help, by their vote at the election, to pro- claim the neiv era—declare that what was morally wrong could never be politically wrong—declare a crusade against drunkenness,profligacy, and gambling; say that no man should he allowed to thrive upon the vices, wickedness, and temptations of Is fellow-men' • and thus they would help to bring in a brighter and better England—a nation whose foundations rested upon truth, righteousness, and equity, MR.
