EN UTSFO RD DI VISION ELECTION.
THE PO LLI NG.

-Tha contest for the election of a member to repre- sent the Snutsford Division of Cheshire in Parlia- ment took place on Monday, the candidates being the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton (Conservative) and Mr. Alexander Mere Latham (Liberal). The appearance of the fine weather caused some appre- hension on the Liberal side as to whether the agricultural voters would be able to leave the fields to record their votes, especially as farmers have experienced such bad times, atmospherically, of late. On Saturday evening, final meetings were held by both parties in the division, and at Knots- ford the Conservatives occupied the Town Hall, and the Liberals held a moss sleeting on the Heath- side. On Monday morning the polling commenced at eight o'clock precitely,and the Liberals claimed that the first vote at Knutsford was cast in their favour. The Liberals also claimed to have had the last vote recorded in their favour at linutsford. On the conclus- ion of the poll, Mr. J. .1. Howitt, from the front of the Liberal Committee-rooms, in Brook-street, addressed a few words to a large number of Liberal:, who responded with loud cheers for Mr. Latham, especially cheering when Mr. Hewitt said that they hoped for a representa- tive for Knutsford, and not for Tattoo.

GR&PPENHALL POLLING DISTRICT. Grappenhall polling district includes the townships of Appleton-with-Hull, Gtappenhall, and Latchford, and there are on the register considerably over 600 voters. Polling commenced early, and continued steadily throughout the morning. Both parties brought a large number of vehicles into use, but there was very little use but there wae very little display in the shape of colours. In the afternoon the proceedings became more lively, and the work of bringing up voters to the polling booth at the Parish Schools was very largely increased. The villave presented quite a lively appearance, there being much interest manifested in the contest by those who came from the adjoining townships to record their votes. The workmen from the Wilderspool Brewery, who form a large proportion of the voters, polled in large numbers in the afternoon and evening, and it was expected that there vould be a heavy poll. The presiding officers were Mr. R. R. Ashworth and Mr. Speakman.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT WIDNES.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT WIDNES.

The last public meeting of Liberals of Widnes, before the poll, was held in Widnes Drill Hall, on Tuesday night. The building was crowded in every , part and the audience displayed the greatest en- thusiasm. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P , presided, and besides the candidate and Mr. J. Herbert Lewis, M. , P., for Flint, there were on the platform : Miss ' Carrie Deacon, Miss Hilda Deacon, Mrs. Shores, Miss Shores, Major Wareing, Messrs. T. S. Timmis, F. H. Pankhurst, F. .J. Poole, F. Hartland, S. Sadler, S. Owens, J. Tilley, T. Baxter' F. Ankers, T. Cosier Dr. O'Keeffe, J. Whitfield, T. Ormerod, J. liaise% J. F. Allen, J. Evans, J. Betney, J. Showan, R. Wilkin- son, J. Latham, 11. B. Shores (agent), &c. The Chairman explained that he was appearini, in the contest rather late in the day, because he had been away and could not return earlier. There was only one thing he could say, and that was he had perfect confidence in their choice of a candidate, a mere suitable man to represent Widnes could not be found (cheers) and it was the duty of the people of Widnes to return Mr. Deacon to Parliament. (Cheers.) Mr. Deacon, who was receivsd with prolonged cheers, and the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow," then , proposed a resolution of cenfidence in Mr. Gladstone I and the leaders of the Liberal party, and expressing the belief that the new Parliament would succeed in passing a measure of Home Rule, which would 11 permanently unite in mutual goodwill the peoples lof Great Britain and Ireland." Mr. Deacon said I it seemed to him that they were more enthusiastic every , time they met in that hall. He was deeply grateful to a large number of ladies and gentlemen who had devot- ed their leisure, their whole comfort in order that the Liberals could gain a victory at this election, and he was delighted to take that opportunity of expressing his thanks in the face of that very large and enthusias- tic ifleeting. (Cheers.) Fie hoped to thank them with a lighter heart on Thursday night. (Cheers.) The Glad- ' stonian majority had begun. (Renewed Cheers.) They had got on the right track and it remained with the electors who bad vet to vote to see to it that the majority was made a large one. He relied upon the men of Widnes to put him in at the head of the poll. It. was there his stronghold lay and he believe] that a great majority of them were going to support him. Dealing with the objections to Home Rulri, Mr. Deacon said the chief reason for objecting was dislike of the Irish, and it was unworthy the consideration of sensible men. A great deal was made of Mr. Goschen's finance, but he had produced his surpluses by reducing the sinking fund. The Tories paraded the fact that they had reduced the duty on tea 2d. a lb. In 1836 the duty on tea was 2s. id. a lb. ; to-day it was 4d. ; it had therefore been reduced by is. 9d. and of that is. 7d. had been taken off by the Liberals and 2d.by the Tories. (Cheers.) There had been a duty of 12s. a cwt. on sugar and the ILiberals had reduced it to nothing so that people could I have cheap sugar. About 50 years ago there were 400 to 500 articles liable to duty, but by the exertions of Mr. Gladstone, backed up by the Liberal party, there were new only a few articles liable to taxation. (Cheers.) In the course of an exposition of his political principles, Mr. Deacon declared himself in favour of Home Rule for Ireland; and the disestablishment and disendow- ment of the Church in Wales, the direct veto, reform of the Registration Laws, one man one vote, large reforms of the Land Laws, leasehold enfranchisement, the taxa- tion of ground values, and improved local government, by the establishment of district and parish councils. In conclusion, lie appealed to the electors whatever might Ibe the issue of the contes,, to maintain order. He I should not like anythiry, to ha poen which would dis grace the fair name. of Widnes. (Cheers.) At the out- set he had said he would fizlit that contest as hard as he could, and hit as straight as he could, but that he would fight in courtesy and good t.seiper and he called upon that meeting to witness that he had kept his pro- mise. (Loud cheers.) The resolution wss seconded by Mr. Titnmis, and sup- ported by Mr. Lewis', M.P.,and' carried and the Meeting term Matt= d.

div.head: RESULT OF THE POLL.
div.p: RESULT OF THE POLL.

iThe last box arrived at 11.30 on Monday evening, and counting was commenced at 9.30 on Tuf_•sdav morning. Mr. J. Cullimore, the Under Sheriff, presided. Both candidates were present with their agents, as were a number of prominent local politicians. The poll was declared by the Under Sheriff at 12.15, and the result was found to be as follows :
Hon. ALAN EGERTON (C) Mr. LATHAM (L) 2,792 Majority CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT STOCKTON HEATH.

A meeting in support of the candidature of the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton was held in the Church Schools, Stockton Heath, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. T. J. Down presided, and there was a good attendance. Those on the platform included : The Hon. A. de Tatton Eger- ton, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M.P., Mr. J. Charlton Parr, Mr. R. Davies, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, Mr. 1.. Wright' Mr. Henry Greenall, Mr. L. Layland, Mr. H. Layland, I and Mr. H. Houghton. The Chairman concluded an address by reading a let- ter from Mr. Long expressing his sympathy with he cause of the Union, and urging the meeting to do their part in rejecting Mr: Gladstone's Home Rule scheme, by I supporting Mr. Egerben's candidature. ' The Hon. A. de Tatton Egerton, who met with a cor- dial reception, said Home Rule was the question before them, and there was no other question on which the electors had been asked for their vote. Mr. Gladstone's policy might be described thus: "Shut your eyes, open your mouth, and then you will see what I'll give you." (Laughter and applause.) ' Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., criticized a speech made by Mr. John Crosfield on the previous Thursday evening in support of the candidature of Mr. A. M. Latham (Liberal.) He said Mr. Crosfield had stated that "the Tory press candidates would persist in telling a lot of untruths. It was a disagreeable thing to say, but if he gave it the proper English word he should say " lies. He (Mr. Pierpoint) did not like that word. they. the Conserva- tives, said if they wanted to look for misstatements of fact they could not do better than refer them to the speeches made by their opponents in that division, and the speech/ of their great leader in Midlothian. (Hear, hear, and analauce.) He had the honour to represent the borough of Warrington—(cheers)—and was naturally somewhat jealous of its honour. Mr. Crosfield sai4 "lie knew the influence in Warrington of the beer barrel." He assumed that that meant the Tory party got the best Or it in Warrington through supplying the people with beer. He had been connected with the Tory party in Warrington for a considerable number of years, and he said it was absolutely untrue that they even tried to in- fluence the electorate in such a way. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Mr. Crosfield further said "it was a consti- tuency that was not fought straight and square." He (the speaker) had been intimately connected with the Conservative party, and he was chairman of that party some years ago. He was now a member of that party, ' and he had just recently been elected as the member for the borough. (Applause.) It was not for him to argue the case for his political opponents. Let them establish it if they could. He made no accusations, but they on. their side had fought the matter perfectly fair and square Mr. Crosfield went on to say that "the Tories were try- ing to frighten the voters in the agricultural districts by telling that their votes would be known." He (Mr. Pierpoint) did not know of any such case, and he did not believe it. (Hear, hear.) The only notice that they knew of being put up in the works at Warrington was at the Dallam works, according to the ordess of the managing director, and it was a simple statement that the men were free to use their votes as their conscience dictated. (Cheers.) Mr. Pierpoint concluded by mov- ing a resolutien expressing confidence in Mr. Egerton. (Cheers.) The Cnairmln (Mr. I) )wo), referring t 9 the statemen about beer barrels, said he wished to nail the lie to the counter. They (Messrs. Greenall and Co.) had done , nothing to assist Mr. Pierpoint's candidature except to lend him a few horses and men to take his voters to the poll. He had never known of a single case where 1 beer was used to drive men to the poll. Messrs. Greenall had in thier employ men of all shades 11 of political opinion, and he could say that not one of them had been coerced or influenced to vote in a par- ticular direction. He had known Sir Gilbert Greenall for a long time, and nobody detested such practices more stronly than he did. (Applause.) Ile vrag quite certain that he would rather have lost any of his elec- tions than be sent to Parliament by any such bribery or corruption. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Robert Davies asked was it likely that they would give beer away, when they knew that one glass of ale under the Corrupt Practices Act would have lost them the election. He pointed out that the Liberal Club was by no means a teetotal establishment, and that the Right Hon. James Stansfeld, whom the Liberals got to finish their campaign, was a brewer. (Laughter.) He also found from the daily papers that a number of gentlemen connected with the drink traffic had been returned as members of the party of temperance. (Laughter and applause.)
MR. JOHN RIGBY, M.P., OF RUNCORN.

An election of especial interest to Runcornians was that decided in Forfarshire on Monday, when Mr. John Rigby, Q.C., the Liberal candidate, defeated Mr. J. W. Barclay, Unionist, by 866 votes. This was a gratifying Liberal gain, Mil. Barclay at the 1886 election having been returned by a majority of 407 votes over Mr. D. C. Guthrie. Mr. Right% who is described as of 76, Jermyn-street, S.W., and 11 New-square, Lincoln's Inn, second son of Mr, Thomas Rigby, late of Runcorn, Cheshire, by Elizabeth, daughter of Mr. Joseph Kendall, late of Liverpool. Born 1834, educated at Liverpool College and Trinity College, Cambridge (8.A., second wrangler and second Stnith'S prizeman 1856. M.A., 1859), Fellow of Trinity College from 1858 to 1666. Called to the Bar at Lincoln's Inn 1860, Q.C. 1881. Bencher of h's Inn 1884, junior equity counsel to the Treasury 1875 to 1881. M.P. Wisbech division Cambridgeshire, 1885-8. unsuccessful candidate , 1886. It is popularly understood that Mr. Rigby was 'born in the Old Bridgewater Arms, Percival-lane, and he comes of an old Runcorn family. His success gave great delight to the inhabitants of his native place. In a , special article on Mr. Rigby under the head of " Our Public Men" the London "Daily News," says --" The new member for Forfarshire would be the acknowledged leader of the Chancery Bar if his position were not dis- puted by Sir Horace Davey. When he first came for ward as a candidate for Forfarshire, and organ of the cultivated classed in Scotland described him as on the look-out for a County Court. Mr. ,Bia.by, it need hardly be said, would consider himself insulted by the offer of a puisue judgeship, and would probably disdain even a seat in the Court of Appeal. There are those who place him above Sir Horace Davey as a lawyer; believ- ing that if less ingenious, he is more sound. Mr. Rigby's massive and powerful underst tria int; can cope succes- fully with any problem presented by the intricacies of equitable jurisprudence. His practice is enormens, and it is a practice of the most lucrative kind. The House of 'Lords and the Privy Council are his favourite hunt- ing-grounds. There never .was a man of more genuine grit, more entirely free frntn alfectatiori and pretence, more thoroughly capable, of holding his own in any, circumstances against all comers.

div.p: THE A.LT itiNgifAxt DIVISION.

The pollingiii the Altrincham Division of Cheshire took place on IVednesday. The Liberal candidate, Mr. Isaac Saunders Leadam, had at previous elections made gallant efforts to wrest the seat from the grasp of the Tories. He opposed the late Mr. J. Brooks in 1635, but a as defeated, and on thatgentleman's death in 1883,he again fought the battle of the Liberal party against Sir W. C. Brooks. Territorial influence was, as•before, too strong for him, though he brought the majority by which Mr. Brooks defeated him—namely, 725—down to 583. At the general election which followed a few months later Sir W. C. Brooks was returned unopposed; but, nothing daunted, Mr. Leadam, at the request of the Liberal party in the division, again consented to contest the seat in their behalf at the present general election. Ile laboured incessantly in the cause of Libe- ralism, and his able and eloquent advocacy of Liberal principles, his skill as a debater, and the manly and straightforward course which he has at all times pursued made him extremely popu- lar in the division. His opponent was Mr. Con- inr,sby Disraeli, a nephew of the late Lord Beaconsfield. Both parties made strenuous efforts tl secure the victory, and throughout the contest innumerable meetings were held. At one of these Mr. A. J. Balfour was prevailed npon to come and plead the cadge of Mr. Disraeli. An amazing quantity of literature was posted upon the walls throughent the division, and the expenditure in printer's ink will form a considerable item in the candid- ate's expenses. The polling places were at Adswood, Altrincham, Carrington, Cheadle village, Dunham Massey, Etchells in Stockport, Hale, Hazle Grove, Hand- forth, Lymm, Northenden, Rostherne, Sale, Stockport, and Timperley. The electorate numbered 12,127, as against 10,497 in 1886. At the close of the poll the ballot boxes were conveyed to the Literary Institute at Altrincham, where the votes were counted, the result being declared as follows C. Disraeli, C • I. S. Leadam, L 5,258
Majority No change.

Majority 1886 : Sir \V. B. Brooks, C, unopposed. LIBERAL MEETINGS AT LYMM.

An open-air meeting in support of the Liberal candi- date, Mr. Leadam, was held at the Cross, Lyinm, on Saturday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. R. Allen, and there was a good attendance, which in- cluded Mr. P. D. Kenny (County Mayo), and Mr. J. Worthington (Wigan).—The Chairman said if they sent Mr. Leadham to Parliament, he would support the " Grand Old Man" in promoting legislation which would be for the benefit of the English and Irish people. —Mr. Worthington, who was greeted with " Three cheers for for the Ince Division," said he had to move that Mr. Leadam enjoyed the confidence of the meet- ing, and that they would do all they could to secure his return. (Applause.)—Mr. Martin seconded the motion, and contended that the men who called themselves Unionists were not honest and consistent men. (Applause) Another Liberal meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Leadham, was held on Monday evening, in the Congregational Schoolroom, Lyrnin. There was a large attendance, and the meeting was addressed by the Chair- man and Mr. W. 11. Holland. I resolution expressing confidence in Mr. Gladstone, and pledging the meeting to support Mr. Leadain, was carried unanimously.

div.head: 111 E NONCONFORMISTS IN IRELAND.
div.p: 111 E NONCONFORMISTS IN IRELAND.
IMPORTANT LETTER TO A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN. Mr. B. Crosby. of Victoria-road, Runcorn, has received the following letter from a Presbyterian minister in Ireland :

Hyde Park Manse, Belfast, July 6th 1892. Dear Sir,— In reply to your enquiries with regard to the probable value of the protest, moiled three years ago, by the non- Episcopal ministers of Ireland, as an indication of the present attitude of many of them towards the Liberal policy of Home Rule for Ireland, I should say it does not amount to much. In proof of this statement I appeal to the fact, that a very persistent attempt was made some months ago, to get the signatures renewed to another protest of a similar kind, but, the result of this effort has not, so far as I am aware, been made known.

In all fairness, when Mr. Gladstone called for the signatures of those ministers in Ireland, who were op- posed to his policy, the names recently procured should have been given, and not those obtained three years ago. We are told, indeed, that more than 6,000 ministers and elders, and officebearcrs of Irish non-Episcopal churches have signed the new protest, and doubtless the statement is perfectly true. When we consider how- ever, that in the Presbyterian Church of Ireland alone not to speak of Congregationalists and Methodists, there are no fewer than 10,526 ministers and elders and dea- cons, the result does not indicate a very strong and uncompromising attitude towards the policy that would give Ireland the right to govern itself, subject to Im- perial control. In short, I do believe that there is a large and respectable minority of our ministers, that is to say of the ministers of the Irish Presbyterian Church, who could hot now be induced to sign a protest of any kind, rhatsoever that might have the effect of hindering ; or embarrassing Mr. Gladstone in his attempt to do full justice to Irelaud. Of course you will be told that this : minority does not contain any of the old or wise or great ' men of the Church. Were Iso disposed, [might furnish some reasons for rejecting such a complacent theory. I shsll not, however, waste your time and my own by dwelling on this a.spect of the subject. lam quite con- tent to accept the position, not only that all the wise and great men of the Church are on the other side. but also that all who are on the other side are superlatively wise and great. All I venture to assert On behalf of mv;elf and the respectable minority of my brethren who think with me, is that we possess average intelligence and claim to be honest.

div.head: I am, Sir, Faithfully and sincerely Fours J. D. CRAIG HOUSTON.
div.p: I am, Sir, Faithfully and sincerely Fours J. D. CRAIG HOUSTON.
Benjamin Crosby, Esq.
IMPOSING FUNERAL OF A RUNCORN

FOOTBALLER. . One of the most imposing funerals that has been seen in Runcorn for many years past, took place in Runcorn Cemetery, on Sunday afternoon. Mr. T.li. Davies was one of the young men who had helped to make the name of Runcorn famous in the foot- ball world, and his name was a household word where- , : ever an interest was taken in the winter pastime, as , played under the Rugby rules. But in addition to the fame be achieved as a football player, he was respected and esteemed for his own personal worth by all who knew him, and the committal of his remains to the grave was made the occasion of a great public display of regret at his untimely end. The funeral cortege con- sisted of no fewer than 400 people, representing all sorts and conditions of men. In front walked about 100 members of the Rose of Sharon Lodge of the G. P.O. of Oddfellows, wearing black sashes, and following were a large number of friends and admirers. There were representatives of the Widnes and Runcorn Football Clubs. The former were Messrs. F. Young, J. EL Smith, F. Smith, T. Laws, T.Showan,R.Wright, George Wright, Gordon. and Thompson. The Runcorn Club Was repre- sented by Mr. P. Speakinan. C.C.,the president; Messrs. A. Jordan, J. Stokes, W. Shore' and W. M. Sowerby, vice-presidents ; with Messrs. .1. E. Longshaw (sec.) and Mr. C. rownall (trea.), and the members of the committee. Immediately in front of.- the coffin marched Mill Brow Brass Band (conductor, Mr. Outhe- , waite) playing the Dead March in Saul. The bearers were the following members of • the Runcorn team:— Messrs. W. Faulkner, D. Massey, G. Lee, W. Cawley, J. 11. Crompton (captain), S. Abrams, I'. Riley, S. Hough- ton, H. Hughes Hate captain), R. Dolan, A. Rampson, and W. E. Evans. The rear was brought no by rela- tives and their friends. The mournful procession as it slowly wended its way through the town from MI Brow to the cemetery; was witnessed he thousands of people who lined the streets on both sides and a -Jarge crowd had assembled at the cemetery to see the last sad rites perform- (1. The. cfficiating minister was the Rev. S. Hanby„ who delivered an address to those around. Mr. Massey read the funeral service of the order of Odd- fellows, and then at the request of Mr. • Speakman, the assembly'sang the hymn commencing " Jesu, lover of my soul." There were placed on the grave a number of flaral offerings, contributed by Runcorn Football Club Committee, the: fellow workers of the deceased at the United Alkali Works, Runcorn, Mr. and Mrs. P Sp( ak- man, Mr. George Shone, Mr. Millinger, Mr. Harrison (Bates Bridge), and the members of the family. The deceased Who had only attained the age of 25 years. leaves a widow and two children to mourn his loss, and as he had been unable to make any provision for them, it is expected that several matches fir their benefit wilt be played.

CATALOGUES FREE BY POST. Messrs. F. WILKINSON AND CO.'S Curtain Factory, the Anglo-Scotian Mills, Peeston, near Nottinyham, of which we gave several illustrations and an extended notice in our last Autumn Number, was distroyed by fire at an early hour on Saturday, the 30th ult. The estimated damage amounts to £lOO.OOO, which is partly covered by insurance. The fire is said to have been caused by the flame of a candle, which a workman was holding, lighting the cotton on a frame as he was adjusting the threads. Owing to the inflammable nature of the stock, the flames spread with great rapidity, and not- withstanding the efforts of the brigades, the whole of the five- storeyed wing was soon alight, and was rapidly reduced to ruins. An enormous stock of lace curtains, curtain machinery, and an entire lithographic plant were contained in the building. Some adjacent property caught fire, and was with difficulty saved. Several hundred hands will be for a time thrown out of employment. Exactly six years prev- iously to the day Messrs. Wilkinson's Beeston factory was the scene of a similar conflagration. It was then that the Borrowish Mill was secured, and this, with the old Chilwell Mill, are both running to their fullest extent. Messrs. Wilkinson, although greatly inconvenienced by the fire, will be in a position to lid their customers' orders. THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JULY 16, 1892.
Mr. Gladstone's THE last of the speeches which _ _ -.last
Mr. GLADSTONE has delivered dur-

Appeal. ing his Midlothian Campaign was made at Penicuik, on Monday. It was so powerful in statement, so close in reasoning and so lofty in tone tilt it must certainly rank as one of his finest efforts. The London "Times" has been lending itself by means of its correspondence to criticism of the great Liberal leader as unfit to govern this country because of his advanced age, but the criticism not only falls fiat, but looks ridiculous in view of a series of speeches which show that "the old man eloquent" is not only intellectually alert and strong, but still stands head and shoulders above all competitors. How fully alive he is to the signs of the times was shown by his reference, in the first portion of the speech, to the fact that, apart from Home Rule, labour problems, taken in the aggregate, have become the main problems for the atten- tion of statesmen and Parliament. This growing factor in politics is one that will require mor(7s at- tention from aspirant 3 to Parliamentary honours than it has hitherto received. The difficulty at present is that the workers themselves are not in agreement as to the best course to tako ; and, until there is something like unaniMity amongst I them, Parliament will find it difficult if not danger- ous to take action. With regard to the mining class, Mr. GLADSTONE intimated that he thought the question of the .hours of labour might be determined on some such principle of local option as is advocated in connection with the temper- ance movement. The experiment if it is to be tried could not be tried in a better way. The opinion may be said to become general that eight hours per day is quite long enough to work under ground; but while one section of miners is in favour of Government regulation the other section prefers that the issue should be settled as between employer and employed. Mr. GLADSTONE'S sug- gestion, if carried out, would be in the nature of a compromise which would be sufficiently flexible to meet the wishes probably of both parties, mid, it might be, of the employers also. It would cer- tainly be a curious turn of fortune's wheel if it should happen that the principle of local option should in the first instance be applied to Labour rather than to Liquor. The Tories, with an audacious disregard for facts, have been trying to take credit for their finance, at the same time posing, for once, as the party of peace. But Mr. GLADSTONE has by per- tinent words and figures utterly shattered their pretensions. It is true that after the Liberals came into office in 1880, they were compelled to enter into various military enterprises; but,as Mr. GLADSTONE points out—" Every one of them with- out exception was to honourably redeem engage- ments that our Tory predecessors had entered into, or else to remove the difficulties which they had created." This was the case with Afghanistan, with the Transvaal, with Egypt, and with the help given to Montenegro and Greece under the treaty of Berlin. For the Tories to re- proach the Liberals with their troubles in these matters is therefore about as ungener- ous and as impudent as it would be for

the spendthrift son to taunt the father in his efforts to settle that son's muddlovli affairs. As to the Tory Government the affairs were settled; they came into office in 1886 with a cleansheet. Thanks to Mr. GLADSTONE'S management of home and foreign affairs,they have had a straight course; and yet they have actually spent more in what they call their time of peace than. Mr. GLApsTosz. spent in his time of war! Thus : " The total expenditure of the Tory Government was 563 millions sterling. The total expenditure of the. Liberal Government was 516 millions sterling.r A balance of 47 millions to the bad in six years as compared with six years of Liberal Government is certainly not a thing to boast of. Limiting the oomparison to military matters alone, it is still found to tell against the Tory party, for while the total war charge of six years of Liberal Govern- ment was 177 millions, the total war charge of the present Government for a like period is 199 mil- lions. And still the nation is asked to admire Mr. GOSCHEN'S finance!

As regards the question of disestablishment in Scotland, which is exciting considerable attention amongst the electors across the border, Mr. GLADSTONE adheres to the principle laid down originally by Lord HAIRTINGTON, namely, that it is a matter which should be left to the people of Scotland themselves. This means that when the voice of Scotland is heard with clearness and something like unanimity, it will become the duty of Parliament to listen to and to give effect to that voice. Another subject which, to the 'edit of Scotland, has not boon disregarded as it has in England is the opium trade and its attend- . ant evils. If the people of this Kingdom could only be made to realise the mischief that is done by the Government connection with the opium trade of India, they would demand its im- mediate restriction, if not entire abolition. Mr. GLADSTONE is definite in his views, for he said that—" subject to the obligations of good faith, I shall be most delighted to see, and even if I can, to forward any measure within the bounds of reason for limiting that connection and bringing it, if it can be done, altogether to an end." The great statesman next proceeded, to doal with the Irish question ; and examined it in relation to six points of good government. Defining these points, he said :

“The first question is, is the present arrange' between Great Britain and Ireland, a convenient method of carrying on the government of that country ? The second question is, is it a. method that contributes to our good fame as a nation third is, does it contribute to public economy, is A cheap? A cheap article is not a! ways jt good article, but still no article ought to be loaded with an unnecessary dearness. The fourth question is. does it cause and breed content? The fifth ques- tion is, does ie create national strength and the sixth question is—is it consistent with common honesty ?” Mr. GLA.DE3TONE showed most conclusively that negative answer must be given to each question ;. and urged the electors to rise to the height of the occasion in seeking to remedy this bad state of things,. by giving Ireland the management of her own aflairs in a Parliament of her own. His appeal will not be in vain. The Liberals are novi assured of a majority, and the Grand Old Man will once more be Prime Minister of England.

THE Liberals have failed in their Local Elections. efforts to gain a seat in the three Divisions of Newton, Knutsford, and Widnes; but they have at least done their duty in making a stronnons effort to advance their principles ;.for, with apologies to Tennyson, it may truly be said that— 'Tis better to have fought and lost, Than never to have fought at all. It seemed at one time as if two of the sitting members were to have a " walk over;" and it was only at the eleventh hour that Mr. LATHAN was brought into the field to try conclusions with Mr. EGVEETON. He rode a gallant fight, and, by his numerous meetings and instructive speeches, he at least succeeded in promulgating Liberal principles in quarters unaccustomed to anything of the kind. And so with Mr. NEILL, in the Newton Division. He has left nothing undone that could be gained by earnest and persistent ad' vocacy of a good cause; but he was handi- capped fm the first by tho fact that regis- tration work had been neglected during the past few years. Here, as elsewhere, the Liberal Union- ists, if not numerous, have been influential ; and by withdrawing themselves and their subscriptions they have seriously weakened the Liberal party. Indeed, in this Division, they were the principal money-finders ; and their going over to the enenlY has been most disastrous. Still, the majority against Mr. NEILL was under 900; amtwith Home Rule out of the way, and the McCorquodales, Gambles, and Pilkingtons working again on the , Liberal side, it is certainly not too much to. expect ' that Newton Division may yet be won for the Liberal party. Widnes has certainly done better than either ' Newton or Knutsford. It is something to have re- c duced the majority by 587; but having made such an advance it is disappointing to still be in a mine,- ' rity of 205. Mr. H. WADErDEACON was an excep- tionally strong candidate for the Liberal party; and he worked long and hard to achieve success. ' He certainly deserved to win; and,, if he can be induced to continue that process of education and conversion of the constituency which he has se well begun, success maybe counted on when he tries again. But even if there were no hope of any of these Divisions returning Liberals at the next . 1 vacancy, we contend that it is the duty of Liberals ' to keep up: their organisation and educate the electors with a view to winning late if not soon As Mr. LEGH himself admitted, after the declare- Con of the poll, it is obvious that other questions besides Home Rule are before the electors; and 1 it is upon the questions that, in the future, the Liberals will gain ground rather than the Tories. Local Option, and the opposition to compensation to brewers, have caused "the trade," during the present contest, to go solid for the Tory party as the supporters of the monopoly and class privileges. But what then? The Liberal party cannot turn back; and, as these issues will, with further dis- cussion, become better understood, the Liberal party will gather strength while the monopolists will be driven to the wall. From all wo can learn the large sums of money which have been spent, in defence of the liquor trade,to say nothing of the free tap which has quietly flowed in so many places —have had much to do with English boroughs Proving less Liberal than was expected. "The trade " has done its worst; and must, if need be, be fought out and out in order that such a reform may be effected as will place the power in licensing matters where it ought to lie, namely, in the hands of the people. And so with "one man one vote," and the taxation of ground rents and mining royalties : we are losing a nura- ber of voters who are personally affected; but, if we show that we have justice on our side, and " keep pegging away," we shall gain two sup- porters where we lose one, and in this way these reforms will be carried out. Besides, there is such a thing as educating the Tories themselves, as

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
We received last week another letter from Mr. J. Dakin on the Railway men's questions to candi- dates ; but, as it reached us "a day after the fair," WO are unable to make room for it.

At present the net Liberal gain is 54, giving Mr. Gladstone a majority of 40. As "Mercutio" said Of his wound—" Tis not so deep as a well, nor so .Wide as a church-door; but 'tis enough; 'twill .serve."

France is improving. She recognises that "Peace hath her victories no less renowned than War"; and, instead of getting up another revolu- tion, she is preparing for an exhibition in 1900. It looks as if the Republic was established. "Vive; la France!"

More money and more timo wanted for the con- atruction of the Ship Canal. It will not be opened this year. nor next ; and how much more money will be required is as yet uncertain. But there is an end of burking or of shirking difficulties. Sir John Harwood speaks out, and, as things are, he is by no means in a despairing mood. The Canal will be completed, but the original cost will be about doubled.

The death of Lord Winmarleigh removes a venerable and respected figura from the stage of life. He played many parts, and he played them well. He may be said to have represented all that Was best in Conservatism ; for he was not adverse to change when, after due inquiry, he was assured that a change would be an improvement. His natural kindneis of heart and courtly manners won him the high regard and esteem of all who had personal intercourse with him.

--- Lord Winmarleigh did much for Warrington; but it is as well to remember in speaking of his benefactions that Warrington did very much more for him. The growth of the town meant the growth of his fortune, for as a ground landlord he secured "the unearned increment" and added riches to riches.

As one of our contemporaries has spoken of him as having given Bank Hall to the Corporation, it should he stated that •he sold the hall and grounds at a fair price, but contributed £3,000 to- wards the Park, the • rest of the money—no less than £o,soo—hclng given by the late Mr. George Crosfield, who still takes rank as Warrington's greatest benefactor. Lord Winmarleigh himself spoke of his contributio.i as being " comparatively small compared to Mr. George Croslield's.” Honour therefore, in just proportion, to whom honour is due.

In another column there will be found the report of the Chief Government Inspector on the Alkali Works of St. Helens and Widnes. It is an interesting document, which sets one • wondering how it is that, with the air more or less poisoned as it is, the inhabitants do not suffer in health as might be expected. Human beings seem to have more power of resistance than vegetation but still, when all is said, impure air is very injurious; and every effort should be made to sweeten both Ut. Helens and Widnes.

-- London suffers from the sulphur produced fret* its coal fires; but its proportion of sulphur is small compared with that of St. Helens. Accord- ing to Mr. Fletcher's report, the sulphur of St. Helens is produced at the rate of 12,000 per square mile as compared with 44 tons in London. It must be that in St. Helens, which is, relatively to London, a smell place, the sulphur gets rapidly away into the comparatively pure air,or life would be intolerable. It is bad enough as it is; and it is to be hoped duo attention will be paid to the recommendations of the Inspector for abating nuisances and purifying the air. --- Dr. Houston, in a letter of thanks to the Press, which will be found in another *column urges the Liberals of Warrington to continue the struggle on behalf of their principles. We believe with him that there is no reason for despondency. The beer interest is powerful, but it is not all-powerful. It has gone completely over to the side of Toryism; and it has done its worst. If the Liberal party be "up and doing with a heart for any fate,' the time will come when Liberalism will triumph in the polling booths of Warrington. -- Last week we printed two letters suggesting that a subscription should be commenced by way of expressing the appreciation which is felt by the Liberals of Warrington for the admirable manner in which Dr. Houston conducted the late contest. The proposal has met with a most hearty response; and measures are being taken to give it practical effect. A contested election means heavy expense, and in Dr. Houston's case the ex- pense has been increased through his not being a resident in Warrington. Councillor H. Roberts has consented to act as treasurer to the Testimonial Fund; and Liberals wishing to contribute may either forward their subscriptions to him, or leave them at the Examiner Office As the object is to let Dr. Houston see that the Liberals of Warring- ton as a party are not ungratpful to him for the splendid service he rendered, it need hardly be said that small as well as largo contributions will be acceptable. Lancashire has done well in the counties if not in the boroughs, and has at last distinguished herself by returning a labour representative in the person of Mr. S. Woods, the new member for the Ince Division. Mr. Woods, like every other labour representative, is a Liberal of more than average ability and intelligence, and he will be a distinct acquisition to the House of Commons. -- Great was the rejoicing at Darwen, on Wednes- day, at the defeat of Lord Cranborne, son of the Prime Minister. Damen is a thoroughly Liberal borough, but the Division is scattered and includes an agricultural district which is essentially Tory. Lord,Cranborne was returned in 1885 by a major- ity of five only; in 1886 his majority was 735 ; but to-day he is in a minority of 214. And that is why the Liberals rejoice greatly. They have never despaired; they have worked hard; and at last they see the fruits of their labours. Now that it is beyond doubt that Ar. Gladstone will have a majority, the Tories are beginning to say that he ought not to attempt a big thing without a big majority. That is the unconstitu- tional doctrine of the Constitutional Party. The Act of Union was carried in one division by a majority of one only ; and it was by a majority of one that the Reform Bill of 1832 was passed.

-- However small Mr. Gladstone's majority, he has a right to work with it if he can. It may come to this, that no member will feel at liberty to be absent from any division of moment without the permission of the Whip. And as to the Home Rule Bill being rejected by the House of Lords, why, instead of resigning not act on the sugges- tion of Mr. T. P. O'Connor? Speaking at Black- burn on Saturday, he said if the Lords threw out the Bill the Irish members would be content to have it sent back to the Lords year after year, Parliament, meanwhile, proceeding with the other reforms in accordance with the Newcastle pro- gramme. Not a bad idea; and it may convi to it.

Party colours in this part of the country vary with each constituency. As a rule, red means Liberal, and blue Tory ; but in the Knutsford Division, the Tories have aprropriated both red and blue, whilst the Liberals have kept to red. In the Northwich Division, the Liberal colours are yellow and blue, which, singular to say, are -colours of the Tory party in Blackburn—the home of the Tory candidate. Mr. Brunner will, of course, win, and Mr. Whiteley will at least have the satisfaction of seeing his Blackburn colours victorious.

DROWNED AT RUNCORN.

The body of a boatman, known by the name of John Jones, was found in the sprinch repairing dock of the Bridgewater Canal, Runcorn, on Sunday morning. About ten p.m. on Saturday, the deceased was seen in an intoxicated condition, and he expressed his intention of going into the town, to the captain of a flat who afterwards heard a splash. He placed no importance on the occurrence, but next morning when Jones was missing, the canal was dragged, and his dead body re- covered. At the inquest, on Tuesday, before Mr. Wor- sley, a verdict of "Found dead" was recorded. The deceased, who had no effects, was a member of the tipper Mersey Watermens' and Porters' Association, and that organisation provided a coffin, &a. ; and had the unfortunate man respectably interred on Thursday.— Shortly after six o'clock, on Thursday morsing, the body of Charles Roberts, aged about 30 years, mate of the schooner Fox, now lying at Weston Point, was found in the Francis Dock, Runcorn. The deceased was last seen by Captain Dunbavaud, of 14, Wellington-st., on Friday morning last week.

When in want ot'a ehasts-S:nd elegant wedding isr birthday present go to PRITCHARD'S, 51, High-st.—Advt. RUNCORN PARISH 'CHURCH DAY SCHOOLS. 'The anniversary services were held on Sunday. In the morning the preacher was the Bishop of Chester, and he delivered his sermon to a very large congregation. He based his discourse on Proverbs xxii, 6, and, referring to the history of the school, said it was put on the basis of free education in 1817 and in July of that year was con- stituted a national school. Although an old school it was still young and vigorous, and there were upon the books to-day the names of 1,017 scholars, of whom 860 were in average attendance. There were no signs of decay and notwithstanding the difficult work, the school was by no means in a weak financial position. It was growing at the present time: it was extending its borders to take in more infants, and increased accom- modation for girls, and his expectation was that those who had the means would give willingly in support of it. Th3y had heard a great deal about undenomina- tional education, but they must cling to their creeds, for if their teachings were taken away there would be nothing but a mangled corpse left. For the sake of their children let them hold fast to the faith delivered to the saints. In the afternoon a flower service was con- ducted by the Vicar, Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, who delivered an interesting address. In the evening the Rev. Canon Dodd of Stretton, occupied the pulpit. The collections realised £lB I2s. sd.

At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday before his honor Judge Ffoulkes, William Mather sued Thomas Clark, of St. Helens, formerly of Runcorn, for 14s. 4d. ; being the amount of money paid into the Benefit Club at the works of the Red Oxide Co. recently removed to St. Helens. Mr. A. Linakar, solicitor, defended the action.—The plaintiff said he was employee! as a labourer at the works until March, when he left owing to the removal of the works to St. Helens. Ma member of the Works Benefit Club he had paid 14s. 4d., and he demanded the repayment of the money but the defend- ant, who was treasurer disputed his claim.—The plaintiff had no witnesses.—Mr. Linaker said when the Club was formed, a meeting of members at which defendant was , present, decided upon a set of rules, which it was intended to have printed, but this had not been done owing to the removal of the works. One of the rules was that if any member left the works before Whitsun- tide in any year, that being the time the dividend was paid, he would not be entitled to receive any money. The works were removed t 3 St. Helens in March, and 1 the plaintiff refusing to go, left the employ of the Com- pany before Whitsuntide and therefore he was not entitled to any benefit.—The defendant and Robert Hoyle and William Cartwright corroborated this statement.— His Honour in giving judgement said the plaintiff had brought no witness to prove that the rules had not been passed by a majority of the members, and he could quite understand that there would have to be arule, in justice, such as the one under consideration. He non-suited the plaintiff without costs.

On Monday evening a fatal accident happened to a youth named Robert Lloyd, aged 18 years, em- ployed at the farm of Mr. Wm. Fairclough, Cause- way Bridges, Burtonwood. It appears that the youth was in charge of a team of horses and cart, and was returning to the hayfield to fetch a load of hay. He was seated on the front of the cart,and when proceeding along the lane the horses took fright. Lloyd immediately jumped from his seat, and in attempting to stop the horses be stumbled and fell, the wheels of the waggon passing over his body, inflicting shocking injuries. When picLed up a few minutes afterwards life was found to be extinct. At the inquest held on Wednesday, a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

The time for argument has evidently passed in the opinion of some of the Tories, who are resorting to miserable personalities, and the concoction of canards against Mr. Brunner and the firm with which he is connected ; and denials and disprovals not- withstanding they are repeated over and over again, Liberals, and tor that matter Tories too, ought to be careful how they receive these baseless assertions.

A KENYON GENTLEMAN BECOMES M.P. FOR LOUGHBOROUGH. - . .

The Liberals in Ket-iiC;;;;i;a-Ch;surrounding dis- trict are very jubilant over the splendid victory which was won by Mr. J. E. Johnson Fergusson, J.P., of Kenyon Hall. Mr. Fergusson was returned for the Loughborough division of Leicestershire in the interests of the Liberals in 1885 by 1,040 votes. In 1886 he again contested the division, but on that occasion was defeated by Mr. E. de Lisle by 135 votes. This time he again contested the seat, and has been able to turn the tables on his opponent by no fewer than 723 votes, a result which has given every satisfaction. The following is the result: J. E. Johnson Fergusson (L), 4,715; E. de Lisle (C), 3,992; majority, 723. TEMPERANCE AT RACE MEETINGS.

And by-the-bye can the doctor tell us what the Salt Union, in which he is so largely interested, has done for the Northwich Division ? It certainly hasn't improved trade. And as to sweating, the doctor's five per cent is earned by far inure sweat- ing than is done a', Wilmington. There the eight hours system is in successful operation, and the wages are the same as when the men worked twelve hour shifts. The men at Wilmington have also a week's holiday each year and their wages paid as though they were working. This does not look very like sweating. There is no harder worked set of men than salt boilers. Will the doctor show his disapproval of sweating by advocating an eight hours day for salt boilers ?

Dr. McDougall should be the last man in the world to mention about anyone not having " a single drop of English blood in his veins." Al- though Mr. Brunner may be of German extraction on the father's side, he was born and bred in the district, and that's more than the doctor can say any way, who even now retains his " foreign" accent, and looks forward to returning across the border to end his days amonghis native mountains. Having all the hatred of " foreign blood," it ts surprising to find the doctorsD !oval a supporter of the " Queen and the rest of the It.iyal family."

Mr. Mond's name may remind ltr. Whiteley of "German sausages and sour krout," but that gentle- man is doing work in the division that does much to smash the Unionist fables, and his speeches will not have less weight because of that coarse re- mark.

This should be a contest en political principles, but an endeavour is being made to win it by all manner of mean, spiteful and lying attacks upon Mr. Brunner's character and upon the conduct of the works of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co. at Winnington. No weapon is too despicable to be used to oust him trom the seat. At the meeting on Wednesday evening, Mr. Brunner replied to his traducers very effectively, and the calumnies can- not well be repeated.

Mr. Whiteley has charged Mr. Brunner with not running straight on the " Sunday Closing Cities- tion." He states that Mr. Brunner, while having expressed himself in favour of Sunday Closing to the Temperance party, has told a deputation of Licensed Victuallers that he was not in favour of Sunday Closing. Mr. Whiteley has the word of" one of the member, of the deputation to this effect." Mr. Brunner denies the allegation in tot°, and his record of votes on the Temperance question gives the canard the lie direct. It is a strange thing that in a county Constituency which adjoins blackburn, a similar charge is brought against the Liberal candid- ate by the Licensed Victuallers, and it is equally devoid of truth. What kind of electioneering is this?

The Tories have during the • North wich election tried to make much political capital out of Cham- berlain's State Aid Pension Scheme. But they have evidently discovered that the workingmen of the constituency are too hard-headed to be taken in by a scheme which offers such a miserable return for the outlay, for now the State Aid Pension is only mentioned in general terms which mean nothing. It wouiff be interesting to learn the averagc num- ber of workingmen who attain to 65 years of age, and would benefit under the scheme.

I came across a member of a trade society the other day, and in a conversation ascertained some of the benefits lie secured by the payment of a shil- lings. week. If on travel in search of employment, there is a donation benefit of 103. per week for 14 weeks ; is. per week for a further 14 weeks, and 4s. per week for a further 24 weeks. There is sick benefit of 10s. per week for 26 weeks, and 6s. per week for a further 20 weeks; and 4s. a week after- wards as long as eickness prevents the member fol- lowing his employment. If a man who has been a member for five years becomes disabled whilst fol- lowing his employment, and cannot follow his trade, he receives £lOO compensation ; if a member over one year and under five years £5O; if a non- free membei under 3ne year £2O. There is also the following snperannuation scale :—lf 25 years a member Gs. per week, 30 years 75., 35 years Bs., 40 years Os., and 45 years 10$. a week. The funeral allowance is £l2 at member's death and .£6 at member's wife's death. Well may Mr. Brunner, at the present time, advise working-men to depend upon their own efforts rather than accept the "miserable scheme " offered for their acceptance. The society under consideration contains many thousand members, and has a splendid reserve fund, and is well able to confer all the benefits enumerated, which are fat beyond any State Aid Pension Scheme yet mooted.

The end of the battle has now come. The polling takes place on Monday, and the day which inter- venes will give an opportunity for quiet thought and consideration. Mr. Brunner has been a con- stant friend and an able and untiring representative of the people of the Northwich Division. In Parliament he has created a record of which any private member might well be proud, and for his arduous and successful labours in passing the Brine Subsidence Act, the ratepayers of the Northwich , and Winsford districts should ever charish grateful memories. But Mr. Brunner is not only a tried and generous friend, he is a politician with a pro- gramme of reform which will be of the utmost benefit to the working classes of this country, and workingmen if they study their own Interests, and are wise will have no difficulty in making a choice between the two candidates. What in common have workingmen with the avowed champion of aristocratic privileges and prejudices, the heredi- tary enemies of those who are the toilers and real wealth producers of the land ? Whatever promises Mr. Whiteley may make, he is asking to be sent to Parliament to support a party whose only object is to retard thq extension of the liberties of the com- mon people, and who have never yet passed a measure for the benefit of the masses unless they have been compelled by an upheaval of feeling they could no longer withstand.

Crewe has shown Northwich an example which must be followed, and if the Liberal party do their duty and work with energy and perseverance until the close of the poll, on Monday night, there is no doubt that Mr. Brinner will again become a member with a magnificent majority, and Mr. Whiteley will be at liberty to return to the com- panionship of those Blackburn Tories of whom it is understood he is the pride and idol.

Mr. Deacon has made a good fight in the Widnes Division. Ile has reduced a Tory majority of 792 to 20.5. The contest proves that the rural districts of the division are most strongly Conservative, but there is good hope that with perseverance and education the seat may yet be won. In Widnes the result is regarded with considerable bitterness, and it is felt that the rejection of Mr. Deacon, who has done so much for the town and district, is most ungrateful.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 16, 1892 GREAT LIBERAL MEETING Al RUNCORN. SPEECHES BY SIR GEORGE TREVELY AN, REV. C. F. AK ED AND MR. BRUNNER.

On Wednesday night Runcorn Public hail was crowded with an audience gathered in support of the candidature of 11Ir. J. T. Brunner, the Liberal candidate and the utmost enthusiasm prevailed, Mr. A. R. Norman presided and on the platform were the Right Hon. Sir George Trevelyan, Rev. C. F. Aked, Rev. ..I. Hanley, Mr. Brunner, Mrs. Brunner, and Misses Brunner ; Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., W. Blagg (Northwich), A. Mond, T. Clegg, E. Marshall, B. I3isbrown, W. Carroll, E. Bellamy, R. H. Posnett, J. Bridgewater, J. D. Jones, J. R. Frith, E. W. Humphreys, W. Handley (agent), &C. The Chairman said he was glad to say that the flowing tide was still with them. They had a net gain of twelve seats that day. (Cheers.) He was proud as an elector in the Northwich Division of Cheshire that they were the first to turn the tide in favour of the question of justice to Ireland. (Cheers.) At the last election they returned Mr. Brunner by a triumphant majority, in favour of Home Rule, and he wanted to know whether it was their intention to alter that verdict. ("No " and cheers.) He hoped they would not be behind Crewe and he did not believe they would if they had fair play. (Hear, hear.) He had heard that they were not to have fair play. (Cheers.) Alluding to Home Rule, the Chairman said the Tory. party boasted that Ireland was at peace under Balfour. That was utter nonsense. There was no doubt that if they continued this great work they had undertaken that victory would crown their cause. (Cheers.) Mr. Wm. Blagg then addressed the meeting. The Rev. C. F. Aked, who had an ovati.m on rising, said it was a great pleasure to assist Mr. Brunner. (Cheers.) They knew the man they were speaking for and the man they were working for. Mr. Brunner was not a stranger ; he was not a carpet bagger coming from the Lord knows where. (Cheers.) His work- people knew him ; they knew what sort of an employer he was. (Cheers.) It was not very much to say that he had been able to make money, but they knew Mr. Brunner had made money honourably, he had used it wisely, and he had ever spent it generously. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner was a man of the people ;he had made his position by the force of his indomitable will, in the strength of his unconquerable industry. He was a man who would represent a working-class constituency fairly and honourably and generously because he knew what the working-man was and what he demanded. (Cheers.) They had to choose too between the repre- sentatives of two great parties. The one party had represented from all generations stupi- dity and cowardice, which represented class in- terests and class prejudices, which represented the determination of the privileged few to tyrannise over the rights and demands of the toiling masses, which represented the spirit of landlord greed and monopoly, which represented that old aristocratic insolent spirit which has through centuries endeavoured to grind workingmen down and to rob him of the wages of his toil. (Cheers.) On the other hand they had a man who was the representative of a party which was identified with the people's hopes, which was pledged to the eman- cipation of the world's heart from the thraldom of the bitter tyranny of man's hate, to plant the banner of British liberty amongst the ruins of class privilege, and the follies of aristocracy and the tyrannies of wealth. (Cheers.) ' The previous speaker could not understand how a workingman could vote Tory. He could if he was drunk (laughter and cheers) and there had been a nreat deal of that sort of voting at that election. (Cheers.) Had they heard anything about free beer and beer a penny a quart,and men with tickets in their hats, telling them which public-house to go to ? He believed that if some of the active, earnest and enthusiastic reli- gious politicians could just sweep one half of the public- houses they might sweep the constituences at election times for Liberalism for morality and for God. (Cheers.) They were told that Mr. Gladstone would not have a majority big enough to give the Irish a Parliament in Dublin. He had got a Majority a great deal bigger than the majority which took the Parliament away from Dublin. (Cheers.) And one had an idea that with his present majority he could sweep away the injustice and inequality of the present system of registration and to I give them one man one vote and one value, and when they had got:that they would show them what o'clock it was. ' (Cheers.) They were going to tackle the land laws and the mining royalties which injuriously affected capital and labour. He who would be free must him- self strike the blow ; and he hoped that they in North- wich Division were going to help to pile up the great majority. They had got a good man, they had got a righteous cause and they were going to send a good man to help their grand old Chief. (Loud cheers.)

Mr. T. Clegg then delivered a speech dealing with : the dis:sstablishment of the Church in Wales, and the broken pledges of the late Government, and urged upon the electors to vote for Mr. Brunner, because of his splendid record in the House of Commcrns, and not for a stranger. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner, who was greeted with great enthusiasm, said their friend the enemy. seemed to be exceedingly short of political argument, and his supporters whom he carried about would rather abuse him than talk ' straight and true. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Whitefey, who at Blackpool said he was coining to Northwich Division to defend the trade of the licensed victuallers, had since declared that he had tee interest in the brewing trade. But he (Mr. Brunner) had seen a letter in a local paper which said he was the son-in-law of a brewer, arid he informed his neighbours of that fact, whereupon Mr. Whiteley and his supporters had been spreading the tale that he (Mr. Brunner) had attacked a lady because he had said Mr. Whiteley was the son-in-law of a brewer. (Shame.) That was throwing dust in the eyes of the electors. He had never in his life attacked a lady nor said anything disrespectful of a lady in public, and he absolutely denied the imputation. All he attacked was the brewer's advocate. (Cheers.) It had been charged aainst him that he was drunk at Davenham the other night. (Loud laughter.) And on the previous day he went in search of a gentleman who had repeated the story, and that gentleman publicly apologised for bay- ing, done to. But was this sort of thing politics ? These were not the sort of arguments he ventured to use be- fore the electors, and he trusted that when Monday came, they would condemn such infamous calumny and , falsehoods. (Cheers.) A hand bill had been circulated stating, that, while he was strongly against coercion in Ireland, he believed in coercion at the the works at Winnington. And this was explained by the statement that when a man entered the service of the firm he was required to join a sick and burial club and pay 4d. a week into its funds. It was perfectly true that it was the rule that every man should Join the , sick and burial club. But the firm did not fix how much they should pay. The men decided how much , they should pay, and how much should be the amount , paid for sickness and burial. And they did not spend all that 4d. a week. They gays £3O a year to Victoria Infirmary at Northwich and they gave handsome sub- scriptions to the Royal Infirmary at Manchester and the Infirmary at Liverpool, and to an Eye and Ear Infirmary. And after all that they lead a surplus at the end of the year which they divided amongst themselves, in the shape of dividend (cheers) and the statement that a man when he left, left money in the club was absolutely untrue. (Cheers.) The man took away all he had put in. Why was there a sur- plus at the end of the year? Because the club did not pay for the doctor ndr medicine, nor for the inspector. Brunner, Mond, and Co. paid for all that for them— (cheers)—at a cost of £6OO a year. (Renewed cheers.) In 1889 Brunner. Mond, and Co. asked their men whether they would have a rise in wages with twelve hours a day or a reduction of wages of ten per cent. with an eight hours day. The result was that the firm gave an eight hours day for shift men, and so satisfac- tory were the results that on the 31st December, of the following year, that was thirteen months afterwards, the firm restored the wages to the old figure and gave for eight hours work twelve hours pay. (Cheers.) The firm had worked trades union hours and paid trades union wages ever since they had begun. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner then referred to trade unionism, and urged the chemical workers to join the Alkali Workers Union, and make it a large and strong union, and then go to the directors of the United Alkali Company, Limited, and prefer before them a respectful request for an eight hours day throughout the alkali trade. (Cheers.) He heard that Mr. Whiteley had made it a matter of com- plaint that Brunner Mond and Cc., had been _ _ . . . . . .

Importing foreign bricks. (Laughter.) That was a strange political argument to use, but as the sub- ject had been introduced he would explain the matter for his benefit. Brunner. Mond and Co., made big dividends because they knew their business, (laughter and cheers) and they always bought as cheap as they could. Now they never bought bricks out of England. because they understood their own business. It was absolutely untrue that they-lever bought a foreign brick since they started in business. They had got some foreign tiles of fireclay of a very peculiar pattern, and they got them from abroad for a very good reason, they could not get them anywhere else but abroad. When they got these tiles they sent a pattern of each to all the large fireclay manufacturers in England, they took a copy of them and for the future Brunner, Mond, and Co., would buy them in England. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner then dealt with political topics upon which he has been previously reported, and in conclusion he said he thanked them from the bottom of his heart for haying placed him in ,the honourable and happy position of being able to serve them during. the past six years. If they would continue him in their service he slibuld be their servant, and tai should believe himself, being their servant, to be the first among them. (Loud cheers.) Sir George Trevelfan, who arrived late, was received with loud and prolonged cheers and the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow." lie said there was no audience deserved better of the Liberals than that he saw before him. Neva; did the Liberal party want a friend more than it did five years ago, and two constituencies which ' Liberals up to the end of time would always regard with gratitude were the constituencies of Spalding and North- wich. (Cheers.) There was an attempt being made at that time to crush Liberalism out of the liousv of Com-

mons and in the couetry—in the House of Commons by listening ill to their speeches, by voting them down in the lobby, and if they did not submit quickly enough, by the closure—and in the country by boycottina. But the Liberal party was a living force to-day, and'. on an evening like that they did not want argument. The time for argument had passed. Speeches made themselves on an evening like that; there was no speech so eloquent as the telegram that he had had placed in his hands, telling him that they had won 13 seats and had only lost one in the course of the day. (Cheers.) And they did not yet know the full tale of victory, even as a general did not know how great his victory was until the cavalry had brought in the guns and prisoners who were captured in the fight. (Cheers.) In one dayon Tuesday, the Tory majority disappeared ; that day it had already been turned into a Lit:Oral r:ajority of 30. (Cheers.) There were people who told them that Mr. Gladstone would require a very great—an enormous—majority to pass Home Rule. That might be the case, but it was only one-half the question. What sort of a majority would the Tories require in order to continue to rule Ireland as it was being ruled at that time? (Cheers.) During the last Parliament they had imprisoned one fourth of the Irish representation. That sort of Government could not be carried out in a free country with Parliamentary institutions unless they had an overwhelming majority. The knell of coercion had been sounded, and without coercion they could not govern Ireland according to the present methods, and that was the great argument for Home Rule. Home Rule was that a majority of the people of Ireland should be allowed to take a part in the adminstration of their own country, and should have the power under the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, of passing Irish laws. That was simply the question Of Home Rule. They were asking nothing for the Irish people they would not give the Scotch likewise. (Cheers.) They ought to manage their own affairs, but at the present time their bills were often voted down by Tories who did not understand the names of the bills, against which they were voting. (" Shame.") It was not the Protestant minority who were in danger in Ireland, it was the Tory minority who were in danger of losing the , unfair monopolias they had so long enjoyed. (Cheers.) After a reference to the immediate need of electoral reform and the payment of members, Sir George Trevelyan mentioned the threat that the House of Lords would obstruct Liberal legislation, and said let the House of Lords look to it. (Cheers.) The business of the eleetws was to 'send members to Parliament to assert the dignity of the people and to stand by their brave old leader in his conflict. (Cheers.) And he would venture to say that if they voted straight on Monday next, that there would stand in their ranks no bolder and more determined defender of the peoples liberties, no man who in private conversation never gave vent to a single word of disloyalty against those sentiments which he uttered on the platform, no man who would stand up more boldly and fearlessly in the face of his mission than Mr. Brunner. their late member, and soon to be their member again. (Loud and continued cheer- ing.) _ _

Ine Rev. David Critchley, of Blackburn, delivered an address, in which he showed that while Mr. Whiteley pretended sympathy with the Nonconformists of North- wich he had none for those at Blackburn, and that he ad in 1.885 canvassed on a Sunday those Irish people who he now described as rebels. (Cheers.) The usual vote of thanks concluded the meeting.
