div.head: SINGULAR DISCOVERY BY BOYS.
div.p: SINGULAR DISCOVERY BY BOYS.

A singular discovery was made at St. Helens on Sunday afternoon. Four lads—named John William Twist, John Whalley, Alfred Twist, and Richard Connolly, all residing in Hanover-street—were walking along Denton's Green-lane when they noticed a woman in a stooping position in one of the fields, some three or four hundred yards away from the road. She appeared to be digging up the soil, and after she had left the spot the lads went there and found a new mound of earth on the edge of a ditch. The lads scraped away the soil, and about a foot from the surface they discovered a bundle, on opening which, the body of a newly-born child was found. The discovery was reported to the police authorities, who took charge of the body. It has since been examined by Dr. Murdoch, of Rainford, and was buried in Rainford churchyard on Monday. No clue has been found as to the woman who so mysteriously buried the child. No inquest is necessary. TIT-BITS " INSURANCR MONEY FOR A RUNCORN

div.head: WIDOW.
div.p: WIDOW.

On Thursday morning, Mrs. Dean, of Oxford-road, Runcorn, was the recipient of a cheque for ..£lOO, on account of the death of her mon, Henry Dean, at Widnes, on the 25th ult. In the current copy of the journal it is stated that " the deceased was hurry- ing home across the railway metals on West Bank estate, and when passing between two waggons, was caught between the buffers and crushed to death. The waggons had been set in motion by shunting operations. The deceased was 33 years of age, and unmarried. He was the sole comfort and support of his widowed mother, who is now 66 years of age, and .in feeble health. From evidence re- ceived, we find that the deceased did not carry a copy of "Tit-Bits" at the time of his death, but that he was a subscriber to the paper through Mr. James Mort, newsagent, Weston, near Runcorn. Mr. Dean had been a regular reader of " Tit-Bits " for the last seven years, and his mother states that he carefully preserved the copies for that period, and was a fre- quent competitor in our competitions. In accordance with the terms of the "Tit-Bits " system of Life Insurance, we have requested the Ocean Accident and Guarantee Insurance Corporation to forward a cheque for £lOO to the next-of-kin of the deceased." Her receipt is appended to the report. RRCOGNITION OF BRAVERY. On Mon lay, at St. Helens Police Court, Chief Constable Woods informed the Bench that about noon on the 3rd June a number of children were playing near the canal bride, close to Messrs. Pilkington's works, when, one of them, named Jobp Thomas Porber, four years of age, fell from the bridge into the water. A young man, named Joseph Burns, saw the occurrence, and immediately dived into the deep, dirty, and muddy water at that spot. He succeeded in rescuing the child, little the worse for its immersion. He (the Chief Constable) reported the circumstances to the Roy al Humane Society, and the Council had awarded a vellum certificate for bravery, signed by the Duke of Argyll. The man Burns was a resident of Bury, but on the day in question was in St. Helens look- ing for work. Though he did not find work he did one good action—that of saving a life. He asked the Mayor to kindly hand the testimonial to Burns. —The Mayor said he had great pleasure in comply- ing with the request. A brave man, he remarked, was a person to be always admired, and he (the Mayor) was almost sorry Burns was not a citizenl of St. Helens. He was a credit to himself and an example to all young fellows. The English people always admired bravery, and Burns had not only been brave, but he had been prompt. Ile would always be able to say that he had saved life, and to save life was one of the best and finest things that any one could possibly do. (Applause.) He then handed the certificate to Burns, who thanked the Mayor. Mr. J. P. Mearns, solicitor, paid the return railway fare of the man Burns, who was said to be in poor circumstances, between Sr. Helens and Bury.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. P. H. Gossage (presided),and there were preteut Messrs. D. Wright, B. Bro am,J. Midwood, R. Cook, G. I Neil, S. Owen. J. Tilley, F. Reyes, J. Taylor, S. Sadler. J. Houghton, h. S. Oppenheim (clerk), S. Hoyle (accountant), Dr. OKeeffe (medical officer), J. Sinclair (surveyor).

div.head: OAS AND WATER.
div.p: OAS AND WATER.

The Gas and Water Committee reported that the illuminating power of the gas during the past month had averaged 17.22 candies. The Engineer had reported to the Committee that the building contract for the Netherley contract was approaching completion. Messrs. Hatboro, Davey, and Co., bad commenced delivering machinery for the engine and pumps. The mean rain- fall for the month had I.een 3.261 inches, and the water in stock was 9.583,895 gallons. The wages required for the Gas and Water Works for the next four weeks was £B5 per week.—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Brown seconded by Mr. Taylor. STREET IMPROVEMENTS.

The Highway Committee reported that Mr. William Owen, architect, Warrington, stated that the contractors for the new Parr's Bank at Simms Cross required the sum of £75 for making the necessary alterations re- quired in the setting back of the corner of the building. The Committee had offered £5O for the proposed im- provement, and Mr. Owen had written accepting this i‘ffer. The Committee recommended that the Surveyor prepare plans and estimates for the sewering, paving, Sze., of the whole of the street lying on the westerly side of Waterloo-road between Church-st. and Hutchinson- at., with a view to notices being served under Section 150 of the Public Health Act. It was further recom- mended upon the request of the owners upon their lg,reeing to pay the cost of the works, that the Board immediately undertake the sewering of the passage in the rear of premises 22. to 68 inclusive in Cromwell-st. The plans k.f two shops in Church-st. for Mr. Joshua Mid wood were approved.— Mr. &idler moved the adop- tion of the minntes, and remarked that the Committee had made a good bargain in regard to the hank.—Mr. Midv.-ood described it as throwing money away.—The minutes were passed without dissent.

HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Health Committee reported that there were three inmates in the Accident Hospital, and two in the Infec- tious Diseases Hospital. The Medical Officer reported that during June there were 109 births and 44- deaths, being at the respective rates of 42-2 and 17.93. The deaths included 19 children under one year, and 5 be- tween one and five. Zymotic diseases caused 4 deaths. Fifteen cases of infectious disease were notified. The Medical Officer added :—" I am glad to be able to state that the township has been almost free from zymotic diseases during the month of June. The death rate is very satisfactory as compared with previous months of the year. It has been reported to me that since my last report two escapes of sulphuretted hydrogen took place, both in the confines of the townships of Widnes and Cuerdley, and both doing some damage to vegetation These escapes took place on the 29th May and 7th June respectively. lam pleased to state that no complaint has been made to me since then of any nuisance from sulphuretted hydrogen, nor have I observed any. The weekly reports from the L.G. Board in regard to the health of Widnes, in comparison 0 most parts of Eng- land, is very satisfactory."—The minutes were passed, on the motion of Mr. Wright.

div.head: FINANCE.-GOOD NEWS.
div.p: FINANCE.-GOOD NEWS.

_ The Finance Committee reported that having regard to the provisions of the Widnes Improvement Act, 1867, with respect to the application of the Gas Works Fund they recommended that as and from the 25th March, 1891, and so long as the Gas Works Fund was sufficient for the purposes of payment of interest and sinking fund of and for gas works loans, and the cost of main- taining the gas works and of carrying the Act, the ccst of public lighting be borne and paid out of the Gas Works Fund and not transferred and charged to the General District Fund (Highway Account) as heretofore. It was further recommended that after the payment of the cost of public lighting in accordance with the pre- ceding recommendation, the baletice of the gas profits be appropriated as follows :--£l,lOO for repayment pf loans; and £5OO to be carried to a depreciation fund in accordance with the provisions of the Improvement Act. The Accountant submitted a statement showing a num- ber of increases which had been made in certain poor rate assessments, and it was recommended that the general district rate be amended as stated, and that notice thereof be served upon the owners and occupiers of the several properties affected. Mr. Miciwood, in moving the adoption of the minutes, referred to the proposed disposal of the gas profits, and said the'Clerk had advised that in leaving the cost of public lighting charged to the Gas Works fund, they would be acting strictly in conformity with the provision of the Widnes Improvement Act, 1867, relating to the disposition of the Gas Works fund. Under these cir- cumstances and having regard to the fact that with gas at the moderate price of 2s. per 1,000, a very large profit was shown, the Committee unanimously came to the !conclusion that it would be only right that the general ' body of ratepayers should be benefited to some cxtent, and they therefore recommended that the practice of transferring the. cost of public lighting to the highway account be departed from. This practically meant that the general body of ratepayers would be relieved to the extent of nearly 2d. in the Z. After dealing with the matter in this manner there would still remain a handsome surplus undispesed of,and it was proposed out of this surplus to re-establish the deprecia- tion fund of £3,000 authorised by the Act of Parliament, by yearly instalments of C5O. which would always be available for reconstruction and repairs of an exceptional character,and so ensure toa greater extent in the future the regularity and equalisation of the profits of the undertaking. Having provided this annual instalment of depreciation fupd, there wonld finally be left a net balance of about £l,lOO, which would be available for redemption of martgages, in addition to the sinkingfund already provided for. The loan capital on gas account which was originally. £513,540 had been reduced by means of the sinking fund and repayments to £46,748, and he trusted the Board would endorse the rreonmii j endations of the Committee. Me new valuation lisl which had ust come out showed an increase of £7,235, and had they known of this some weeks ago,the new rate would have been 2d. in the £ less than it was. However there would be left a balance of £940 to be carried to next year's account.--Mr. Wright suggested that the Gas Committee might abolish meter rents, but Mr. Brown replied that the Act of Parliament would not permit it. The subject should receive consideration.— Mr. Brown also pointed out that the Committee last year spent about £l,OOO in improvements, which was not charged to capital account. The minutes were . adopted.
TEE PROMENADE.

On the recommendation of the General Purposes Com- mittee it was resolved that the tender of Messrs. Roberts Bro., £226 153., for the repair of the Promenade will be accepted. It was stated that the Ship Canal Co. would pay £l5O of this amount.

div.head: BOWER'S BROOK.
div.p: BOWER'S BROOK.

IThe Clerk had reported to the General Purposes Com- mittee, with respect to Bower's Brook, that he had waited upon Mr. Manson, solicitor to the L. Sr N.-W.Ry. Co., and had received an assurance from both that gentleman and Mr. Stephenson, the Engineer to the Co., that the remedial works which the United Alkali Co. proposed should be executed by the L. & N.-W. Ry. Co., would be taken in hand without delay.

div.head: PROPOSED TECHNICAL SCHOOL-GIFT OF SITE.
div.p: THE PROPOSED TECHNICAL SCHOOL-GIFT OF SITE.

IThe minutes of the Technical School and Free Library Committee contained the following.—The Clerk sub- mitted and read letters dated 30th June and Ist July, from Messrs. Rowcliffe, Rawle,and Co., intimating that Madame de Falbe and Captain Gerard Leigh, the trus- tees of the Leigh Estate, had agreed subject to the ap- proval of the Court of Chancary,to accede to his request to give the proposed site for the schools and library, and asking that the plans might be submitted to them for approval by Madame de Falbe and Captain Gerard Leigh previous to the Board's adopting the same. The Sur- veyor submitted and read draft instructions to architects as settled by the Clerk,which were approved.and instruc- tionsgiven to forthwith advertise for competitive designs. The Chairman said it was a very handsome gift, an. he proposed "That the thanks of the Board be tendered to Madame de Falbe and Captain Gerard Leigh, the owners of the Leigh Estate, Widnes, for their very valuable gift of land as a site for the Technical School and Free Public Library, and that the Clerk be directed to send copies of this resolution to Madame de Falbe and Captain Gerard Leigh."—Mr. Midwood seconded. Be had heard the site valued at £2,000 and £1,500, and it would certainly be cheap at £l,OOO. It was a very generous gift.—Mr. Owens suggested that the record of their thanks should take some embellished form, and remarked that he should like to see some other gentleman connected with the town surprise them with a handsome gift.—The Chairman said the thanks would be written on vellum ' paper and made as nice as they could be, and he thought that would be as much as the trustees would care to receive.—The motion was carried.
TELE HORSE AMIIIILAMCE.

Mr. Vero C. Driffield had writton complaining of the delay in taking the horse ambulance to Gaskell Deacon's Works on the occasion of a recent accident, and to obvi- ate this in future, the tender of Mr. J. H. Lee to house and look after the ambulance for £3 3s. a year and 2s. 6d. each journey was accepted.

div.head: WIDNES ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES ELECTION.

The polling for Widnes division took place on Thursday, and the contest was one of the keenest that has taken place since the constituency was formed. Both sides were confident of success, and strained every nerve to achieve the victory. In 1885 and in 1886 Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss was re- turned by large majorities, but almost on the eve of the battle, this gentleman retired through ill-health, and the Conservative party, after meeting with decided re- fusals from influential gentlemen in the district, at last secured as their candidate Mr. .7. Saunders Gilliat, J.P., a Liverpool and London merchant, and a director of the Bank of England, and member for Clapham in the last Parliament. For at least twelve months Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., of Appleton, had been before the electors as the Liberal candidate. Connected with Widnes all his life, and having been a large etnploser of labour, and taken an active part in every good work in the town, both public and private, he was considered to have an admirable chance of wrest- ing the seat from the Tories. Of unimpeachable cara.lter,sterling ability,and sound political convictions, he was highly popular in his native gown, which is the principal place in the division, and had the election depended upon the Widoesians, it would only have been a question of how large his majority would be. The outlying districts, however, are strongly Tory and Mr. Deacon laid siege to these with an ardour and persever- ance.that appeared to have made considerable impres- sion. For the past three weeks meetings had been held in the constituency nightly and the amount of litera- ture circulated was immense, while canvassing was carried out with great persistency. Mr. H. B. Shores acted as agent to Mr. Deacon and Mr. W. T. Husband filled a similar office for Mr. Gilliat. THE POLLING.

IThe register contains the names of 10,354, electors of whom 4,950 reside in Widnes, but after allowing for i duplicates and removals the electorate would not num- ber more than 9,000. The election was conducted by Mr. W. W. Rutherford, of the firm of Miller, Peel, Hughes and Co., solicitors, Liverpool, the Sheriffs agents,and the arrangements were admirably conceived and executed. At Widnes there were two polling dis- tricts, one at Simms Gross, where there was a polling booth at Simms Cross Board School, with six stations ; and a second at West Bank school where there were three stations. During the day both candidates drove through the division, and both were loudly cheered. In the course of the day Mr. J. T. Brunner, Liberal candidate for Northwich, voted for Mr. Deacon at Widnes and in the evening Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, who had come from France specially, recorded his vote at Roby. The contest was god humouredly conducted on both sides, and although Superintendent Keighley had a large force of policemen in reserve, the town was free from disorder and their services were not required. . - .

After the close of the ballot at 8 o'clock the boxes were conveyed to Widnes Town Hall, the last box arriving from Gersten at 9.10 p.m, and the counting was immediately commenced In the Board room. Both candidates watched the counting, and they were repre- sented by the following gentlemen :—For Mr. Deacon : Major Wareing, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. K. Muspratt, F. H. Gossage, E. Carey, F. Gaskell, H. Gaskell, junior, s. Deacon, T. Cosier, W. B. Bowring, F. J. Poole, and 11. B. Shores. For Mr. Gilliat : Major Cross, Alderman J. T. Wood, Messrs. Gilliat, junior, H. Lewis, J. White, A. S. Mather, E. Charles, T. A. Bullough, J. C. Crauford and Mr. Husband. .
By tea o'clock a crowd of 8,000 people had assembled in the square opposite the Town Hall and at 10-25, the returning officer announced the result as follows, amid a scene of the wildest excitement :

GILLIAT . . 3,866 DEACON The announcement was received with mingled cheering and hooting, the latter preponderating. Afterwards in the counting-room Mr. Gilliat proposed a vote of thanks to the returning officer and said it gave him great pleasure to tender his respect and thanks to his oppon- ent for the extremely courteous, and gentlemanly way in which he had conducted that contest. (Hear hear.) Mr. Deacon seconded the motion and reciprocated Mr. Gilliat's kindly words. They had each done their best and they could do no more.—The motion was carried and Mr. Rutherford having replied the proceedings con- cluded. Mr. Deacon went at once to his home, and he was cheered to the echo en route. Mr. Gilliat proceeded to the railway station escorted by pelicemen, and he was followed by a large crowd which alternately cheered and hooted.

div.head: BETHESDA. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH
div.p: BETHESDA. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH

RUNCORN. Partially destroyed by fire in September last year the church has now been restored, and the re- opening services were commenced on Tuesday evening last. The upper portion of the building, a well as the organ, were completely destroyed, and the expense incurred in the renovation was £2OOO, the greater portion of which has been defrayed by the General Fire Insurance Co. The interior of the sacred edifice presents a hiR hI y improved appearance. The roof has been raised 61t. Din., and the ceiling is formed into panels, supported by pitchpine prin- cipals, stained and varnished, and the effect is very fine 'I be gallery has been entirely remodelled. It is circular in shape, and,made of polished pitchpine,adds much to the appearance of the structure. At the chancel end a noble looking stone arch has been erected. Tne ceiling and walls are painted in charming and harmonious tints, and the whole effect is pleasing. The communion is now a raised platform made of pitchpine, and there is a new pulpit of the same material, the joiners' work being of the finest description. The organ chamber is filled with an instrument built by Mr. Monk, of London, and was recommended by Mr. Minshall, organist of the City Temple, London. The instrument is a very powerful one, of the most sweet and excellent tone, and consists of two manuals and radiat- ing pedals containing in all a total of 958 pipes, and with the three couplers, 20 stops. The reopening ser- vices were commenced on Tuesday evening, when the Rev. F. Heber Evans, D.D. chairman of the Congrega- tional Union of England and Wales, who has been described as a prince of preachers, deli vered an eloquent discourse to a large congregation. He took his text from Hebrews ii, 8-9 verses.—On Thursday evening the fortnal opening of the organ took place, when an organ recital was given by Mr. E. Minshall, of the City Temple. The church was well filled by an appreciative audience, who thoroughly enjoyed the rich musical treat provided. Mr. Minslcall's performance included selections from " The Water music," " Elegy and prayer," " Characteristic piece" and " 0 Sanctis- sima," and his auditors was charmed. Mr. Bantock rierpoint, of London, sang the air, "Shall I in Mamre's fertile plains," the song" Nazareth " and " 0 God have mercy.''and his vocalisation was characterised by power, expression,and trinefulners in a very marked degree. Mr R. W. Pierpoint capitally executed the cornet Sole "The Lost Chord." An augmented choir, under ti. • conductorship of Mr. W. Handley, rendered seyerttl, anthems with admirable effect. The audience frk, 4 quently showed their appreciation by applause,and there. were several encores,
FICKLE ENGLISH CLIMATE.

The variable climate of our country often give rise to a variety of ailments and com- plaints, which assuming at first the form of only a slight idisposition, if neglectest and unheeded may bee me the germ of serious diseases. wh.ch will undermine the constitu- Q tion, and finally resulting long and lingering UININE illness, and perhaps terminate fatally. The changeable and unaeasmable weather of the past few months makes it incumbent on all persons to exercise wise and prudent precau- tions to counteract the evil effects which the BlTT- variable weather we have lately experienced ITTERS. may have is on their health and comfort. Already we frequently hear such complaints as '• no appetite," " these frequent head- aches," " this languid feeling," and a dozen other expressions which all point to the urgent need of some tonic. Several tonic mixtures are being offered to the public, but none which have ben so uniformly successful as Gwilym Evans' Quinine Bitters. It has never been known to fail. %._.X WILY M. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
SAVING IT FROM BLOWING DOWN.

. At the Warrington tgiitrates' Court, on Thursday, Thos. O'Neill, shoemaker, lodging at Bailey's lodging- house, was charged with stealing. the previous evening, from the shop door of Wm. Craddock, clothier, Butter- market-st., a lady's veollen jacket, value 6s. 61. Evi- dence was given by P.C. Bell and Robert Robinson, manager for Mr. Craddock. The constable saw the pri- soner with something under his coat coming along Hill- st., and as soon as he saw him he turned back rather hastily. Witness followed and found that what he had under his coat was a cape. The prisoner said he took it to save it from being blown down. There was attached to the cape a hook and a piece of copper wire by which the cape had been attached to the door. The manager identified the cape. The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. SHAMEFUL ATTACK ON A CONSTABLI.—Thomas Pritchard was charged with being drunk drunk and disorderly in Green-st., on Saturday night, also with assaulting m. Jinks, of the Green Man. Jinks did not appear, and the charge of assault was not dealt with. The defendant was fined ss. and costs on the first charge.—John Kelly, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., the same night, 54.—John Longshaw, in Cambria-place, that night, ss. and costs.—Mary Lomax, in Glazebrook-st., on the Ist inst., was dismisssed.— Jane Tickle, in Winwick-st., on the 2nd inst., was dis- missed.—John O'Donnell, in Buttermarket-st., on Sun- day morning, ss.—Thomas Rowley was charged with being drunk and dissrderly at Bridge Foot, on Sunday morning, also with assaulting P.C.'s Clough and Taylor. P.C. Clough said he met the prisoner on the bridge early on Sunday morning, and he asked him where he could get lodgings, and he told him on Friar's-green. He said he would not go there, as he had been there and had paid sixpence and been turned out without being paid back his money. Wit- ness was going with him to see why he was turned out, and the prisoner suddenly struck him.—P.S. Taylor corroborated and said the prisoner attempted to strike him, and kicked him, and striuzgled all the way to the station. Witness hal had some "bother with him on Saturday night.—The prisoner now said that the lodg- ing-house house keeper offered him his money back, and he refused it. He asserted that Clough used his baton on him, but this was denied. _ WIFE ASSAULT.—CbarIes Bancroft, 19 Carlisle-st., was charged with assaulting his wife Eleanor Bancroft, on the 10th inst.—The complainant, who had a black eye, said about a quarter to three on Sunday afternoon, her husband came in for dinner, and before he took off his at said "Has he been here again 2" He had found the gate open, and he was jealous of her father coming to her house. He was 72 years of age. He had not been there that day. The defendant used very bad language about him. She said " Are'nt you ashamed of yourself to talk like that of an old man .72 years of age ?" and he struck her and gave her the black eye. He was drunk at the time.—The defendant said the complainant struck him twice, but he did not.strike her. She got the black eye by accident.—The defendant was ordered to pay the costs, and bound over in Ills own recognizances of £lO and two sureties of £lO each to keep the peace for six months. Cockhedge-lane, was charged by Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., with having in his possession cer- tain wild birds, namely thrushes. contrary to the Act which prohibited this at this time of the year.—The chairman remarked that the law was a peculiar one.— The defendant was fined 3s. 6d. costs.—Hannah Horton 78, Cockhedge-lane, was similarly charged by Mr. Dowty, and was fined 23. 6d. costs. CHARGES OF CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Frank Daniels, 44, Dallam-lane, was charged by Inspector Dowty, with cruelty to a horse by working it while in an unfit state, and Robert Nelson, manager of Arpley Coal Yard, was charged with causing it to be so worked.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defendant. Mr. Dowty said Daniels was driving a lorry full of children to whicn the horse was attached, to St. James's Schools on Walking Day. The horse was in very good condition, but excessively lame, there being great inflammation around the coronet. Witness told Daniels he could drive the children to the field where they were ulti- mately going, but he must take the horse back then. —P.C. Bell said the horse was working in great misery. —Mr. Browne characterised the case as a paltry one.— George Devonport, shoesmith, employed by Mr. Fer- guson, said he shoed the horse two days before Walking Day, and he shoed it too tight in consequence of which it went lame, and the day after he had to loosen the shoe.—Mr. Ferguson, veterinaly surgeon, said at Christ- mas he attended the horse for a roughness in the coronet, and cured it.—The Chairman said Mr. Dowty was quite right in bringing the case, but the Bench thought there was no culpable negligence. The case was therefore dismissed. .

...... CHARGES OF THREATENING.—MORE WOMEN'S ELECTION Rows.—Catherine Gerrard ,13, Hopwood-st.,was charged with threatening Mary Griffiths, 11 Hopwood-st. The complainant fainted in the box just when the case was being commenced, and she was taken out of court, the case having to stand over till her recovery. She said the defendant got hold of her by the hair of the head, and later struck at her with a poker, and threw stones at her, threatening to take her life. —A female witness said the defendant struck the complainant and then got a jug of water and threw it over the complainant's mother and sister. The cause of the row was "the elections."—Two other female witnesses corroborated.—The defendant said the complainant had written on her shutter" 585 Kit" in reference to her having been sent off for 7 days, and sent her granddaughter to kick at her door. .She (the defendant) shouted Houston, as they were shouting Pierpoint.—Mrs. Evans said she saw " these people" write 585 on the defendant's shutter, and the complain- ant said to the defendant "Kit Majority." The defen- dant replied " You should have made your bother 7 day at the time. The election is not to-day." They abused the defendant scandalously. The defendant had no poker, only the baby in her arms.—Mrs. Heaton corroborated.—The defendant said she had had a life like a dog since the election was started. The CRSO was dis- missed.—Mary Peel, Haydock-st„ was charged with threatening Martha Birchall. married woman, 19, Hay- dock-st., on the 11th inst. div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

Secretaries of Cricket Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office. Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

WARRINGTON Y.M.C.A. v. GREENINGS' FITTERS AND TURNERS.—This match was played on the Association's ground on Tuesday evening, and the home side were again victorious, though the margin of runs was reduced by the visitors. The Y.M.C.A. hit up 43, Wright (not out 11) and Jenks (8) being the chief scorers. Crompton bowled in good style for the Association,and the only one able to do anything with him was Forbes, who was top scorer for the Fitters and Turners with six runs, Chad- wick following with 5. The total reached 29, the Y.M.C.A., thus winning by 14 runs.

div.head: DUKE OF CONNAITUHT AND VYRNWY WATER.
div.p: THE DUKE OF CONNAITUHT AND VYRNWY WATER.

The Duke of Connaught on Thursday performed the ceremony of inaugurating the supply of Vyrnwy water to Liverpool by turning on a silver tap attached to a pipe in front of St. George's Hall. His Royal Highness left Newsham House in the morning, and first proceeded to the Seamen's Orphanage, where he unveiled a memorial tablet to the late Mr. James Beazley. After- wards the Prince proceeded by way of Hartington-road to the Royal Hospital—where he opened a new operat- ing theatre—and thence to St. George's Hall to perform the chief function of the day. This duty accomplished, he was entertained by the Mayer at luncheon in the Town Hall, many of the leading citizens being present. After luncheon he left Lime-st., for London._ _ _

- The accident at Fiddler's Ferry, an official report --- announces was made good at an early hour on Thursday morning, and in the course of the day 144 millions gallons of Vyrnwy water flowed in the Prescot reservoir, this being It million gallons in excess of the estimated quantity.

div.head: SHOCKING BOATING FATALITY,
div.p: SHOCKING BOATING FATALITY,

A distressing boating fatality has occurred at Bala Lake. Mr. Geoffrey Hignett, of the firni Of Hignett, Bros., tobacco manufacturers, Liverpool, along with his tutor and Miss Parry, a barmaid at Llangollen, were boating op the lake, when some spectators on the land- ing-stage called attentiom to the fact that the craf: was over-loaded. Shortly afterwards it capsized, and Miss Parry was drowned, the two gentlemen being rescued by onlookers.

div.head: AMERICAN RIOTS.
div.p: THE AMERICAN RIOTS.
12 NON-UNION MINERS MASSACRED.

WASHINGTON, THIIRSDAY.—Senator Dubois, of Idaho, has received a despatch from Boise, Idaho, signed by the Attorney-General of the State, stating that the Governor has proclaimed Shoshone County to be in a state of rebellion. The despatch adds, " Twelve dead non-union miners were found yesterday in the Fourth of July Gulch, having been Massacred on Tuesday."

div.head: Ma. GLADSTONE AND HIS ELECTION.
div.p: Ma. GLADSTONE AND HIS ELECTION.

Mr. Gladstone left Aberdeen at 12.30 on Thursday for Braemar. In the course of a brief interview with the president of the Aberdeen Liberal Association, Mr. Glad- stone said :—The falling off in the Liberal poll was not due to the Irish question, but about 2,000 voters out of 13,000, speaking roughly,voted against me on the Church question under the influence of the strongest and incess- ant exertions of the clergy, applied from the pulpit and otherwise. On the election generally, Mr. Gladstone expressed himself as confident of the final result being in favour of Rome Rule, and he remarked with satisfaction that "the counties were doing their duty."

div.head: DREADFUL EXPLOSION ON GENEVA
div.p: DREADFUL EXPLOSION ON GENEVA
LAKE. LOSS OF 26 LIVES.

A most disastvus boiler explosion occurred about noon on Saturday, on board the saloon steamer Mont Blanc, at Ouchy, on the Lake of Geneva. The steam rushed into the first-class saloon, scaldigg the occu- pants. Nineteen persons were killed and forty injured, thirty-five of them severely. Among the victims are a number of English and French visitors, including women and children. The death roll has reached in all twenty-six. L&IISANNE, WEDNESDAL—After hls examination to- day by the Juge d'lnstruction, the Director of the Lake of Geneva Navigation Company was placed under arrest and lodged in gaol.

By a fire which broke out on Monday, in a jute, flax, and hemp warehouse in Commercial-st., Dundee,damage was caused to the amount of £5,000. Mr. Justice Mathew, who opened the commission for the Carnarvonshire Assizes, at Carnarvon, on Tuesday, was presented with a pair of white gloves, there being no criminal cases and only three civil actions. Intelligence received by way of Vienna is to the effect that Baku has become practically depopulated owing to the outbreak of cholera. The factories are stopped, and only a few persons are left in the place.

div.head: EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, J ULY 16, 1892, WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. I TERRIBLE CATASTROPHE IN THE ALPS. 140 LIVES LOST,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, J ULY 16, 1892, WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. I TERRIBLE CATASTROPHE IN THE ALPS. 140 LIVES LOST,

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. R. Heaton presided, and there were also present Rev. G. P. Roberts, Messrs. Balharry, Davies, Shaw, Pilling, Hood-Wright, llill, Muir, Dobson, Aukland, Dignum, Turton, A. J. Jolley, Ratcliffe, Clarke,W. Houghton. J. Houghton, Nlather, Hibbert, Smith, Longton, A. Jolley, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and other officers.
VILLAGE SWEPT AWAY.

PARIS, TUESDAY.—A telegram from Bonneville, Savoy, announces a serious catastrophe in the Alps, near Cita- mounix, a landslip having occurred in the mountains, above the baths of St. Gervais, 13 miles from Cha- mounix. A large number of houses have been over- whelmed. BONNEVILLE, TUESDAY, FOUR P.M.-ThO disaster at St. Gervais occurred at three o'clock in the morning, when everyone was in bed. The Bionnaray Glacier became detached from Mont 3lanc, and sweeping down the mountain, utterly destroyed the bathing establishment of St. Gervais and the hamlet of Dufayet. All the houses were carried away bodily by the torrent. More than 150 corpses have been recovered from the river Arve, the surface of which is strewn with debris of all kinds.

BONNEVILLE, HAUT SAVOIE.—A later telegram saws— Last night, the large hotel erected at the sulphur springs of St. Gervais, a little off the road leading from Geneva to Chamounix, was reduced to ruin, a neighbouring village was ahnost entirely destroyed, and upwards of 100 lives were lost, through one of those convulsions of nature to which mountainous regions are peculiarly sub- ject. The catastrophe arose in this manner. The lower end of the glacier of Bionnaray became detached from Mont Blahc, and fell into the torrent beneath, carrying away with it the little village of the same name. The masses of ice and the wreck of the village formed a dam, which held up the waters for some time, until they sud- denly broke through tho obstruction, and berst like a cataract into the mountain stream known as the Bon Nant, which flows by St. Gervais lea Rains. The thermal springs, the medicinal virtues of which attract many visitors to the hotel during the year, rise in the wooden ravine of Montjoie, through which the on Nant, or Good Stream, passes on its way to meet the river Arve. The gorge in which the establishment des Bains, erected at an altitude of 2,066 feet above the level of the sea, stands, or rather stood, is narrow, and the hotel consisted of five separate buildings joined to- gether by walls of stone roughly hewn from the moun- tain side. At a quarter-past two this morning, or there- abouts, the people in the hotel were awakened by a terrific noise of rushing water, and the crashing of rocks one against the other. Then a further gust of wind drove through the gorge. The next moment a torrent of water, carrying with it fragments of rock, trees, and debris of all descriptions, hurled itself upon the hotel. Of the five buildings, three were utterly destroyed and another nearly so, while the fifth remained almost un, hurt, owing its safety to its position, which was high above the course of the Bon Nant. Passing down", the valley, the torrent struck the village 60 f he Favet, which was almost entirely demolished. The wreckage of the houses was swept down the stream for miles into the river Arve, on the surface of which corpses and debris of all kinds have been seen floating all through to-day. The number of those who perished still remains uncer- tain. So far, the most trustworthy estimates place the number of dead at 40.

div.head: PADGATE SCHOOLS.
div.p: PADGATE SCHOOLS.

The Schools Committee had passed a resolution that the school band be allowed to go to Martinscroft on the occasion of the Wesleyan School treat on the 26th July. On the motion of Mr. Davies, seconded by Mr. Heaton, the Committee resolved that a vote of thanks be given to the Superintendent and Matron for the neat and clean appearance presented by the Children on Walking Day. The Superintendent of the Schools reported that Walking Day had passed off successfully. Mr. Joseph Houghton placed a field at their disposal, and Mr. Thos. Houghton lent a horse and lurry and man to convey the little ones to Warrington.—The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: REGISTRARSHIP FOR NEWTON AND HATDOCK.
div.p: THE REGISTRARSHIP FOR NEWTON AND HATDOCK.

A letter was read from Haydock Local Board asking the Guardians to appoint a registrar of births and deaths for Haydock, as apart from Newton. It was pointed out that the Haydock district contained a population of 7,000, and that it was found to be an inconvenience, a loss of tim2, and an unnecessary hardship and cost to the ratepayers of the district to have to go to Newton for the purposes of registration. The distance from the lilackbrook end of the township was four and a-half miles, while it was at least three miles from any part of the township. It was also mentioned that owing to the sinking of new pits by Messrs. R. Evans and Co., scores of cottages were being erected, and that the new rail- way which would pass through the district would materially increase the population. Mr. Balharry moved that Haydock form a sub-district and that it have a separate registrar.—Mr. Turton seconded this proposal.—Mr. Hood-Wright did not think it would be I fair to divide the Newton district now that they had advertised for a registrar and had applications sent in. By a division of the district the salary would be considerably reduced.—The Clerk said the only question they had to consider was whether they would recommend the Registrar General to make Haydock a sub-district. The payment of the registrars, he pointed out, was not a fixed salary but by a fee on each case registevd.—Mr. 'HEBERT opposed the dividing of the Newton district,but on a vote being taken Mr. Balliarry's motion was carried by 18 votes.—Mr. 13ALHAERY afterwards proposed that Mr. J. Mathews, the clerk to the Haydock Local Board, be recommended to the Registrar General as the registrar for the Haydock district.—Mr. Hoon WRIGHT and Mr. HIBBERT opposed this proposal on the ground that it looked like a " hole and-corner" business. They thought the appointment ought to be advertised.—The CLERK said that unless they made the appointment now it would pass from them altogethor.—Mr. Balharry's motion was then carried by 16 votes.—There had been 12 applications for the post of registrar for Newton, and these were gone into by the Guardians. Ultimately Mr. T. Bowes, relieving officer for the Newton district, was appointed.

div.head: ALKALI WORKS OF ST. HELENS
div.p: THE ALKALI WORKS OF ST. HELENS
AND WIDNES. GOVERNMENT REPORT.

Mr. Alfred E. Fletcher, the chief inspector under the Alkali, etc., Works Regulation Act, 1881, has just presented his 28th annual report to tbe Local Government Board. We extract the portions bear- ing upon the Alkali Works of St. Helens.

div.head: TANK WASTE OF THE ALKALI WORKS.
div.p: TANK WASTE OF THE ALKALI WORKS.

In dealing with this subject Mr. Fletcher says, "The enormous deposits of this material in Widnes and in other districts where the Leblanc process of soda manu- facture is carried on, still remain as a proof of the indus- try, and we must add, of the ignorance of the past." He then says :—" During the long years that have passed before any practicable method was devised for economi- cally dealing with the tank waste of the Leblanc soda process, the constant nuisance arising from this material has been keenly felt, and it was on all hands acknow- ledged that when any such method should be devised , even if no distinct profit were found to follow its work- ing, it would be incumbent on all manufacturers to adopt it, in the interest of the district round their works. The question therefore arises, should it not now be obligatory on all producers of alkali waste to desulphurise it by the Chance-Claus process or by sonse other method. In section 6, Alkali Act, it is declared that ' Alkali waste shall not be deposited or discharged without the best practicable means being used for effectually preventing any nuisance arising therefrom.' Ihe time seems,there- fore, to have now come when manufacturers of alkali should be called on to desulphurise their waste, and when the depositing of untreated waste should be consi- dered an offence under the Alkali Act. In anticipation of this statement I have written to the directors of the United Alkali Company, who are now the chief pro- ducers of alkali waste, and have received their assur- ance that as to St. Helens the whole of the waste pro- duced there shall be brought under desulphurising treatment within six months, and that of Widnes within twelve months from the commencement of 1892."

div.head: NUISANCE FROM CHEMICAL WORKS.
div.p: NUISANCE FROM CHEMICAL WORKS.

In spite of the continued action of the inspectors under the Alkali Act, and the increased care taken by the manufacturers, it cannot be denied that cause for com- plaint still remains of unpleasant smells, and occasion- ally of injury to vegetation, arising from the districts where chemical works are congregated. The smell of sulphuretted hydrogen has certainly been prevalent in Widnes, and has been carried to a considerable distance by the prevailing winds. In the earlier part of the year that was accounted for the imperfect action of the Chance-Claus sulphur recovery process. There is, how- ever, no discharge of that gas from this source now. When the nature of the nuisance was perceived, prompt steps were taken, and the evil was stayed. Latterly there has been a somewhat increased discharge of this offensive gas from the waste heaps of this district. I have in consequence insisted that, over the defective portions of the banks, a thick layer of inert material shall be spread, and that in future an improved method of laying the waste shall be adopted. It has been arranged that it shall be deposited in successive beds of moderate thickness instead of in embankments twenty to thirty feet high, so that it may be more consolidated with a view to a complete exclusion of the air. When this improved system is carried out I trust the annoyance will in great measure cease, bup it cannot be expected that no unpleasant odour will be perceived, for the drainage must continue, and this liquor will for a long time be a source of discomfort. Unfortunately some of this drainage liquor, charged with sulphides, finds its way into the sewers, where some amount of acid would appear to meet with it,since from some of the gully holes and grids sulphuretted hydrogen is exhaled. This is, however, not in sufficient quantity to be a source of nuisance at a distance, and it may be hoped that now the chief cause of annoyance will be found to have been greatly diminished.

INJURY TO VEGETATION is meat to be feared in thee neighbourhoods of both. Widnes and St. Helens, not from the gas just alluded to, but from the sulphurous acid which proceeds from various sources,principally from the combustion of coal. In both of these places the amount consumed is about 1,000,000 tons annually, and the class chiefly burnt is the mferior.small coal locally termed "slack." This contains more sulphur than is found in the large coal from which it has been screened. There are also copper 'smelting and other works, both at Widnes and St.Helens, the smoke from which is more highly charged with sulphurous acid than is that from the chemical works.

The following calculation has been made to show the amount of acid gas thrown annually into the air of St. Helens. It is nearly all either sulphurous or sulphuric acid. The hydrochloric acid escaping from the chemi• cal works is taken as its equivalent of sulhur acids, and added with the rest. There is then

div.head: ACCOUNT OF AN EYE WITNESS.
div.p: ACCOUNT OF AN EYE WITNESS.

130NSEVILLE (HAUTE SAVOIE), TUESDAT.—One of the visitors at St. Gervais-les-Bains,who was staying in that portion of the hotel which miraculously escaped destruc- tion during the fearful catastrophe, gives the following thrilling account of the disaster. In all about 80 ladies and gentlemen who were taking a course of the waters sat down to the table d'hote in the hotel yesterday evening. The staff of the establishment numbered some 25 persons. I was somewhat fatigued after a long ex- cursion which I made during the day, and retired to bed bed about half•past ten. Suddenly in the early morn- ing I was aroused from my sleep by a terrific shock which seemed to shake the hotel to its foundation. I The walls of my room were partly destroyed, and the 'furniture was thrown all about the place. I rushed to the window,the glass of which was completely shattered, and saw a large volume of water rushing through the courtyard of the hotel with tremendous velocity, and sweeping down with it large blocks of stone, some of which were its big as cottages. The roar made by the ' flood, and the crashing of the rocks against each other, were indescribable. Three of the five wings of which the hotel was composed were consequently carried away with their contents, and furniture of every description was borne along in the waters. The fourth wing was partially destroyed. but that in which my room was situated escaped with comparatively little damage. In the midst of the confusion which followed the disaster the occupants did not know which way to turn for escape, as all the mear.s of exit were blocked. At length one of the visitors climbed down through the window on to the mountain side by means of a rope which was made out of the bed sheets. He then ascended in the semi-darkness to the viliage of St. Gervais up the wooded path which leads there from the eitablishment,when parties of rescue were immediately organised. It was some time, however, before they could reach the hotel, and even when they succeeded in doing so it was only by wading through water breast high. The hamlet of Le Fayet preents a derlorable aspect of desolation. On all sides are ruined houses. The bridge over the bon-Nant, by which coaches pass on the road to Chamounix, remains standing, but it is so damaged as to render it unsafe for vehicles to cross it, and the service of diligences is accordingly inter- rupted.

SALLANCIIIIS, WEDNE;,DAY.—It has now been ascer- tained that fully 140 persons perished in the disaster at St. Gervais by a fall of a portion of the Bionnassay glacier from Mont Blanc, and the bodies of upwards of ene-half that number have been recovered. They were all in a inost piteous condition, some of the victims having been decapitated, while many lost either arms or legs. The spectacle was the most distressing of any remembered in the whole district. Evidence on all hands showed that most of the victims were overwhelmed while asleep and swept down the rushing torrent, in which they were instantaneously drowned. Among the most tragical of fates, was that of a Dane who after escaping from the explogon which took place on board the steamer Mont Blanc' at Duchy, on Saturday, came on to St. Gervais, where he was one of the first victims of the disaster.

Arrangements are being made for the funerals, and in the meantime public subscriptions are being raised on behalf of the so fferers from the calamity. The latest theory as to the cause of the disaster is that a lake formed in the interior of the Bionnassay glacier, immediately above the village of Bionnay, and that the sudden eruption of the pent-up waters bronght about the catastrophe. The water at Bionnay reached a depth of 30 metres, or nearly 160 feet.
WARRINGTON GAS WORkS.

div.head: • REPORT OF THE GAS MANAGER.
div.p: • REPORT OF THE GAS MANAGER.

Mr. W. S. Haddock, manager of the Gas Works, has presented a report to the Gas Committee, in which he states:—" The gas manufacturing plant has been kept in a good state of repair. The largest quantity of gas made in 21 'hours at Longford was 667,000 cubic feet on January 15th, and at Mersey- St. 555,600 cubic fee:, on December 24th. The largest quantity made in one day was 1,140,000 cubic feet, on December 18th. The largest quantity sent out in one week was 7,253,500 cubic feet, for the week ending January 17th. The smallest quantity sent out in one week was 2,057,400 cubic feet, on July sth.. The increased make of gas is 15-i per cent, upon last year's production. This very large increased make is due, to some extent, to the severe weather in the early part of this year, as is shown by the largest output being three weeks later than the shortest day. To enable us to keep pace with the large increased output, it will be necessary to enlarge the works, which will cost not less than £6,000 for new purifiers, condensers, scrubbers, retort house, coal store, &c. The contracts for the gas- holder are let at about £14,000, and the work is in pro- gress, and we expect to have the holder completed early in 1893. The outlook for the coming year is very un- favourable. The price of coal may be slightly less, but cannel rather tends t 9 increase in price, and in several works experiments are being made to substitute the cannel with petroleum oil, it being a very powerful enricher. On the other hand, sulphate of ammonia is 120 per cent, lower than it was two years ago. lar is not worth more than about half of last year's prices. Coke is also lower, and spent lime is not selling at is. 6d. per ton. In other words, our expenditure increases, but our income decreases per ton of coal carbonized. In several towns it has been necessary to increase the price of gas to enable the gasworks to be carried on at a profit."
A MOTHER MURDERED BY HER SON.

A drunken man murdered his mother on Saturday afternoon, at Heyside, a village two miles north of Oldham. Patrick Gibbon, a labourer and ex-soldier, aged about 26, resided with his parents, at Water-st., Heyside. The father, mother,and son have been drink- ing together since the Oldham election, and frequent quarrels have ensued. These disagreements culminated on Saturday about three o'clock. During the tempor- ary absence of his father, the son seized a razor and cut his mother's throat, infhctiocr' a terrible wound, which extended from ear to ear. Death ensued almost im- mediately. The culprit went outside and invited the neighbours to see what he had done. It is said that all the three were drunk at the time. The murdered woman's name was Bridget Gibbons, and she was 62 years of age. Patrick Gibbons was committeed for trial at Oldham, on Monday, charged with Murdering his mother. It is alleged that he cut his mother's throat as she lay in bed asleep. Prisoner denied any knowledge of the tragedy.
. Mr. Cyrus Field, whose illness has been becoming daily worse for some time past, died on Tuesday.
THE GENERAL ELECTION. MORE LIBERAL SUCCESSES.
WEDNESDAYS' DECLARATIONS.

The poll declared on Wednesday afternoon con- siderably altered the political situation. The Liberals gained twelve more seats, and lost only one -a net gain of eleven. With the three seats which they were to the good in the morning they thus had a balance of fourteen seats in their favour, 'giving them a majority of 26. The change in majorities may be explained in this way: At the Dissolution the Government had a majority of 68. At the polls down to Wednesday afternoon, however, Mr. Gladstone had in all won 70 seats and lost 22. This gave him a net gain of 48. Of these, 34 sufficed, on being transferred from one side to the other, to wipe out the ministerial majority of 68, and left a balance of 14 gains, counting 28 on a division. At night another Liberal gain was announced, from Argyllshire, making the Liberal majority 30. Among the polls declared on Wednesday was that for Mid-Lothian, where Mr. Gladstone was re-elected, but by a diminished majority-690. At the last general election he was returned without opposition, and no comparison therefore can be instituted between 1886 and 1892. But in 1885 a poll was taken, and the right hon. gentleman's majority reached the large total of 4,631. This has now been reduced to 690. It will be found, we believe, that the Disestablishment question is largely responsible for the diminished sup- port which has been accorded to the Liberal leader at the polling booths. Turning now to other constituencies, we harve the satisfaction of announcing two more Liberal gains in Lancashire. Darweu (represented in the late Parliament oy Lord Cranborne, son of Lord Salisbury) and North Lonsdale have been captured-in the former ' case a Tory majority of 735 being converted into a Liberal majority of 214, and in the latter a Liberal majority of 284 taking the place of a Tory majority of 1800. The Colne Valley division of Yorkshire has been wrested from the Unionists, while in the Houghton-le-Spring • division of Durham a Teeny great Liberal victory has been won. W.; have also gained'a seat in each of the following constitnen- des :-The Gainsborough division of Lincolnshire, East Norfolk, East Essex, Radnorshire, the From division of Somersetshire, Dumbartonshire, South Ayrshire, aLd Roxburghshire. div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The annual meeting was held at the Cemetery office, on Wednesday. Present—The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. W. Littler, 11. Coleburn, S. Taylor, E. unison, W. Whittaker, and W. F. Salkeld (sec.). The proceedings commenced by a vote of thanks to Mr. Coleburn for his able conduct in the chair during the past year, Mr. Taylor moving, and Mr. Imison se- conding the proposition.—Mr. unison proposed, and Mr. Taylor seconded, that Dr. Gastaldi be the Chairman for the ensging year, both gentlemen speaking in compli- mentary terms of, the personal character and ability of the rev. gentleman. The motion .was unanimously carried, and Dr. Gastaldi took the chair, and said he would endeavour to fulfil the duties of the office to the satisfaction of the Board.—Mr. Thomas Handley was then appointed vice-chairman, on the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Coleburn.—The secretary sub- mitted his report, which showed that the interments for the three months ended June 25th, were 113 ; last year 149 ; decrease 36. The fees received during the same- period amounted to £ll5 103.8 d.; last year £l3l 125.6 d.; decrease £l6 is. On the recommendation of the Fin- ance Committee accounts amounting to £2O 10s. were passed for payment--The executors of Messrs. M. A. Smith, ef Whitley, offered to renew the mortgage of £750 at 31 per cent. The Committee instructed the secretary to see if he could not obtain 31 per cent. —A letter was read from Mr. John flindley,of 28. Union-st., wrote complaining of damage done to a tombstone in the Cemetery do Sunday last, and asking the Board to replace it.—The Secretary explained that the Cemetery officials with the assistance •of the police protected the property in the Cemetery as well as possible. After dis- cussion the Secretary was instructed to reply express- in,g regret for the'occurrence, and stating that the Board took all the care they could, and were not liable. The Board of CommisSioners applied for permission to place a seat in a recess in Victoria-road anti the privi- lege was granted OCI thopayment of an ackeowledgement of is. a year. _

div.p: ENO lIMOUS DEFALCATIONS.

It has been ascertained that the total defalcations in connection with the speculations of Lunt and Wilson, the Liverpool cotton brokers clerks, now in custody, amount to upwards of £190,000. About £llO,OOO of this is believed to have gone in cotton speculations, and about £BO,OOO on the Stock Exchange.

div.head: CHOLERA OUTBREAK IN FRANCE.
div.p: THE CHOLERA OUTBREAK IN FRANCE.

MADRID, TRURSDAY.—The report of the Commission of the Spanish doctors sent to Paris to report upon the nature of the epidemic in the suburbs of that city affirms the disease to be Asiatic cholera. Precautions to prevent the introduction of the epidemic will shortly be adopted by the Government along the Pyrenean frontier.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS'S SCHOOL CASE. ACTION FDE DAMAGES IN THE COUNTY COURT.
div.p: THE ST. BARNABAS'S SCHOOL CASE. ACTION FDE DAMAGES IN THE COUNTY COURT.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, 'before Mr. Wynne Ffoulkes. Judge, an action was brought by Miss Mary Eliza Parsons, formerly head mistress of St. Barnabas's National School, Warring- ton, and now mistress of the Weaver School, Bays Green, Winsford, Cheshire, brought an action against Robert Proud, Richard T. Smith, T. M. Pil- kington, and William Parr. as managers of St. Barnabas's school,claiming £5O damages for wrong- ful dismissal, on January 20th, 1890, from her office as head mistress of the school, or in the alternative, damages for being wrongfully obstructed by the defendants in the performance of her duties as schoolmistress and prevented by them from earning her salary. The plaintiff had also included the Rev. G. Allton, vicar of St. Barnabas's, as one of the defendants, but the action against him had been withdrawn. Mr. Henry Lynn, barrister, instructed by Messrs. Baker and Nairne, solicitor!, of London, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. John Tomlinson, solicitor, of Preston, appeared for the defendants, Mr. Unsworth, of the firm of Messrs. Jenkins and Unsworth, solicitors, Warrington, represented Mr.. Allton, in the proceedings. Mi. Lynn announced the withdrawal of the action against Mr. Allton, who, he said, although a manager of the school, took no part in the proceedings which were ground for the*action. Mr. Unsworth made application for coats on behalf of Mr. Allton, and this was acceded to.

Mr. LYNN said the circumstances were before his honour two years hp, the dispute being then as to whether certain persons had the right to act as managers of the school. The claim was for damages for loss of alary accruing to the plaintiff, through the action of the defendants, who had terminated her engage- ment by a months' notice, although she was entitled to at least three months' notice. When the notice expired, she, not recognising their right to I dismiss her, refused to accept their notice of dismissal. The defendants, accompanied by Mr. Tomlinson, solici- tor, proceeded to the school, and Mr. Tomlinson, though in the most gentle way, put his hand on her shoulder, and told her she must go. Miss Parsons then, of course, having other remedies left: The question of the technical assault had been already before the Liver- pool Assizes, and ultimately a verdict was entered for the assault against Mr. Tomlinson. An attempt was made to upset that verdict In the Appeal Court. but that court upheld it. Mr. Lynn.read a resolution of Septem- ber, 1887, according to which the plaintiff was appointed subject to three months' notice on either aide, and she was to have the fees of the school and half the grant earned at the end of each year, a copy of which was sent to her and returned with her acceptance of the terms endorsed thereon. She was ejected from the school on January 20th, 1890, and was out of employ- ment till September following, in consequence of which she claimed the damages. Mr. Lynn contended that Messrs. Proud and Pilkington were not managers of the school having never been duly qualified. He said the vicar and his son were appointed managers under the trust deed, and were appointed when no vacancy had I occurred in the committee of management. An entry appeared in the minutes of the meeting of the 23rd of May, 1891, "A. G. Allton retired. No business." A. G. Allton was the Vicar's son, and the entry merely meant that he had looked in and gone away because there was no business, though the defendants had acted as though it meant his resignation. Mr. Proud was elected treasurer, and at a subsequent meeting it was resolved that Mr. Proud be elected treasurer, and also a manager on receipt of Mr. A. G. Allton's resignation. There was no intimation of any resignation, and yet on the 11th of Oct., neither the Vicar nor his son being pre- sent, Mr. Proud was elected to the chair in the Vicar's absence, and on the motion of Mr. Smith, seconded by Mr. Proud, Mr. Pilkington was appointed a manager. Mr. Lynn contended there being no vacancy both ap- pointments were invalid, and Mr. Pilkington's was also so, through the motion for it being seconded by Mr. Proud who was not himself a manager. A considerable discussion took place on this and other points between His Honours Mr. Lynn, and Mr. Tomlin- son, and Mr. Lynn asserted that it formed no part of the actual decision of the Court of Appeal that Mr. Proud was I a manager, but was merely an °biter dictum on his part. Mr. Lynn read the decision of the Master of the Rolls in the appeal Court, and His Honour held that a statement there was a judgment to the effect that Mr. Proud was a duly qualified manager, and on Mr. Lynn, pointing out that the other judges present had not mentioned the point, replied that that might be, because they villtre satisfied with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. His Honour said that he was bound by this decision,and he considered that if Mr. Proud was a manager Mr. Pilkington was. Mr. Tommisos in his argument for the defence con- tended that the plaintiff had refused to obey orders of the managers and set them at defiance. She refused to attend any of the managers' meetings, and refused to pay into the bank school fees received, or to render accounts of the fees received for the month of Novem- ber, 1889, or of expenditure, and refused to produce to the committee of management schedules relating to the school grant, and she locked them oat of the school. Her conduct, he said,would have justified the committee in dismissing her without any notice. Miss PARSONS was sworn. She said she was ap- pointed head mistress of St. Barnabas's school in the year 1887. She corresponded with the Vicar while in the office. He was the correspondent of the schools.

The JUDGE here suggested Eo Mr. Lynn, who was ex- amining the plaintiff, that he should not raise any bye- points. There was, his Honour remarked, evidently a great deal of ill-feeling,and thee bye-points only tended to inflaming this.

Mr. LYNN: There is no suggestion that there is any ill-feeling on the part of the plaintiff. His HoNotra : I think there is from what I have heard on both sides. Examination continued : She received a month's notice on December 18th to leave. Sha did nOt accept it, and on the morning of January 20th, 1890, Mr. Smith, Mr. Proud, and Mr. Pilkington, with Mr. Tomlin- son, came to the school about a quarter to nine, and Mr. Tomlinson told her she was to go. She did net leave till he toucked her on the shoulder, and he then turned her out. She gave Mr. Tomlinson a letter of protest which she had ready. She did not get employment till September Ist, 1890. After she received the notice she went and saw Mr. Parr, and asked him if he had signed any papers for the master and mistress to leave, and he said he had not. She asked him if he had signed a notice of dismissal. He said' it was not a notice to go, but a fresh arrangement of the books. She had had no complaint as to the way in which she did her duty. By Mr. TOMLINSON : Something was said about Mr. Proud being appointed treasurer. She did not know he was a manager. She did not know it was her duty to attend managers' meetings, and mark the register. Had she known he was not a manager she would never have allowed him to come and look at the registers. The vicar told her not to recognise Mr. Proud as a manager. She did not know that she expressed the intention not to mind any notice issued by Messrs. Pilkington and Proud. She took no notice of Mr. Pilkington's written reqaest to her to put into the Manchester and Liverpool District Bank the moneys she received. She would have obeyed the order if it had been sent by a person she recognised as a manager. She might have ren lered an accpunt, but would not have gone against the agreement unless she had something else to work upon. She refused to render an account, because it was always in the summary at the end of the week. She did not know that it was ex- pressly provided in the code that before any fees were paid into the bank they.must go through the treasurer's hands. • Mr. LYNN : I know the code pretty w:11 by heart, and I don't know that. .

WITNESS, in further reply to Mr. Tomlinson, denied locking her door against the managers or being a party to or having knowledge of Mr. Woolacott, the head master, locking them out. In reply to the Judge as to whether she refused, when requested, on the day of her ejectment to give up the keys of the drawers containing , the registers, she said " I made no reply. I did not give ' them up."

By gr. TOMLINSON : I did not say I refused to recog- nise the authority of any of these managers except the vicar and his son. By the JUDGE: It was my duty to hand up my keys when required to the managers. We were persuaded by the Association of Teachers in London not to give up the keys in case they should be demanded. We put the case in their hands. By Mr. TOMLINSON : When she saw Mr. Parr about the notice she asked him to sign a paper to say that she was not dismissed, and he desired her to come to his house nekt day. She did not take the notice as one of dismissal. She was not told it was to enable her to make her peace with the persons who claimed to be acting as managers. She said, "There are no managers except Mr. Sunth." She said this because the Vicar had told her this.

By Mr. LYNN : she had always been receiving the fees and using them for herself. For part of her salary she had to wait a year. She had never been asked be- fore for them. The Rev. G. ALLTON was then called. Ile said he was an ex-officio manager of the schools. He built the schools, appointed the managers, and had been a manager ever since. He was appointed correspondent of the schools by the managers. He acted as such till the defendants forced themselves into the schools, and Messrs. Proud and Pilkington took upon themselves the position of managers.. Since then he had ceased to visit the schools, or have anythiug to do with them. Witness gave the explanation as to the entry respecting the retirement of Mr. A. G. Allton which had already been given by Mr. Lynn. He had told Miss Parsons that Messrs. Proud and Pilkington had never to his recollection, been elected. He did not agree with her that she was not to obey orders. She acted entirely on her own responsibility. Mr. TonixaNsoN submitted that he had ne case to answer. The plaintiff herself admitted disobedience to
orders of persons whom His Honour held to be legally constituted managers. She professed to have acted on the advice of the vicar, but the vicar denied the truth of this.

The JUDGE said he felt sorry for the plain- tiff, because he thought she had been led into error by the advice of others. He should have been more sorry if she had given her evidence a little more ingenuously, but he dared say she felt aggrieved, and that was some reason why she was not quite so satisfactory in her answers as she might have been. She certainly did not take the notice as a. notice of dismissal, and the notice was very peculiarly worded and did not read like a notice of dismissal. It did not speak of terminating her engagement, but made use of a curious expression, " existing arrangements."' Therefore he did not think he could hold that notice to be a notice of dismissal. Whatever the plaintiff did she did honestly enough. She thought she was acting upon her rights because she had been so advised, hut it might have been wiser, whatever advice was given to her, to have at least assented to what three managers • required her to do. and to hav,e let it be considered in a proper place whether they were really managers or not. He considered that in refusing to pay the lees- into the bank she was right. Her agreement stipulated that she was to have these, therefore what right had the managers to call upon her to do this ? The account had been rendered by the weekly summary and by that all the managers could see how they were disposed of: With , regard to the locking of the doors,her evidente was very unsatisfactory. He could come to no other conclusion ' ' than she knew perfectly well that the doors were to be*, locked by Mr. Woollacott. She said "WA" laid our ' case before the association, and the locking of the doors was done by advice she was willing to carry out. He was inclined to think she was a party to this act. In answer to his question as to whether she refused the keys she did not say she refused but replied" I did not give them up." That was a piece of special pleading and quibbling unworthy of an educated woman in her posi- tion. His Honour nonsuited the plaintiff, with cjits fondle defendants.

NOTES ON GA.MES AND ATHLETICS. - CYCLING. Sixteen inembers of the Warrington Cycling Club left their native heath at noon on Walking day for a tour in North Wales, the party including a lady rider. Chester was reached in good time, and, after a slight halt, the. wheelers left for Wrexham, where an excellent tea greatly refreshed the party. Llangollen was reached about next morning. A number of the party visited Bala Lake, going via Corwen, the splendid scenery of this part of the country being greatly enjoyed. Tha party returned to Llangollen in the evening, and a jolly time was spent.

The party here divided, one section runninl' Llandudno, and the ride through llettwys-cood wiil be remembered for a long time, the hedges being covered with wild roses and honeysuckle. Conway Bridge and ' Castle were passed just before sunset, Llandudno being reached about seven o'clock. The party returned home by boat to Liverpool on Monday, . reaching. Warrington about eleven o'clock, all looking better for the outing.

The other portion of the members returned home from Llangollen by way of Chester, several taking the oppor- tunity. the latter place offers of a row, and going no the .Dee. Whilst enjoying the pleasure of this healthy exerciee a boat containino• some ladle's was oh;erved aground. The gallant cyclists went to the assistance of the fair ones with that expedition which characterises the Warrington youth, but one eager cyclist, in pulling off the boat fell into the river, whence he emerged at wetter and a wiser man.
Is.low that Mr. Battersby's 1892 Patent Loco Cycle is creating such a sensation, it is Interesting to learn that . . .

the iden"tical invention was protected by W. C. Berton, of Warrington, in August, 1899. Later in the year he superseded the invention by similar connecting rod mechanism, which patent mechanism gives greater leaverage, &c , and wilt be introduced by the Burton Cycle Co., on a long base safety, in a few months • al- though at the same time Mr. Burton considers his chain- less anti-friction gearing far superior to all ether systems. Strange to say, the superseded mechanism mentioned above, has also been patented this year by , an expert, but the manufacture was stopped by the Burton Cycle Co., giving notice of the infringement. -- Speaking of the Burton chainless safety, it may be mentioned that J. G. B. Johnson, of Scunthorpe (a. stranger to7Cheshire roads), in a trial of one of these. machines (71), geared), on Monday night, rode froM Chester to Stretford,. a distance of 38 miles, in 2 hours 15 minutes. lie faced a strong wind, and was unpaced 15 miles, the pace-making being done by indifferent riders, and he rode within record time to Altrincham wherehis pace-makers failed him. Mr. Johnson will, we believe,within a few days make an attempt to break the the record between Chester and Manchester. which is at present held by Wisemantof Manchester. . CRICKET. The representative cricketers of Scotland made an- other very poor show against Surrey, and another one innings defeat was the result. It is evident that Scot- . .

tish cricket is not quite first-class just yet, whatevrT it may become eventually. The highest scorer among the Scotchrnen was FT. J. Stevenson, the well-known Inter- national full back at Rugby football.

• Middlesex are sending a pretty warm team north this week end to play Lancashire and Yorkshire, and with. such batsmen as Stoddart, Scott, Webbe; O'Brien, Jar- dine, and M‘Gregot in [IA eleven, they should want a lot of getting out.

Frank Sugg does not vary much when he makes his mind to score a century, and on the three occasions on which he has so distinguished himself during the present season his contributions have been 105, 106, and 107. They are vet useful to a aide, and would corne. in handy against Kent or Middlesex this week. ATHLETICS.

Athletics are as a rule says the" Athletic News," are very particular as to their appearance when engaged in competing at sports, but now and again a rough dia- mond is discovered whose views of cleanliness are of the prehistoric order—or any time before soap and towels were used. An illustration of this kind was afforded the other day at some sports in the North of England, where one of the competitors was observed to be carry- ing a liberal quantity of real estate on his legs. It was at first presumed to be black socks, but a closer survey revealed the truth. The man won his heat, but one of the officials called the runner's attention to the " good , old annual "state of his legs, and told him to go and get them washed before he turned out again. The sprinter looked at his limbs, and to the amazement of the official replied, " What's use o' weashin' um. They'll he a.s black again in another week." Evidently that man had tried the experiment once before. We believe he is now waiting for the trip to Blackpool.

It is said that James Southworth, the crack sprinter of the Blackburn Rovers, will retire from the amateur running path at the end of the present season. He in- tends to sign the professional foottmll form, and will nO &Mk be seen occasionally operating AI full baek for the Rovers. He is not the same class of football player as his brother John is, but he is a useful exponent of the game, and is served by his great speed.

FOOTBALL. With regard to the new Lancashire Rugby La ague,ma only are the eight clubs selected full of enthusiasm over the scheme, but many of the junior organisations are watching the proceedings with interest,. Already a pro- posal is on foot to form a second body, and amongst others mentioned as being the pick of a likely lot are Manchester Rangers, Widnes,Leighjyldesley, Walkden, St. Helens, Blackley, Pendleton, Mossley, Rochdale St. Clement's, and two other clubs. If this body was formed, a.nd Manchester, the two Liverpool clubs, and Rochdale Hornets were drafted iuto No, 1 League in time for season 1893-4, the Rugby game in Lancashire would be something like the genuine article.

BALL CLUB. . The annual general meeting of the members of this club was held in the Co-Operative Hall, on Thursday, when there was a fair attendance. Mr. W. Mullins presided, and in opening the meeting said they had not had such a prosperous season as they hat! hoped. The gate receipts were greater than the previous season. but the expenses were heavier. The Secretary (Mr. J. Waddington), in. submitting the balance sheet, said they, all knew what sort of a season the elbla had had; and the composition of the team. It however finished well in the Liverpool league with 13 points, but there was only one other club below them. They were in an unenviable position, but at any rate the clubs yvhich were in front, had only got one or two points more than their club. They had really only won two matches before last January, owing to the fact that they had only a poor team. Their prospects for the coming season were much brighter, because they had got some of the old team to sign for the coming season. The statement of accounts showed receipts- E 73 124. 7d., including a balance of 63. 31. from last wear, and the expe4uiture was £B9 17s. 9d., leaving a deficit of £l6 53. 31. The balance sheet was adopted on the motion of Mr. J. Lewis. The election of officers resulted as follows : President Dr. Patterson, secretary, Mr. J. Waddington, treasurer, Mr. W. Mullins, auditor, Mr. R. Reade. Com- mittee: Messrs. Edwards, Wyatt, Moss, R. Appleton, Dowker, Hamblett, Lewis, Tyrer and Dearden.

HONOUR TO WHOM HONOUR Is DuE.—The manufac- turers of the celebrated Sunlight Soap have just been honoured by a Special Royal Warrant of Appointment, as Soap Makers to the Queen, which is the highest honour that any manufacturer can hope to gain. It IS also worthy of mention that such has been the unpar- alleled increase in the sales of Sunlight Soap that the firm have given instructions to their architect to more than double the size of their works, already the largest of their kind in existence.
