ANECDOTES OF ACTORS.

A stupid fellow once charged Sheridan with inconsistency, when the wit replied that the accusation reminded him of the reasoning of the entertainer of a convivial party, who hearing his friend observe that it was time to take leave, as the watchman was crying past three, observed: "Why you don't mind that fellow, do you? He changes his story every half-hour." Sheridan evidently meaet it to be understood by this Blue- tration that any seeming change in his opinions or statements were only such as were demanded by the change in the times. A drama was presented to Sheridan in which the characters amounted to no less than fifty-six. "What's this," said Sheridan. "the new army. list 1" "Nothing of the kind, sir," answered the introducer; "it is on an Irish story, and by an Irishman." Sheridan glanced over a few leaves, and saw that it was altogether inadmissible. " Tell toy countryman," said he, "that as a drama there "an be no hope of its success; partly owing to the d uced population of London. But it might turn to a history of the rebellion, and the list at the 'tinning would do for the muster of the levy es 2.4,4.55 e." Suett, the famous coraedian, being one evening at his usual quarters,. 4rery conceited young man volunteered a song, which he sung very ill. Upon his asking Suett how he liked it, " Why, sir," said Suett, "your song is like the small-pox." "How's that?" "A good thing when it's over." The person immediately got up in a rage and made an appeal to the company, but an appeal against such an antagonist was a dangerous proceeding; every part of his remonstrance was turned into ridicule by the witty address and eccentric manner of Suett, who concluded a triumphant reply amidst roars of laughter with these words— " Swans sing before they die; 'twere no had thing Should certain persons die before they sing."

At the theatre, one evening behind the scenes, Suett observed a performer put something under his cloak ; he asked him what he had got there, at the same time putting his hand under the garment. "Oh, only my dagger," said the player. Suett drew out a small bottle, and having ascertained that it contained his favourite beverage, drank the contents and returned him the bottle with these words—" There's the sheath." • "The candles you sold me last were very bad," said Suett to a tallow chandler. "Indeed, sir? I am sorry for that." "Yes, sir; did you know they burnt to the middle and would then burn no longer?" "Good Heavens 1 you surprise me. What, sir; did they go out ? ' " No, sir—no; they burnt shorter."

One day Joe Hams, the comedian, was arrested by two bailiffs for a debt of £2O, just as the Bishop of Ely was riding by in his carriage. Quoth Joe to the bailiffs :—"Gentlemen, here is my cousin, the Bishop of Ely;. let me but speak a word to him, and he will pay the debt and costs." The Bishop ordered his car- riage to stop, whilst Joe, close to his ear, whis- pered—" My Lord, here are a couple of poor waverers who have such terrible scruples of con- science that I fear they will hang themselves." "Very well," replied the Bishop. So calling to the bailiffs, he said, "You two men come to me to-morrow, and I will satisfy you." The bailiff's bowed and went their way. Joe (tickled in the midriff, and hugging himself with his device) went his way too. In the morning the two bailiffs re- paired to the bishop's house. "Well, my good men," said his reverence, "what are your scruples of conscience ? " "Scruples!" replied the bailiffs; "we have no scruples. We are bailiffs, my lord, who yesterday arrested your cousin, Joe hams, for twenty pounds. Your lordship promised to satisfy us to-day, and we hope you will be as good as your word. The bishop, to prevent any further scandal to his name, immediately paid the debt and costs.

div.head: ENLISTING A LAWYER,
div.p: ENLISTING A LAWYER,

An old reuruiting-sergeant tells the following "It was on the 11th of May, 1829, I 'listed a a recruit in Dublin, and put the question to him, as is usual, and gave him the shilling, and walked him to the barracks as fine as a fiddle. Well, in a few days lie was claimed as a 'prentice, and so he was had up before the Mayor, and he committed him for trial. At the following 'sizes I was called as a witness, and the lawyer that defended him told me that I did not 'list him, 'I did,' says I. 'Did you put the question to him rightly?' says he. I did,' says I. •By the virtue of your oath, now,' said he; just ask me the questions, for I don't believe you asked him.' 'Row do you know t' say for by this and by that you weren't by." Nona' of your business,' says he ; and he held out his band; and accordingly I pulled out a shilling and clapped it in his fist, and then I asked him the questions, and he said 'Yes 'to them all. Were those the same questions you put to the prisoner?' says he. 'Yes, they were,' says I. Well, here's yer shilling back for you, says he. 'I can't take it, sir,' says I. Why not?' says he. 'Why?' says I. Why, shure, I can't take it back till ye go before the Magistrates and pay the smart money' (which every recruit must pay if he wants to be released from service). You be hanged says he, and he put the money in his pocket ; and I called to his lordship on the bench for a witness that I had listed him; and, oh, but there was a .roar in the Court! Begorra, the Judge laughed till the tears ran down his face. Well, the decision ,of the Court being in my favour, I axed the Judge If I might take away my new recruit, and they all roared again, and the counsellor got as red as a turkey-cock and nearly marl. At last he made the best he could of it, and says I to the counsellor, Bays I, 'Don't 'list in the Line next time, sir.' What, then,' says he, snappishly. Oh, yer 'oner,' says I, stick to the rifles—that's more in your way.' Well, begorra, when I told the Major, I thought he'd die; and when he'd done lauein% he bid me keep the smart ineney' for myself.

THE following glimpse of an old lady's phar. Macopceia in the middle of last century is got from a letter of Mrs. Delany's, written in January, 1758 " Does Mary cough in the night? Two or three snails boiled in her barley-water or tea- water, or whatever she drinks, might be of great service to her ; taken in time they have done wonderful cures. She must know nothing of it. They give no manner of taste. It would be best nobody should know it but yourself, and I should imagine six or eight boiled in a quart of water and strained off and put in a bottle would be a good way, adding a spoonful or two of that to every liquid she takes. They must be fresh done every two or three days, otherwisethey grow too thick. ' A TivE,E with only ten feet of timber in it may 'nave quite done growing, while another of five times the contents may be putting on a great bulk of Wood every season. A "ripe'' tree has always a " stodgy" appearance, especially about the topmost branches, among which small leafless twigs will begin to show themselves. If the work of selecting trees for felling be left to subordinates, the biggest, not the ripest, trees will generally be chosen. But this involves very serious loss ; for the larger a tree is the more wood it will put on every year, lilt Is still " growing"; and, since an oak is usually not timber at all until it is twenty-five or thirty years old, ovary additional year's growth, up to fifty to sixty years of its age, ought to be reckoned as containing two years of its entire increase. A GREAT MANDARIN of tho palaces a distinguished physician, discovered the secret of making a very fine paste with the bark of several trees and old silk stuffs, by boiling them in water. He made with this iste different kinds of papers. To-day the chi—which is the name givento paper in China— is manufactured with divers materials. They make it of hemp, of mulberry bark, with that of the cotton tree and several other trees, particularly the bamboo ; of rice and wheat straw, and, lastly, of the little skin which is found in the cocoon of silk- worms. THE highest use of a friend is his friendship, and In some•respects a friendly bock is the very best of friends. Speech is silver, silence is golden. A book is a bi-metallic friend; it will give you either silver speech or golden silence, as you prefer. IT is not sufficient not to intend to do wrong; we must intend to do right, and carry out our intentions also. Not to think is in such cases a crime.

WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.

The 25th annual festival in connection with Widnes Athletic Club was commenced last evening week, and continued on Saturday evening, in the Sports Field at Farnworth. The Committee were not favoured with the best of luck, as the weather' was showery on Fridaievening, and on Saturday afternoon there was a steady downpour for several hours. Notwithstanding this drawback, there was a large attendance of spectators on each occasion, it being computed that there were 3,000 in the enclosure on the concluding day. The candidates for the division, Mr. Deacon and Mr. Gallia were both on the field in the course of the afternoon. The Committee had spent a portion of last year's profit in improving the course, and the improve- ment was gratefully acknowledged by the numerous competitors. The total number of entries was 340, a figure which is about 30 less than last year, the flat races accoonting for the decrease. There was an in- crease of entries in the bicycle events. The prizes were of the usual value and excellency, amongst them being a silver goblet presented by Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., the President, for competition in the quarter mile flat race confined to the district Mcssrs. Elkington' of Liverpool, who had supplied the various articles, had also presented a handsome pair of Benares vases, and covers. A number of crack runners and bicycle riders competed in several of the events, and there were a number of very close and exciting finishes, as the record below will show. A Widhesian in the person of A. E. Barlow, who ran under the An- field Bicycle Club colours, won the two miles bicycle race in splendid styla,and he came in for an ovation. Another popular victory was that of G. Wright in the mile handi- cap, the runncrs displaying pluck and endurance of a high order. ' The general arrangements of the sports were of the most complete and admirable character, and the officials whose names follow are to be congratulated thereon':—Judges : Messrs. T. W. Grace, Manchester , (N.C.A.A.), C. E. Barlow, and Major Wareing. Clerks of the Course: Messrs. Arthur Carey, I Carr, J. Edgar Dennis, Guy W. Gossage, W. H. Longton, H. Auer,Geo. E. Sayce,and H. S. Timmis. Field Finance Committee: Messrs. W. S. Callander, T. C. Haddock, and J. P. Fraser. Handicapper, official timekeeper, and Referee: Walter Platt. Starter :J. Wilkinson. Hon. Secretary : Arthur F. Brundritt. Secretary: James Walter Davies.

I FIRST DAY. 150 Yards Flat Race Handicap.-Winners of heats: J. S. Craig, Widnes F.C., scratch ; H. Webster, Warrington F.C., yard ; H. Green, Warrington 7 yards; E. Osborne. Warrington Y.M.C.A., 5 yards ; J. Massey, Warrington H., 3 yards. Final heat : 1, Osborne ; 2, Webster 3, Green. A good race, Osborne winning by a yard. Few inches separated second and third. Time, 122-5 secs. Two Miles.Blcycle Handicap.-First hee, : 1, A. E. Barlow, Anfield, B.C. scratch ;2, D. Dagleish, Widnes C.C., 175 yards- 3, Sherratt, Widnes C.C., 160 yards. Second heat : 1, W. Leatherbarrow; Warring- ton Ct., 130 yards; 2, J. S. M'Lean, St. Helens Y.M.C.A., 175 yards ; 3, T. Bate, St. tlelens C.C., 160 yards. Third heat: 1, J. Buxton, Warrington C.C., 140 yards ; 2, W. R. Toft, Anfield 8.C., 140 yards; 3, M. Bailey, St. Helens 8.C., 100 yards. Deciding heat: 1, Barlow ;2, Leatherbarrow ;3, Toft. A most exciting race. For the last three laps'Leatherbarrow led Barlow, Toft, and Buxton ; and for three quarters of the last lap the four riders were abreast. Twenty yards from home Barlow put on a spurt, and won a grand race by t wo feet, amidst loud applause ; a foot separated second and third, Buxton being close up. Time, 6 mins. 14 secs. Quarter-mile Flat Race Handicap.-1, J. Clarke, Wid- nes, syards ; 2, J. a. Craig, Widnes F.C., scratch • 3, E. Davies, Widnes, F.C., 10 yards. The winner took the !cad early on, and held it tbroughout, eventually winn- ing in rather easy fashion. Time, 534-S secs. One Mile Flat Race Handicap.-1, G. Wright ;2, J. Barlow ;3, J. Peel. Wright won easily, while three yds. divided second and third. The above were all confined to the district. THE SECOND DAY. 120 Yards Flat Handicap.-There were eleven prelimi- nary heats and two trial heats. The winners of the preliminaries were :-W. Rawsthorne,St. James's,Liver- pool F.C., 10-lvds.; J. A. Gould, Newport, syds. ; S. R. Huson, South London H, nyds. ; D. M. Little. Liver- pool H, lOyds. ;S. H. Williams, Crewe A.A.C. 9fyds. ; H. M. Warner, Salford H, siyds. ; G. Osborne, Waning- ton Y.M.C.A., 104yds. ; C. A. Bradley,Huddersfield A.C., scratch ; G. H. McDougall, Stanley P.C., lavds. ; T. Freeman, Salford Harriers, 77ds ; H. Stephens, Liver- pool Police AC., nyds. First final heat: 1, E. H. Williams; 2, S. R. Huson ; 3, A. J. Gould. Second trial heat: 1, C. A. Bradley ; 2, G. H. McDougall; 3, G. Osborne. Final :1, Bradley.; 2, 13uson ;3, Osborne. Won on the post after a good race; six inches between second and third. Time a yard outside 12 seconds. One Mile Bicycle Handicap.-This race was run in four heats. The first heat resulted as follows :-1, E. Blakey, Southport, 165 yds • 2, W. Leatherbarrow, Warrington, 150 yds.; 3, W. f.owe, Rainhill, 145 yds.; Second heat: 1, G. F. Kelson, Waterloo, 160 yds. ; 2, J. O'Neil, Oxford, 170 yds.; 3, A. E. Barlow, An-field, 85 vds. Third heat :1, I. Lyon, Liverpool, 95 yds. ; 2. H. Humphreys, Carlton, 155 yds. ; 3; F. Parry, North Liver- pool, 145 yds. Final: 1, E. Blakey.; 2, A. E. Barlow; 3, W. Leatherbarrow. The winner led almost throughout, and a grand attempt to overhaul him by Barlow failed, but he would have succeeded had there been much further to travel. Won by two yards, same distance between second and third. Time: 2 minutes 53 seconds. :Scratch.-In this event only three ran and they finished : -1, W. J. Holmes, Barrow; 2, J. Kibble- hite, Essex Beagles ;3, G. H. Morris, Salford. H. Morris made the pace until about 300 yards from home, when he was passed by Holmes and Kibblewhite, the former winning by ten yards, Morris being 20 yards be- hind Kibblewhite. Time : 2 minutes, 8: seconds. 100 Yards Scratch.-1, C. A. Bradley, Huddersfield ; 2, S. R. Huson, London; 3, A. J. Gould, Newport. Only the three placed ran. Bradley won by a yard and a half. Gould walked in. Time lot seconds. One Milo Handicap.-1, G. Wright, Widnes, 95 yards ; 2, G. Jennison, Blackburn, 125 yards ; 3. E. Wilkinson, Barrow, 120 yards. Jennison led at a good pace, and was leading by 20 yards when the last lap was entered upon. Wright, who was running with great gameness, put on a grand spurt and overhauled the leader in grand style, winning a capital race by three yards. The third man was eight yards away. The winner was loudly cheered for his splendid performance. Time 4 min. 23 4-5. One Mile Scratch-Three started, 1, J. Kibblewhite, Essex Beagles ; 2, G. H. Morris, Salford ; 3, F. Dickson, Widnes. Kibblewhite mode all the running and won with the utmost ease by 30 yards, Dicksontwho merely ran to secure third prize, was lapped. Time 4 min., 47 sec. _ _

120 Yards Hurdle Ilandicap.-1, A. J. Gould,Newport, owes 15 yards; 2, C. Robertson, Wirrall H. & H., owes 2 yards; 3,M. Sullivan, Seaforth, owes 3 yards. Gould, who won very easily, was greatly superior to his oppon- ents in taking the hurdle. He also won the heat, his chief competitor, Huson, having a spill. Time 19sec. Three miles Bicycle Handicap.-1, Isaac Lyon, Liver- pool, 35 yards; 2, A. N. Deakin, Anfield 8.C., scratch ; 3, W. Leatherbarrow, Warrington, 165 yards. Ten ran. Lyon went to the front two laps from home, closely pursued by Deakin, who was defeated by half a card ; a foot between secomA and third. Time 9min. sq. Half Mile Handicap.-1, W. F. Daniels, West Cheshire, 53 yards ; 2, E. Wilkinson, Barrow, 55 yards ; 3, W. J. Holmes, Barrow, scratch. A hundred and fifty yards from home, Daniels took the lead, and although Holmes came with a tremendous rush at the finish, he could not reach the leader. Five yards, a foot. Fahey ; six employes at Widnes Alkali Works, captain, George Williams; six employes at Sullivan's works, captain, M. Duffy ; six employes at Gaskell Deacon's Works, captain, Z. White ; six employes of Messrs. T. Bolton and Sons, captain, J. Campbell; six employes of Messrs. T. Bolton and Sons, captain, S. ' Mosley ; six employes of Widnes Alkali Works, captain, N. Seabury ; six employes at Sullivan's Works, captain, W. Houghton ; six employes of the Liverpool Silver and Copper Works, captain, F. Collins; six employes of Mr. Hardman, Plasterer, captain, J. W. Hardman ; six employes of Messrs. Gossage and Sons, captain, T. Hughes. The final lay between Widnes Alkali and Messrs. T. Bolton and Sons and the former team won. At the close of the sports Mr. A. F. Brundrit distri- buted the prizes.

div.p: LetttrO to the Obitor.

THE BOROUGII SURVEYOR AND ALTRINCHADI ELECTION. Sir,—lt cannot be said that the Warrington public have any immediate concern in the election for Altrinchatn Division, but there is a phase of the recent one held there in which, I venture to think, ratepayers of this borough will be inclined to manifest some little interest. I understand that Mr. Longdin, surveyor to the Corpor- poration, has absolutely been acting in the capacity of a paid official on the occasion of the polling in a part of Altrincham Division. It seems to me that a public offi- cial in the pay of the ratepayers of Warrington ought hardly to be devoting a day of the time for which they pay him, in order to swell an income which is certainly not to Ise considered inadequate. His contribution of his services as presiding offizer is, moreover, doing an Injustice to others to whom circumstances are such that a day's employment is of much more consequence to them than to the Warrington Borough Surveyor. If there is no restriction in these matters, it seems to me there ought to be.—Yours truly,
ARGUS.

div.head: MR. JOS. CHAMBERLAIN ON .LORD SALIS-
div.p: MR. JOS. CHAMBERLAIN ON .LORD SALIS-
BURY. "See what a desperate homicide this Salisbury is."— Shakespere. "lila characteristic inacceracy."—Chamberlain.

Sir,—Seeing that Mr. Chamberlain is now hand and glove with the Conservative party, it is a matter of some interest to know what is really his opinion of the indiscreet and truculent Tory chieftain, Lord Salisbury. The following is taken from a speech made at Birming- ham, in March, 1883:—" Lord Salisbury is the same to- day as ever he was, and his rhetorical manifesto is only a concession—a mere literary concession—to the exigen- cies of the hour. By the very circumstances of his birth, education, and social status, he is precluded from exhi- biting any genuine sympathy for either the peasan- try of Ireland or the labouring-classes of England." Again :—" Lord Salisbury has always expressed his scorn for remedial legislation." Further:—" Lord Salisbury cares nothing for the bulk of, the Irish nation. He has no sympathy—at least he expresses none—for the great mass of the population, whether of the Loyal Ulster or of the other provinces of Ireland,who have been subjected to undeniable tyranny and oppression, and whose wrongs cry aloud for redress. He can express to you in eloquent terms his sympathy for the Irish land- lords who have had to submit to a reduction of twenty- five per cent, in their rents, but I find nowhere any expression of syrnpatlly for poor tenants who, for years under the threat of eviction and the pressure of starva- tion, have paid those unjust rents levied on their own improvements and extorted horn their desperate toil and hopeless poverty. I say that in this matter as in so many other, Lord Salisbury constitutes himself the spokesman of the class—of the class to which he him- self belongs who toil not neither do they spin, whose fortunes, as in his case, have originated in grants made long ago for such services as courtiers render kings." How is it Mr. Chamberlain does not say these things now ? Has Lord Salisbury changed, or is it Mr. Cham- berlain who has gone over to him P—Yours, LOOKER-ON.

div.head: DR. HOUSTON THANKS THE PRESS. Willington Hall, Tarporley. July 9, 1892.
div.p: DR. HOUSTON THANKS THE PRESS. Willington Hall, Tarporley. July 9, 1892.
Dear Sir,

I am penitently conscious of a grave omission that I made when speaking at the Liberal Club on Tuesday night. I should have expressed, in more definite terms than I did, my sense of the obligations under which I lay to the Liberal press in Warrington, for the splendid work they did for the cause and the candidate ever since I was selected to contest the seat. Their reports were admirable, their articles were able, their political intelli- gence was excellent, and, what is perhaps most important of all, their tone was lofty and dignified, worthy of a great occasion such as the momentous struggle in which we were engaged. All this I ought to have expressed in my speeches at the Club, but, in the excitement natural at such a moment, forgot to do so. You will perhaps allow rue to take this opportunity of saying through your columns one thing that I should like to impress upon my supporters, namely, that the Liberal party in Warrington have no cause whatever to despond. No ground has been lost. In the direction of political education much ground has been gained. The elector- ate has been stirred to its centre. Never was a finer feeling of loyalty to principle aroused. On the other hand, the forces ,making against us will grow weaker day by day. The strange spell which the "yellow coach" still casts over the minds of misguided men will pass away. They will soon awaken to the absurdity and folly of continuing to worship this Fetish—a worship that is making them ridiculous in the eyes of Lancashire, and of the very Tories who are taking advantage of it, while they are laughing in their sleeves at their poor dupes. With this influence, let us hope, will pass away to,-) the evil, the drunkenness, the degra- dation, and the misery, that are inseparably associated with Greenallism. The working-men will cease to lie down and let the Juggernaut of Beer roll over and crush them. Then perhaps the late revolting alliance between the Church and the Intemperance party that has shocked the piety of Warrington, and almost driven to despair those who are working to redeem its people from des- truction, will be dissolved. But if the Church will persist in the vain attempt to serve God and Mammon, on their own heads be it. I remain,

div.head: Yourg faithfully, ARTHUR HOUSTON.
div.p: Yourg faithfully, ARTHUR HOUSTON.
THE SHIP CANAL.

MORE MONEY REQUIRED. "A VERY SERIOUS OUTLOOK." On Wednesday afternoon, in the Manchester City Council, in reply to Mr. Gunson, who asked when the promised report on the Ship Canal affairs would be pre- sented to the Council, Sir John Harwood said he thought the question was quite reasonable. He did not think when he promised the report that there would be any difficulty in obtaining the necessary statistics from the engineers. He saw the engineer the previous day, and . he also sent a letter to the Mayor stating that he and his colleagues were waiting for these statistics. Meanwhile, the Council might be interested to learn that they had let four of the contracts. That, at all events, was a good thing to say, and he could assure the Council the work would be done more economically than would have been the case under the old dispensation. (Hear, hear.) Up to the present they had not been able to come to any salsfactory agreement with regard to the work beyond Runcorn to Weaver Pool, and there was a possibility of their having to do the work themselves. The dredging of parts of the canal had turned out most troublesome and expensive work, and there was no probability—not the slightest hope—that the canal could be finished before January, 1894. Another thing which ought to be stated was that they would require more money beyond the £3,000,000 sanctioned by the Corporation. He did not think the.sum required would be a very great deal ; it certainly would not be the large amount which some persons seemed to expect. They had £822,000 worth of first and second debentures not sold, and next year they would have some £390,000 in the bank which could not be used for the construction of the canal. But the whole matter—the question of the dredging of the canal, the difficulties at Weaver Pool, and the other financial questions—were such as made it impossible for them to make any further claim to the Council without they had the statistics asked for before them. For instance, there were several arbitrations going on, and they aid not know what to put down for them. Although, it was a very serious outlook for them he thought they would be able to meet it calmly ; that they would be able to deal with it, and that by and by their work, which seemed at one time almost impossible, would be accomplished. (Hear hear.) The discustion then terminated.

div.head: – it* ,
div.p: - it* ,
WINMARLEIGH HOUSE.

ployed workpeople in the cotton manufacturing dis- tricts, and during the whole period of that calamity he served on the central committee at Manchester. pie last few years of his lordship's life were spent in retire- ment in Winmarleigh, though, notwithstanding his ad- vanced age, he not unfrequently took a prominent part in gatherings of a public character. Of his two sons, one died young and unmarried ; the elder died also during his father's lifetime, leaving an only son. Lord Winmarleigh was then himself past the conventional term of threescore years and ten. and it was a striking instance of the irony of fate that he should live to see his grandson come of age, and then that the young heir should die within a twelvemonth after. There is now no heir either to the title or (in the male line) to the estates. The Pattens of B nk Hell— en ancient family, of which, according to the authorities William of Waynflete, the founder of Magdalen College, was a member—have been settled at Warrington for over 250 years, but the main branch ceases in the male line with the death of him who was perhaps its most dis- tinguished representative. The deceased peer had three daughters, one of whom is still living and resident at Winmarleigh. The others were marriad—one to Mr: 'l'. H. Lyon, of Appleton Hall, and the other to the Rev. Robert Rolleston, some time curate of Warrington, and both died within a year of their marriage. WINMARLEIGH HOUSE AND MANOR.

Winmarleigh, from which the deceased nobleman took his title, is the name of a sequestered township in the Fylde country of North Lancashire, situate two or three miles westward of the great high-road from Preston and the country to the south of Lancaster and the north. It contains a population of some three hundred souls, domi- ciled in about fifty dwellings, farmhouses and cottages for the most part. The occupation of the inhabitants is husbandry or agriculture. About 20 years ago,there was no building or natural or artificial feature in the township which the most observant of travellers through the district would have turned aside to see. At last the place was retrieved from its age-long obscurity and insignificance by becoming the home of a proprietor who had attained a national reputation as a politician, as well as a social eminence as the promoter of many movements for the public welfare, and the name of Wi nmarleigh was brought into familiar usage in the Imperial Parliament and the highest circles, royal and aristocratic, as part of the titular designation of a nobleman whom all England knew and respected. The name is one which has under- gone many variations from its original orthography. It is spelt at least twenty different ways, from " Winmer- lee)," in the reign of Henry 111. (AD. 12d); and " W vn- merles," a century later (1.343); to" Winmerle " in 1476; " Wilmerlegh," in 1500 ; ‘Vyromersley," in 1561 ; " Winmerley," in 1868 ; and" Winmarley " and" Win- , marleigh," in the present century. _ . - • •

, . - Although the recorded history of a rural township like this is almost nil, yet there are interesting relics of prehistoric times in the neighbourhood, some of which have been deposited for exhibition in the Warrington Museum, and others are preserved by Lord Winmarleigh out of whose land they were dug up. i

Of the earliest owners of the manor estate of Winmar- leigh mentioned in ancient documents, it may be re- marked that they bore the township name as their surname ; and that when they passed away, a daughter and heiress of the last of them, Roger de Wynmarleigh, married Henry de Plesington, lord of Plesington, near Blackburn, and their daughter and heiress, Isabella de Plesington, became the wife of Richard de Radcliffe, who with her had the manor of Winmarleigh with other estates. The hadcliffes first appear as lords of Win- marleigh in the second half of the 14th century ; and they continued in a male succession to hold the manor during about 200 years, until the reign of Queen Eliza- beth in the latter part of the 16th century. Sir Gilbert Gerard, Kt.' some time Attorney-General an d master of the Rolls, held Winmarleigh in right of his wife, Anne Ratcliffe. Sir Gilbert Gerard died in 1592 ; and the estate passed to his son and heir, Sir Thomas Gerard, created in 1603, Baron Gerard of Gerards, Bromley. Winmarleigh afterwards became the inheritance of Elizabeth Gerard, daughter of Dutton. Lord Gerard ; she married the Hon. Wm. Spencer, of Ashton Hall, near Lancaster, and bore issue Wm. Spencer, whose daughter, Elizabeth, became wife of Robert Hesketh, Esq of Rufford, and the only child of this marriage, Elizabeth Hesketh, married in 1714, Sir Edward Stanley, afterwards eleventh Earl of Derby. It was in order to raise money to pay Lady Derby's por- tion, says the historian of Garstang parish, (Mr. Fish- wick) that the Spencer family sold, in 1763, the Win- marleigh manor estate to Thomas Patten, Esq., of Bank Hall, Warrington, by deed dated 18th and 19th March, 1744. Thus the Pattens have owned Winmar- leigh nearly 150 years. Winmarleigh Hall, the old manor house, long the domicile of the Ratcliffes, having ceased to be the resi- dence of the lords of the manor after the death of Wm. Ratcliffe, Esq., in 1560, had fallen into neglect and decay. No doubt it was used for a farmhouse until, being dilapidated, it was demolished in the latter end of last century, and upon its site another house was built, which is the farmhouse of the home farm formed under the direction of Lord Winmarleigh himself. The situa- tion of this structure and the site of the Old Hall is a few hundred yards away from the modern mansion close by the entrance to the grounds from the public road. The farmhouse, has, of course, no historic interest, but there is an ancient yew tree in the orchard near the house which may have been planted by a former lord of Winmarleigh who dwelt in the manor-house. The land of the hall farm includes some of the best on the estate. Respecting one field, there is a tradition that in a certain year when corn was at its highest price, probably in the war-time eight year:, ago, the crop of wheat grown upon it yielded when sold a sum equal to the estimated value of the fee simple of the land. With regard to Winmarleigh House, the following architectural description will be read with interest. The front presents a good architectural aspect emboldened by projecting bays on two stories, having large win- dows. mullioned and transomed, and terminating in a handsome parapet of Gothic stonework at the east end of the frontage, and in a gabled upper story at the west end. The style is domestic Elizabethan, and the mate- rials used externally are red bricks and fine freestone. The stonework is enriched by sculptured heraldic shields and other appropriate devices. The other block, of considerable length, extends from the back of the prin- cipal building. Its salient feature is the main entrance to the house, underneath a fine porch, having two Tudor-arched doorways, above which the walls are decorated with moulding and carved panels, and finished with arcaded parapets, flanked by turreted buttresses. Behind the porch, covering the entrance hall, rises a square tower ot three stories, its front pieced with win- dows, the larger one on the first floor mullioned and transomed. The tower has bold pillared parapets, and a root of high-pitched pyramidal form, in the centre of which a weather vane is fixed. The tower is flanked by corbelled chimneys, and dominates the other structures from any point of view. Large and handsomely-designed chimneys rise from the gables and roof-ridges, as shown in the engraving ; and, together with several gabled buildings of different elevations, the tower, roof, gables, Am., impart that picturesqueness of sky-line which con- stitutes the peculiar beauty of Gothic architecture in its uses, whether for ecclesiastic, civic, or domestic edifices. Mr. Paley, of Lancaster, was the architect of Winmar- leigh House, and It is a work which does credit to its designer. It is not ambitious in scale, elaborate in plan, or overplied with ornamentation in detail, but it is a

beautiful country house worthy of its patrician owner. Respecting the interior, we can but say that the library, drawing-room, and other chief apartments are spacious, lit by fine Tudor windows deeply embayed and elegantly appointed. The library contains the subscription portrait of Lord Winmar- leigh in his military uniform as colonel of the 3rd Royal Lancashire Militia—a portrait which belongs to the 'regiment—ana numerous other portraits old and by modern artists. It contains also a very beautiful piece of sculpture, a female head and bust in marble, repre- senting " Adoration " executed by a sculptof whom Lord Winmarleigh met wlth as a youth studying in the War- rington School of Art and encouraged to develope his artistic gift. The situation of Winmarleigh House has been judiciously chosen. The ground naturally undu- lates slightly, and the soil is a rich loam, with porous subsoil, upon a deep bed of gravel. The grounds were laid out by Mr. Thomas, the celebrated landscape gardener. The gardens, shrubberies, and surrounding plantations have been planned in the most effective manner. The kitchen gardens and conservatories are ample. From the garden walks at the front of the house? the prospect to the eastward, where the plain is bounded by the lofty and shapely fells of Bleasdale, is exceedingly impressive. The estate fairly well timbered, affords a pleasing foreground and middle distance. We should have Mentioned that the house was built in the year 1871; that, at least, is the date cut in stone upon the porch, with the initials of the builder and master—" J. W. P." (John Wilson-Patten).

Patten " I know you as the member for . Mr. boy in Warrington and have carried many parcels to Bank Hall. It appears that Mr. — left Warring- ton when young to make his fortune, and started to walk to Liverpool. When part of the way there he be- came tired and his heart was just failing him, when a gentleman drove by and offered him a "lift " which he accepted. This gentleman is now dead but he recol- lected and corroborated this before his death. Arrived in Liverpool Mr. --got a. situation in a shop, and out of his first savings, bought an elephant's tusk, which he cut up and sold in small pieces at a great profit. He pro- ceeded to buy another and another until at last he was able to buy a small cargo, and eventually to purchase shares of ships. On looking round for some investment for his money an opportunity presented itself of buy- ing some land in the vicinity of Liverpool, and shortly after this became bnilding land, and brought him an immense fortune. In short all his speculations pros- ' Dered, and he became a Member of Parliament, and died ' a Baronet.

div.head: DEATH OF LORD WIMMARLEIGH.
div.p: DEATH OF LORD WIMMARLEIGH.

The news of the death of Lord Winmarleigh was received nowhere with more regret than in War- rington, with which town he and his family had been for so long a time intimately connected. his lordship, who had reached the advanced age of 90 years, had been in feeble health almost during the 1 whole of the present year,and more than once within ! recent months his demise was almost hourly expected His life was, indeed, probably only prolonged by the careful medical attention be received and the assiduous and devoted nursing of his two daughters. As soon as the news was made known in Warring- ton all the usual tokens of public mourning were displayed. The nags at the Town Hall, at the Liberal and Conservative Clubs, and the Cricket Ground and other public and private places were exhibited half-mast high. Reference was also %bade to the event at the Police Court, and in the evening the United Brass Band, instead of playing in the Park its intended programme of dance music, sub- stituted for it one of sacred music. In fact, Warringtonians in general recognised the death as a public loss. The family to which Lord Winmarleigh belonged ia mentioned, it is said, among those who came over to England with William the Conqueror. Mr. John Wilson- Patten, afterwards created Lord Winmarleigh, was the ' eldest son of the late Thomas Wilson-Patten, M.P., of Bank Hall, Warrington. Ile was born on the 26th of April,lBo2, and was educated at Eton, and at Magada- len College, Oxford. Among the offices that he filled I were those of A.D.C. to H.M., Vice-Lieutenant of Lan- cashire, and honorary colonel to the 3rd Lancashire Militia. He was also Chairman of Committees of the whole House in 1852-3, was Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster in 1866-8 ; and was Chief Secretary for Ire- land in 1868. He was created Baron Winmarleigh, of Winmarleigh, county of Lancaster, in 1874. Winmar- leigh, it may here be mentioned, is a sequestered town- ship in the Fylde county of North Lancashire, and it is situated near Preston. For a long series of years the Wilsen-Patten family were closely connected by residence with Warrington and the neighbourhood, the late Lord Winmarleigh, then Colonel Wilson-Patien, only remov- ing from Bank Hall, Warrington, to the mansion at Win- marleigh, some 14 or 15 years ago. At that time ther- was a pretty general feeling in favour of a town hall and park being procured for Warrington, and Colonel Wilson-Patten intimated to the Corporation that he would be prepared to make some personal and pecuni- ary sacrifice if he could thereby secure to his fellow- townsmen the possession of Bank Hall and gardens as a town hall and park. Steps to secure that end were at once taken by the Town Council, with the result that Warrington became possessed of its present town hall and well-laid out grounds. Towards the cost that was of necessity incurred the late Mr. George Crosfteld gave the sum of £9,500 and Colonel Wilson-Patten gave £3,000. The father of the late Lord Winmarleigh was a man of note in Lancashire. He was Mr. Thomas Wilson- Patten, M.P., and was born in February, 1770. Mr. Thomas Wilson-Patten in 1800 married the eldest daugh- ter. of-Mr. Nathaniel Hyde,of Ardwick,and of the marri- age there were issue two children—one son and one daughter. The son was the late Lord Winmarleigh. His father died in December, 1827,at the age of 57, and his son and heir was then about 25 years of age. Oa leav- ing Oxford he spent three years in visiting foreign coun- tries, and it was immediately after returning from his travels that he entered into possession of his inheritance. On the 15th of April, 1828, he was married to his cousin, Anna Maria Patten. fourth daughter and co-heiress of Mr. Peter Patten Bold, of Bold, Lancashire. Lord Winmarleigh commenced his parliamentary career in the old unreformed House of Commons in the year 1830, when he was elected one of the representa- tives for the County Palatine of Lancaster, which was I then undivided. His lordship entered Parliament as a Conservative, but on the introduction of the first Reform Bill he voted for its second reading. Feeling unable, however, to pledge himself definitely to all its details, he was obliged, in 1831, to yield to the strong expression of public feeling in favour of "the Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing but the Bill," and retired. His absence from Parliament was brief. In 1832, the county of Lancaster having been divided by the Reform Act, Mr. Wilson- Patten was invited to stand for the northern division, together with the late Earl of Derby, then Lord Stanley, and was returned unopposed. From this date he sat as member for North Lancashire uninterruptedly in the Parliaments elected in 1832, 1835,1837, 1841, 1847, 1852, 1857, 1859, and 1865 ; that is to say, in nine sur,cessive Parliaments, extending over a period of 33 years. On the division of North Lancashire into two parts by the Reform Act of 1867, which came into effect before the election of 1868, Colonel Wilson-Patten decided to stand again for the northern division, was elected, and sat in the House of Commons until his ele- vation to the Upper House in 1874. Lord Winmarleigh !during the Parliament which followed the general elec- tion of 1832, was a supporter of of the late Sir Robert Peel. When that great statesman resolved to repeal the Corn Laws in 1848 Mr. Wilson-Patten gave invaluable help, and as a consequence, at the general election of 1847, he last the support of some influential men of his party in the county. He was, notwithstanding, re- elected, with Mr. James Heywood, a Liberal free trader, for his colleague. Mr. Wilson-Patten took a leading part in the promotion of all measures affecting the commerce and the manufactures of the country, and of Lancashire in particular. He also seconded th,e motion for the abolition of the truck system, which for many years had caused ,a;reat discontent amongst the labouring classes. He supported a Bill for the closing of public- houses during a portion of Sunday, which, however, was defeated subsequently in consequence of a reaction ,on the public mind. In 1866, Mr. Wilson-Patten was appointed Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and was created a member of her Majesty's Privy Council. In 1868 Mr. Disraeli appointed him Chief Secretary for Ireland, with a seat in the Cabinet, and in 1874 he was raised to the peerage. Long and eminent as were the services of. Lord Win- marleigh to the country generally, and 'to*Lancashire in' particular, in both Houses ,ef Parliament, they did not exceed the duties of citizenship honourably and ably dis- charged by his lordship. During a period of 60 years he served in various ranks of the military service. For 50 years he was in the 3rd Royal Lancashire Regiment, during which time he was 30 years in the position of . colonel-commanding and 13 in that of honorary colonel. In 1855 he accompanied the regiment to Gibraltar, dur- ing the Crimean War, and on his return his services were favourably mentioned by her Majesty's Govern- ment in both /louses of Parliament, and her Majesty was pleased to appoint him one of her aides-de-camps. In Lancashire Lord Winmarleigh was conspicuous as a promoter of important improvements in agriculture,and the county and local agricultural societies found in him a Liberal and zealous patron. On the occurence of what is known as the cotton famine in 1862-65 his lordship showed his hearty and practical sympathy with the suffering operatives by presiding Over the first public meeting to raise subseriptiens for the relief of the unem-'

div.head: LORD WINNIA.RLEIGH AND WARRINGTON.
div.p: LORD WINNIA.RLEIGH AND WARRINGTON.

During his long residence at Bank Park, Lord Win- marleigh naturally took a prominent part in the public affairs of Warrington. For many years he acted as governor of the Grammar School, and at times on the annual" speech day" he distributed the prizes to the successful stuants. Tie was also at one time president of the old Mechanics' Institute, his connection with that institution dating so far back as 1348. He was one of the principal promoters of the Waterworks Co., and was chairman of that company during nearly the whole of its existence. He assisted in the formation of Warrington Savings Bank,and presided at its first annual meeting. He was an ardent churchman, and several of his most notable benefactions went in aid of the church. He gave sites for St. Anne's Church, and for Holy Trinity and St. Paul's Heath Side Infant Schools. Quite ' recently he gave £2,000 towards the endowment of a separate district for the Bank Quay part of Holy Trinity parish, and added £l,OOO to the building fund of the proposed new churc'n in Liverpool-road. He also promised £l,OOO towards the cost of the projected, now schools in connection with the Parish Church to be built in Manchester-road. Lord Winmarleigh was also a warm supporter of the volunteer movement, and gave liberal help to the local corps. Owing to the growth of manufactures in Warrington and the construction a the Cheshire Lines railway,Bank House became a much less suitable residence for a nobleman of Lord Winmarleigh's position than it formerly was ; and it was in consequeace of this that he left Warrington in the autumn of 1872 for his new hall at Winmarleigh. The occasion was taken advantage of by the Corporation to,acquire Bank House and grounds as a Town Hall and Park. Towards the purchase money the late Mr. George Crosfield contributed no less a sum than £9,500, and out of the £22,000 which was paid him Lord. winnearlaigh also contributed £3,000. After the completion of the bargain, both Lord Winmarleigh and Mr. Crosfield were entertained to a banquet by the Cor- poration, and as a permanent commemoration of their generosity, the marble busts of these two gentlemen were set up in a place of honour in the vestibule of the Town Hall, where they may still be seen. In his speech at the banquet held on the occasion of the opening of the Park in June, 1873, the deceased (then Colonel Wilson-Patten, M.P.) said he could not pretend for a moment that whit be had done with regard to the pur- chase of the park and gardens was to be compared to the munificient gift of his friend Mr. George Crosfield. He did not deny that for years past it had been a great object with him to obtain for Warrington what was new secured, namely, the benefit of a park and recreation ground, He had been in consultation with Alderman Holmes for years as to the best mode of accomplishing that object, and if honour was due to anyone it was due to Alderman Holmes. A park and recreation ground had become a desirable acquisition to every town, and to every place in which there was a large number Of inhabitants; but in their great Lancashire towns those advantages had become almost a necessity for the welfare of the working-classes of the town, and they should be properly looked after. There had been a want of the means of common recreation to those en- gaged in factories and workshops, and other vocations during the greater part of the week, and it was not to be wondered at if in the absence of these advantages, the moral and physical condition of the town had not been so satisfactory as many of them wished it had been.

div.head: INCIDENTS AND ANECDOTES.
div.p: INCIDENTS AND ANECDOTES.

-- --- The death of Lord ‘Vinnaarleigh has naturally given occasion for the repetition of a number of incidents and anecdotes relating to his career. A local tradesman tells the following story relating to the deceased, who, at the time to which it refers, was a young man. Mr. Patten was particularly fond of boating on the Mersey, and on one occasion, accompanied by a friend, he went down to the river side, having previously given instruc- tions to a youth in his service to clean the boat and put in the cushions. Mr. Patten, however, had donned a boating costume for the occasion, and was net recog- nised by his servant. He called to the lad to bring the boat, which was moored in the middle of the river, to the side, so that he and his companion might get into it. "I sharn't," was the reply. A moment or two after- wards, this time in a more peremptory tone, Mr. Patten again requested the lad to come to him but still he re- fused. The lad was evidently indignant. and this time, instead of using the words "I sharn't," he said—" I, will see thee at first. I shall bring it to no- one till Jack Patten comes." The surprise of the recently- deceased lord may be better imagined than described. He took the refusal in good part,however,and presented his " faithful servant" with half-a-crown for refusing to surrender the boat to one whom he believed to be S. stranger. The lad was equally surprised when he dis- covered that it was Mr. Patten to whom he had spoken so disrespectfully. Another amusing story is related of him. Miny years later, shortly after the then Colonel Wilson-Patten had carried his Bill through the house of C3RIMOrIS for the earlier closing of public-houses, he was in Preston in command of the 3rd Lancashire Militia. He had occa- sion to call at one of the hotels, it is said, to make an, inquiry from one of the officers who was staying there. It was Sunday eveniog.aand the house had just been closed for the day. The colonel demanded tt be admitted, but the laudlord refused to.allow him to enter the house, whereupon the colonel (under the impression his identity was unknown to the worthy host)exclaimed ;:oßusuet.! amintsitieeacdo,lohnoelw, eavnedr,insolfst puropodnuccionmg ing into thethedesired effect the landlord remarked " Certainly not ' • Mr. Pat- ten must abide by his own Bill." div.head: 'REFERENCES AT THE POLICE COURT.
div.p: 'REFERENCES AT THE POLICE COURT.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, the Mayor (Alderman Greenell) at the close of the usual business, said he was sorry that he had to refer to the death of Lord Winmarleigh at 8 o'clock that morning. Most of them knew the gentleman, and would be sorry to lose him. He had been agood friend to the town, and the inhabitants. He was afraid such men as he were all dying out. He only heard just now from Mr. White of his lordship's death. He was sure Alder- man Harrison would join him in regretting the occur- rence.—Alderman Harrison, who sat on the Bench with the Mayor, said he regretted most sincerely the death of Lord Winrnarleigh. It was a very great loss indeed. He was a well known figure in Warrington. In every sense of the word, he was a most estimable man. No man stood higher in his sovereign's regard, than Lord Winmarleigh.—Chief Constable Hunt : When we saw Lord Winmarleigh we saw a nobleman.—Alderman Harrison: That we did, one of nature's noblemen—a nobleman independent of his position as a peer.—Mr. Hunt : I remember when I came here I thought he looked like those I had been accustomed to see in the town I came from.—Alderman Harrison : He was noble in every sense of the word.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

On Thursday the remains of Lord Winmarleigh were interred in the family vault at Warrington Patish Church. In the morning the coffin was conveyed from Winmarleigh Hall to Sc ,rton the nearest station, and was followed by the Winmarleigh tenants of the deceased nobleman. It was thence brought by train to Warring- ton Bank 14uay Station,which was reached shortly after two o'clock. At Warrington the funeral partook of a public nature, there being in the procession the Mayor and nearly all the members of the Town Council. a large deputation from the Conservative Club, and numerous leading townsmen. Amongst the mourners present were the Hon. Ellinor Wilson-Patten, the Marquis and Mar- chioness of Headford, Miss Evelyn Wilson-Patten, the Hon. Captain Osbert Lumley, Lord Cross, Mr. W. H. Cross, M.P., Sir Charles de Hoghton, &c. There was an impressive and solemn funeral service at Warrington Parish Church, and it was witnessed by a crowded con- gregation. . •

The Mayor has received the following message from the Hon. Elfluor and Elizabeth Wilson-Patten : " Please accept and convey to the inhabitants of 'Warrington our deep appreciation of the respect and warm feeling shown by all classes towards our dear father, yesterday."

A case of attempted murder, followed by suicide, is reported from Silvertown, East London, yesterday afternoon. It appears that Mr. Christian Grey, son of a managing director, of the Silvertown Telegraph Works, war met in Winclsester-St., yesterday by a discharged servant of the company named Reed,who lived in Twy- rord-st. The man attacked and stabbed him in the Ciroat, afterwards committing suicide by cutting I his own throat. Mr. Grey's wound has been stitched up, and is not considered dangerous.

div.head: NET LIBERAL GAIN
div.p: NET LIBERAL GAIN
LIBERAL MAJORITY

There was a marked decrease in the amount of excite- ment prevalent in political circles yesterday, the final result being regarded as now settled, while it is not believed that the polls to come have many surprises in store. Forty contests took place on Thursday, and in seven of them the results were declared on Thursday night. Of the 83 results yesterday, 21 are in English counties, including the Leigh division of Lancashire, and the Eddisbury division of Cheshire, both of which remain unchanged, the former returning a Liberal Riad the latter a Conservative ; Mr. Tomkinson has the satis- faction of slightly reducing the Conservative majority. The poll was a heavy one on both sides. One of the earliest results declared yesterday was in North Dorset, where the Conservatives captured a seat which was strongly Liberal in 1885, and which returned a Liberal ' by a majority of 255 in 1886. The return of Mr. Arch in West Norfolk, ousting Lord Henry Cavendish Bentinck, gave a gain to the Liberals, thus balancing the day's results. In North Meath Mr. Michael Davitt defeats the late Parnellite member, Mr. P. Mahoney, and thus enters Parliament in support of the Nationalist party. Another notable result of Thurs- day's polling is the seating of Sir Charles Dilke for the Forest of Dean by a majority of nearly two to one.

The declaration on Thursday of the results of polls taken on Wednesday brought up the net Liberal gains to 54. The Government majority of 68 in the late House of Commons disappeared on Monday, and the Liberals were placed in a majority. Later polls show a long list of Liberal gains, and Mr. Gladstone's majority, counting each net gain as equal to two votes on a divi- sion, is now as above.

EDDISBURY ELECTION.

On Thursday the polling in the Eddisbury Division of Cheshire took place at twenty-five polling stations. The candidates were Mr. James Tomkins)n, of Willingtcpa Hall, Tarporley, who unsuccessfully contested the diva-, ion in the Liberal interest in 1886, and Mr. H. J. Tollemache, of Dorfold Hall, Nantwich, the old Conservative member. The campaign has apparently been conducted between both parties with good feeling. Since 1886 nearly 600 voters have been added to the register. As Mr. Tomkinson was defeated by 669 in that year, the Conservative appeared confident of success. On the other band, the Liberals averred that during the past six years the agricultural labourer had been educated On political questions and that Liberalism had undoubtly been progressive. Large numbers of vehicles are engaged in conveying votes to the poll. The electors number about 10,200, and the poll was expected to be a very heavy one, as many of the labourers would be influenced to vote upon questions dealing with land. The result of the poll was declared on Friday as fol- lows H. J. Tollemache (C) James Tomkinson (L) Majority 1885—Tollernache, 4,285; Irwell (L), 4,164. 1886—Tollemache, 4,357; Tomkinson, 3,678.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON DIVISION. GENTLEMEN,— Having again been elected as your representative, I desire to tender my most sincere thanks to those who have given me their support. I desire to especially express my gratitude to those numer- ous and devoted workers both Conservative and Liberal Unionist, whose exertions have contributed so greatly to the increased success of the Unionist cause in this division. While again thanking you for the honour conferred upon me, I may add that I shall always endeavour to support such legislation as may conduce to the general welfare of the con- stituency. I am, Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, T. W. LEGIT. Newton-le-Willows, 12th July, 1892.

KNUTSFORD DIVISION ELECTION, 1892. GENTLEMEN,— I beg to tender my sincere thanks to those 2,792 Electors who polled in my favour on Monday. 11th July. From the flrst. I recognised that the task before me was a heavy one, and that the influences which can be btought to bear against the cause of Liberalism in Cheshire are many and varied. In the face of these influences I am most grateful to those who preferred political freedom to private advantage, and kept their pledges to me. I also return my thanks to those who struggled so manfully and worked so hard on my behalf, many of whom I hope 1 shall have an opportunity of thank- ing in person. Those, however, whom I may not be fortunate enough to see, will. I trust, accept this intimation of my gratitude, and preserve as pleasant rectllections of the con- test as I do myself. I remain, Gentlemen. Yours truly, A. M. LATHAM. 1, Temple Gardens, London, E.C.

PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTH WICH DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. G ENWEstEN. , It is nigh upon twenty years since I settled among you, and during thoseyears I have served you in every public office to which you could elect me. There is no community in all England than can show a nobler record of work done during those years for the well- being of all the dwellers within its borders. Northwich, Runcorn, Winsford, and Middlewich, in taxing themselves uncle.. the Public Libraries Acts, have given to their people free access to the thoughts of the noblest minds of all time; in adoptitg the Technical Instruction Act they have gi-en to the young an opportunity, eagerly embraced by large and Increasing numbers, of training for hand and eye and mind, fitting them for fuller, brighter, happier lives. Verily this is a community a man may be proud to represent. With all this work I have sympathised, and to the fullest extent of my powers have joined, with all my heart. As I have worked and voted hitherto, I pledge myself to work and vote hereafter, if again you do me the hononr to return me to Westminster. As President of the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council I fully endorse the platform it has adopted, every point in which has nay heartiest approval. Five years ago I asked for your suffrages as a supp rter of Mr. Gladstone, and after a contest, during which the argu- ments for and against Home Rule were presented to you with a clearness and fnlness rarely, if ever, equalled, you elected me by a majority as emphatic as it was decisive. To-day the same issue is before you, and my attitude towards it is unchanged. Once more I come before you as a devoted adherent of the statesman who, in the sixtieth year of his public service—a service as unprecedented in its term as in the noble quality of itsachievements—is now and for the last time appealing to his fellow.countrym en for their approval and support. At such a time I may well be pardoned if, omitting any state- ment of my own. I refer you to his address to the Electors of Midlothian, and say that it is the dearest wish of my heart to be permitted to aid in the work of 'carrying to a successful issue the reforms therein set forth, so fraught with happi- ness to millions of our fellow-men. Finally. I would ask every man in the Northwich Division to remenaber on the Polling Day that a vote given for me is a last vote for sir. Gladstone—a last opportunity of rewarding for a life's serviicte the man who has laboured so long, so stead- fastly,and so successfully for the people's good. I remain, Gentlemen Your faithful servant, JOHN TOMLINSON I3RUNNER. Winnington Old Hall, Northsvich, 35th June, 1892.

The sulphur is burnt and passes into the air as sulph- uroqs acid, some of it as sulphuric acid. Taking it as sulphurous, the amount would be 72,216 tons, or if; bv further oxidation it is converted into sulphuric acid it must reach 110,580 tons, an enormous amount to be sent into the air in the course of a year The area covered is about three square miles, so that there is sulphur at the rate of 12,036 tons per mile as against eleven tons in London. This comparison may explain the great difference to be observed between the condition of the trees in London and those in the mann- facting towns of the North. It explains, too, the wide extent over which the injury to vegetation is perceived. In the concluding paragraph of Mr. Fletcher's report he says that the inspection of the Irish works will devolve on Mr. Ballard, who is now relieved of a portion of his work in Lancashire by the duties undertaken by Dr. Affleck in Widnes. In Dr. Affleck's report for Widnes, there is the following passage: "No new chemical works, outside the Act, have been started during the year, tut a new copper smelting works is at present being erected in Widnes, by Messrs.
